This study examines the fluctuations of a specific angle, known as $\Psi_n$, and its associated magnitude, known as $v_n$, which indicate particle distribution patterns and movement velocities within the fragments produced by heavy-ion collisions. Researchers at the Large Hadron Collider's ALICE facility evaluated these fluctuations for the collision of heavy nuclei at an energy level of 13 TeV by analyzing data from the ALICE experiment. Analysis of the resulting data was performed on a variety of heavy-ion collision outcomes, each produced by creating either proton-proton or heavy-ion collisions, and comparing them to predicted theoretical models. The observed data fluctuations align with predictions made by Monte Carlo simulation software, but also exhibit distinct patterns of fluctuations for specific angles and velocities, particularly for the most evenly distributed particles, known as midrapidity, and within the fragments produced by the collisions, known as charged particle midcentral. The ALICE experiment's findings also revealed a positive correlation between fluctuations in the angle and magnitude, known as the correlation ratio, which was observed across a range of heavy-ion collision outcomes. The results from the ALICE experiment also compared with previous findings from the same research group using the same methodology but at a lower energy level of 2.76 TeV. The energy-dependent patterns of fluctuations observed at the lower energy level did not hold true at the higher energy level of 13 TeV. The ALICE experiment's current findings align with predictions made by Monte Carlo simulation software referred to as JAM but exhibit a greater level of fluctuations in the angle and magnitude than those observed in the heavier-ion collisions produced by the Monte Carlo simulation software referred to as AMPT, which exhibit level of fluctuations similar to those observed in the proton-proton collisions produced by the same software. The observed data fluctuations also exhibit distinct patterns across different collision outcomes, known as central and peripheral collisions, which show distinct patterns of fluctuations for specific angles and velocities, particularly for the most evenly distributed particles, known as midrapidity, and within the fragments produced by the collisions, known as charged particle midcentral. The ALICE experiment's findings also compared with predicted theoretical models, which show that the observed fluctuations are influenced by the way the particles interact with each other, known as collective effects, and the way the particles are produced, known as thermal effects. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. Finally, we present an experimental scenario demonstrating the capabilities of our approach. This research is an extension of our previous study entitle "Handling Inconsistencies in Tables with Missing Values and Functional Dependencies" published at EDBT'22. Unlike the original work, this extension includes an improved algorithm for computing the truth status of data tuples, known as FourVal, which offers a significant performance improvement (up to 100x) than its counterpart, TwoVal, presented in the original work. The FourVal algorithm was initially designed to address query validation and related problems, and not proposed as a general-purpose data repair approach. Additionally, the research issued a challenge to develop a data repair approach that achieves a better performance than TwoVal and FourVal algorithms combined, which remains unresolved at the time of submission but has been addressed since then. The FourVal algorithm is an instance of a broader class of algorithms called Join-Order-Optimised Algorithms (JOAs), which was unaware at the time of submission but has been confirmed since then to be a distinct category of algorithms from the one identified in the paper that compared 12 algorithms for computing data tuples' truth status at TBMS workshop in 2019. The research was supported by the following grants: NSF IIS-2034386, NSF IIS-2133777, and NSF CCF-2039134. The data and code for this research are available at https://github.com/zhonghuajiayuanbigdata/P4VC. The experiment environment used for this research is available at https://github.com/zhonghuaji

Object manipulation tasks require a deep understanding of scene transformations and object symmetries. Neural Descriptor Fields (NDF) achieve compelling representations of objects by utilizing Neural Descriptor functions, but do so without considering the full SE(3) symmetry of 3D geometry. In order to refine these representations, we introduce Neural Descriptor Symmetry Networks (NDSNet) that learn the exact Neural Descriptor functions for both a target object and its transformed counterpart. This allows for the precise computation of the difference between these two representations, effectively capturing the underlying symmetry of 3D geometry. When applied to a variety of tasks, NDSNet demonstrates improved performance compared to models without symmetry learning. When integrated into Neural Descriptor Fields, our framework yields a more sophisticated model called NDF-SE, which achieves state-of-the-art results on both the ModelNet40 classification and ShapeNet segmentation datasets. Furthermore, NDF-SE is capable of accurately reconstructing transformed 3D objects from partial point clouds, setting a new benchmark for the task. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhongyuri/NDSNet.

We found that the precision of aerosol depth measurements is significantly higher when using the latter method. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two groups based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping and correspondence learning. We integrate the projection grouping technique from the training data into a neural network, forcing the network to predict correspondence for projected points on the 3D object shape. Additionally, we introduce a novel loss function, Projection Consistency Loss (PCL), which learns correspondence from 2D-to-3D point projections. PCL learns the correspondence between projected points and the 3D object points, thereby obtaining intermediate cues and correspondence for the pipeline's second stage. We further enhance correspondence accuracy by projecting the 3D object points for a given image through the neural network and compare our approach with current state-of-the-art methods for benchmark datasets. Our contributions are straightforward to incorporate into existing two-stage pipelines. The proposed PCL loss can be applied to any two-stage pipeline that employs virtual control points or uses the coordinate class network as the backbone. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/leehoseini/6dR-PCL.

Numerous numerical methods for biomolecular models rely on configurational averaging, a technique that simplifies the interaction with solvent. The accuracy of this averaging can vary greatly depending on the application and location within a protein. The Stokes operator, a key component in solving the equation for the velocity of a solvent, is crucial in assessing the validity of this averaging. The study compares the accuracy of three numerical approaches – finite volume, finite element, and pseudospectral methods – in simulating the Stokes operator on a model protein surface. The results indicate that the finite element method yields the most accurate results in a average sense, while the finite volume method performs better in the average sense with respect to special tensor product basis. The study also highlights the challenges in directly solving the Stokes problem on a complex biomolecular surface, and presents a preconditioning strategy that combines an efficient solver for a simplified problem with the Littman-Clark preconditioner, demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach. The research was motivated by the needs of an explicit molecular simulation method known as the multiple domain dynamical method. The Stokes operator simulations were conducted using realistic models of a protein and ubiquitin, and the results were compared to the output of an implicit simulation, and the differences were found to be negligible. The most efficient code for solving the Stokes equation was made available as part of the Gromacs simulation package, following the same licensing terms. The code was tested on high performance computing systems, and achieved efficient execution, and the precomputing step could be distributed among 100 processors. The research was conducted at the University of California in San Francisco, and the University of California in Berkeley, and was supported by grants from the National Science Foundation and the National Institutes of Health, and computational resources were provided by the National Science Foundation and the University of California in Berkeley. Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by applying it to real-world datasets, including a collaboration network and a financial transaction network. These examples showcase the benefits of considering inter-layer relationships on centrality values and highlight the algorithm's efficiency. Our approach provides a versatile solution with practical implications for evaluating influence or credibility in complex, multi-faceted social structures. Furthermore, our approach can be viewed as a generalisation of existing methods for calculating eigenvector centrality in single-layer networks. Our approach has the potential to be expanded to other applications of eigenvector centrality, such as community detection and network ranking. Our code is available online for public use. This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require reexamination for intermediate-speed impacts. High-speed impact research relies on high-speed cameras, whereas low-speed impacts employ high-speed cameras alongside underwater visualization via high-speed lighting. Underwater observation during the pinch-off time reveals a surface seal pattern characterized by a central hole and six distinct ridges, with ridges' height inversely related to the speed of the incoming sphere. Furthermore, a notable dent ("indentation") forms on the water's surface below the point of impact, with a depth also inversely related to the speed of the incoming sphere. A prior model proposing the pinch-off time be directly proportional to the viscosity of water and the square of the diameter of the sphere, while being inversely proportional to the atmospheric pressure and the difference in pressures below and above the water's surface, requires adjustment. The need for adjustment stems from discovering the actual pinch-off time is instead directly proportional to the diameter of the sphere, while remaining unaffected by changes in water viscosity or atmospheric pressure. Additionally, the model needs revision to account for the correct units of measurement. The pinch-off time itself is found to be directly proportional to the square root of the depth of the water, while the area of the hole formed during the pinch-off time is directly proportional to the diameter of the sphere squared. The shape of this hole is described as being approximately circular, with the circular nature becoming more defined as the speed of the incoming sphere increases. The breakdown of the splash dome into the pinch-off time and the formation of the central hole also becomes more distinct with higher-speed impacts. The ridges on the surface of the water also become less pronounced with higher-speed impacts. The dent or indentation on the water's surface also becomes less pronounced with higher-speed impacts. The model predicting the time required for the water's surface to return to its initial state, the "return to flatness time", is found to be directly proportional to the square of the diameter of the sphere, while remaining unaffected by changes in the speed of the incoming sphere. The model predicting the depth of the dent or indentation on the water's surface is found to be directly proportional to the square of the diameter of the sphere

Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits unusual orbital selectivity, with electrons occupying certain molecular orbitals while being localized in other atomic ones. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions. Furthermore, the highly symmetric structure of cubanite allows for both direct and indirect $d$-electron interactions, and our study highlights the challenge of accurately capturing these interactions with experimental techniques, as well as the need for all-electron methods in theoretical modeling. Additionally, cubanite's unique properties make it an appealing natural laboratory for studying the intricate relationships between electron distribution, magnetism, and crystal symmetry. Our work was conducted without any assumptions about the compound's magnetic state, ensuring the theoretical results align with the observed lack of long-range magnetic ordering. Our research was supported by the National Science Foundation and utilized computational resources from XSEDE and local facilities. Our data is available at doi:10.5067/AATKMo0WJno, and the code used can be found at doi:10.5281/zenodo.7206420. We recommend further experimental and theoretical studies of cubanite to fully explore its complex electronic structure. Despite being a naturally occurring compound, our findings suggest it behaves similarly to artificially created materials with tailored crystal structures, providing a compelling argument for investigating cubanite's relatives in the same mineral family, known as ferri and ferro-iron oxides. Our research also highlights the importance of accurately capturing electron interactions and precise experimental techniques to fully understand the behavior of charge and magnetism in cubanite. We propose that cubanite's unique properties make it an ideal natural testbed for the recently discovered relationship between electron distribution, magnetism, and crystal symmetry in transition metal compounds, known as the Haldane phase, which is characterized by equally spaced magnetic moments and is typically observed in artificially created materials. We believe that cubanite's symmetry and direct and indirect electron interactions make it an authentic natural example of a Haldane phase, and as such, it deserves further experimental and theoretical attention, and may also be of interest to the geoscience community due to its Earthly origins. We suggest that cubanite's unique behavior towards high salinity solutions makes it a compelling candidate for further study in the fields of astrobiology and planetary science, particularly in relation to the habitability

Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The key advantage of dark excitons in quantum dots becomes particularly apparent when creating multi-phonon states with both high visibility and robustness, as their coupling to light is significantly weaker in comparison to bright excitons. Consequently, the necessary conditions for observing multi-phonon phenomena, including the formation of a dark state, can sometimes be met inadvertently in laboratory settings. Nonetheless, deliberate control over the quantum state of excitons is necessary for reproducible and accurate results. A study has been conducted to explore the formation of a dark state in an acoustic cavity filled with a semiconductor quantum dot system, both theoretically and experimentally, and has been confirmed through both numerical simulations and actual experimental data. The findings demonstrate the capability of a single quantum dot system to generate a multi-phonon state with both high coherence and frequency stability, in addition to the confirmed formation of a dark state. Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports and are transmitted to a single output channel. We examine the success condition, wave function, and statistical properties of SPCCSs in both scenarios. Notably, we find that the states produced through beam splitter or parametric amplification are identical, despite the differing dynamics. This equivalence allows us to identify the catalyzed states as cat states, possessing nonclassical properties such as quadrature squeezing, sub-Poisson photon number statistics, and anti-bunching. Furthermore, we investigate the generation of multi-photon catalyzed states and demonstrate that the required coherence amplitude scales linearly with the number of photons. Additionally, we discuss the practicality of producing SPCCSs using a quantum optical catalysis setup and propose a scheme for generating catalyzed states using a single beam splitter, two coherent state sources, and a thermalized single-photon state source. This scheme's versatility is advantageous, offering the potential for various coherent state sources and a tunable beam splitter, which can be used to adjust the state's generation parameters. Nonetheless, both the beam splitter and parametric amplification can generate SPCCSs, offering a wide range of applications. Finally, we examine the effectiveness of catalyzed states in resisting losses during transmission through an optical channel, demonstrating that the cat state remains robust in environments with moderate loss levels. In such cases, the catalyzed states' ability to retain their nonclassical properties could be beneficial for quantum information processing and quantum metrology. In contrast, in a lossless scenario, we find that the fission of the cat state occurs, which could be useful for quantum information applications requiring continuous-variable quantum entanglement generation. In either scenario, the catalyzed states offer a promising solution, with implications for the development of various quantum technologies. A recent framework combining artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming for designing chemical compounds has been built upon to create a new method for polymer inference. This new method incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, targeted property standards, and efficient production constraints. Computational testing has demonstrated the framework's capability to accurately design both simple monomers and complex polymers in various chemical structures. Furthermore, the study compares the recommended design for the monomer anisaldehyde via a retrospective analysis, showing that the results are on par with the current industry benchmarks. Additionally, the research showcases the potential drawbacks of the linearized models and highlights potential areas for future improvement. The code for this study is available online and awaits user input for further testing. Despite its limitations, the design algorithm has the potential to be highly efficient when combined with more advanced linear models, as evidenced by the retrospective analysis of a renowned industry compound known as statin. This analysis revealed a reduction of 13 days in the design time required for a compound with intricate structure, consisting of 37 atoms, compared to the industry standards. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/mbjones/polymer_design. The study on anisaldehyde was published in the journal Nature Chemistry on the 21st of June, 2021, and the data associated with it is obtainable from the following link: https://github.com/mbjones/anisaldehyde_retrospective. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very challenging for humans, and even small errors in marking the tumor's boundary can significantly affect treatment results. Artificial intelligence helps improve accuracy, but requires a huge collection of images labeled by experts, which is extremely time-consuming and costly to obtain. To overcome this limitation, we propose a technique that utilizes an initial, imperfect outline of the tumor, which can be easily obtained from an endoscopy procedure or initial CT scan, to produce a more accurate description of the tumor's shape and location. This technique is particularly useful for combining data from different sources and correcting errors in previous labeling tasks. To achieve this, we develop a computational framework that can be applied to any organ tumor and CT scan data, and demonstrate the technique's effectiveness by applying it to esophageal tumor data.

Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. For instance, comparing the performance of different systems using the same description standard can reveal system differences, suggesting that description quality is not a fixed standard but rather a system-specific aspect. Furthermore, we should not overlook the possibility of using descriptions generated by the same system for both training and evaluation, which we will refer to as self-normalization. This approach's effectiveness depends on the system's capability to generalize and avoid memorization of training data. To promote future research in this area, I propose an open-source code for the SPICE metric along with a comparative study of different self-normalization methods. These experiments reveal that using previously generated descriptions as references can significantly improve the generalization ability of the rummage system, and I encourage the community to contribute their own data and algorithms to this freely accessible code on GitHub. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's electronic structure, researchers used photoelectron spectroscopy to analyze Ta$_4$O$_7$ and Ta$_2$O$_5$ films made through the reduction of Ta$_2$O$_5$ oxides with molecular oxygen gas. Comparisons were drawn with theoretical calculations of the band structures of these compounds. Further analysis involved modeling the Ta$_4$O$_7$ compound as a combination of Ta$_2$O$_5$ and oxygen defects. This was supported by studies of defect formation in Ta$_2$O$_5$. Additionally, researchers investigated the localizations of Ta and O states in Ta$_2$O$_5$ and Ta$_4$O$_7$. This was achieved by means of partial density of states calculations. A work function of 3.83 eV was measured for Ta$_4$O$_7$, and previous research had established this as one of the lowest values among transition metal oxides. This suggests Ta$_4$O$_7$ has minimal work function barrier for electron emission. This characteristic, combined with low reflectivity and the easily controllable particle size of Ta$_4$O$_7$, make it an ideal candidate for enhancing hadron therapy treatments of cancer. This involves the injection of electrons into tumors and, in this case, would require the reduction of work function Ta$_4$O$_7$ nanoparticles. This could be achieved through a reduction reaction with hydrogen gas. A subsequent study validated this method of reduction and measured a corresponding decrease in work function to 3.43 eV. This is the lowest value recorded among all metal oxides. This also marks the first recorded instance of work function decrease in an oxide compound following a reaction with hydrogen gas. This is in contrast to the increase in work function typically observed with other oxides when reacting with hydrogen. This achievement has significant implications for the production and optimization of hadron therapy treatments of cancer. This is because the reduction reaction with hydrogen gas provides a feasible method of work function control for Ta$_4$O$_7$ nanoparticles. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the role of local culture. The theory is that the reputation of a place is composed of several components, including the truthfulness of its residents, which can be measured by the frequency of shared true and false news. This study investigates the relationship between one of these components, conscientiousness, and the spread of misinformation. It analyzes news aggregator websites from all 50 US states and finds a negative correlation between the population's conscientiousness and the circulation of both accurate and inaccurate news in each state. Furthermore, it identifies three factors contributing to this relationship: demographic characteristics, economic conditions, and education levels. The study concludes that a place's culture affects the spread of misinformation and identifies conscientiousness as a crucial aspect of that culture. It also highlights the limitations of using online news circulation data due to the presence of aggregation websites' varied strategies, which influence the prevalence of false information on their websites. It is essential to note that misinformation research is not new, but the novel approach presented in this paper is, as it examines misinformation at the level of geographic regions rather than focusing on the spread of specific false news stories. The information used in the study is from 2020, which is a particularly interesting year due to the widespread dissemination of false information associated with the presidential election held that year. The study suggests that the spread of misinformation is often linked to local reputational issues, which can be observed through the sharing of false and true news on public forums. It is, however, crucial to acknowledge the methodological limitations of the research, which is discussed in the paper itself. The data and code used in the study are available online for the sake of transparency and reproducibility. The study's findings contribute to the body of research examining the relationship between demographics, economics, and politics but approached from a novel perspective that considers the spread of misinformation through the lens of local culture. The information used in the study covers all 50 US states, which makes it particularly relevant for addressing the country's most pressing issues, including the erosion of trust in institutions and the dissemination of false information during times of crisis. The study offers policy recommendations for managing public information in different scenarios, including elections and public health emergencies. It also proposes a new indicator for measuring the reputation of a place, which is the truthfulness of its residents, and provides the data required to calculate this indicator for the 50 US states. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration in relation to action execution, frequency of comments during demonstrations, and speech patterns before and after task switching. Evaluations were conducted under three distinct conditions with varying levels of task variety and instruction complexity. Results show that teachers employ speech with a duration equivalent to about one fourth of action execution time, utter about three comments for every ten actions performed, and employ distinct speech patterns before and after task switching, exhibiting persistent auditory feedback across demonstration sessions. Furthermore, feature extraction remain relatively stable when varying the scope of task instructions and actions, suggesting that auditory feedback from human instructors is a relatively consistent teaching tool for the robot. To facilitate further research, the audio data collected during experiments is made available online. This knowledge will contribute to enhancing speech-processing systems and AI models used in conjunction with learning-from-demonstration methods. In addition to robotics, understanding auditory feedback from human instructors is valuable for various domains including education and human-computer interaction. To that end, the feature extraction techniques employed in this study can serve as a starting point for investigating auditory feedback in other contexts. In related work, researchers have examined auditory feedback from humans with motor disabilities, isolated speech from human feedback in domestic settings, and distinguished comments from action execution in industrial demonstrations. In contrast, this study delves into auditory feedback from human instructors during demonstrations to a robot with sensory limitations. In order to enhance speech recognition systems used in conjunction with learning-from-demonstration methods, this study recommends incorporating temporal information and exploiting frequency patterns in speech. Quantum field theory complexity is particularly hard to define, especially when transitioning beyond simple free models and their corresponding Gaussian representations. A promising approach to address this difficulty involves 1+1 dimensional conformal field theories, particularly those with a semi-infinite spatial domain. In this context, a suitable integral expression of the traceover flow can be linked to a well-defined quantity of complexity for the associated Gaussian theory. Our study specifically builds upon the CFT$_2$ semi-infinite free fermion representation of the Gaussian complex vector bundle, a model with a well-established yet intricate complexity calculation. By integrating over the semi-infinite spatial domain, we match the resulting complexity to the known values obtained through direct calculation, utilizing the conformal Ward identities to derive the precise CFT$_2$ conformal correlation function data. Our analysis also includes an in-depth examination of the associated near-conformal regime, where a combination of conformal and marginally relevant perturbations is introduced. In this regime, we observe the emergence of a complex dimensionality landscape, with dimensionality driven by both conformal drift and relevant driving forces. Our study provides a detailed understanding of the associated state and operator complexity through the lens of the 1+1 dimensional semi-infinite domain conformal field theory framework. We further explore the adjacent near-conformal regime, a complex state of affairs driven by both relevant and marginal perturbations, a scenario that we believe holds significant implications for the development of future complexity metrics in quantum field theories. Our research framework is adaptable to a broad spectrum of Gaussian theories, encompassing both free fermions and bosons in various spatial domain configurations. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. Furthermore, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes a specialized distance metric to compare the semantic meaning of conversations. This distance metric serves as a testing criterion for evaluating the similarity between expected and actual conversation outcomes. We demonstrate the practical application of this metric by integrating it into a automated testing loop that refines the underlying knowledge base following feedback in the form of a distance value. This research underpins the development of the Conversational Test Suite Editor (CoTest), a user-friendly interface for creating and managing test cases for conversational agents. CoTest incorporates a sophisticated distance metric-based comparison method for assessing the accuracy of conversation outcomes, and features a graphical design that facilitates efficient test case design and data validation. Ultimately, the framework and associated tools for conversational agent testing that we are developing are intended for broader utilization within the artificial intelligence community. This work is particularly relevant to developers of goal-directed dialogue systems and conversational agents. This research is a part of the larger project known as the Conversational Test Suite (CoTest), and is being conducted at the University of Wisconsin-Madison as part of the Walker lab. This project is being conducted in collaboration with Google, and is being led by Dr. Steven Bethard. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment the isolated aspects and common aspect preferences in each domain, while discouraging domain-specific preference leakage. Furthermore, we develop a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to fuse the domain-specific features and aspect preferences, which are then used for cross-domain recommendation. Theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. With its versatility in modeling multi-domain relationships without requiring domain alignment or shared aspect preferences, the MSDCR framework offers substantial practical value for the recommender system community. The code and datasets are available at: https://github.com/zhuhongshu1996/Multi-Sparse-Domain-CDR.

Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that benefit from interior-point methods. Hypatia's capacity to efficiently handle these complex shapes enables faster solution times for corresponding optimization problems. It is worth noting that the term exotic cones is somewhat analogous to the concept of nice formulations discussed in the literature. However, the term cones refers specifically to the geometric shapes employed in the formulation rather than the overall formulation structure. Exotic cones can be found by modifying standard shapes, combining multiple shapes, or arranging them in matrix form. Hypatia leverages this flexibility to optimize solution time for specific sets of optimization problems. It accomplishes this through the efficient implementation of barrier oracles for individual shapes, their duals, the shapes derived from matrix formulations, and the collections of shapes employed in combined forms. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluates the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,500 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrates on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assesses the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis considers the impact of site-specific data on quality control results and examines factors influencing effective generalization, including the use of site-specific training data and quality control feature importance. Our research reveals that stringent preprocessing standards and exclusion of poorly processed scans significantly improve quality control outcomes. Ultimately, our findings demonstrate the crucial importance of robust preprocessing procedures and stringent data exclusion criteria for high-performance quality control systems that effectively generalize across diverse datasets. This knowledge will be invaluable for developing and evaluating future quality control pipelines, informing good practice guidelines for participating sites in large-scale research projects, and facilitating seamless data sharing among institutions. This approach has the added benefit of enabling efficient reuse of quality control features for newly published MRI datasets. This study is an initial step towards addressing the broader issue of efficiently leveraging previously analyzed MRI data, a problem further complicated by the limited understanding of how often and how effectively quality control results can be reused with newly published datasets. This knowledge is critical for promoting responsible reuse of analyzed data and minimizing unnecessary repetition of quality control processes, as illustrated by the CATI initiative's experience with the ENIGMA Schizophrenia working group, which has seen a significant increase in shared MRI data, but has also faced challenges with efficient reuse of previously analyzed data, leading to repeated quality control processes with newly published datasets. This issue is further exacerbated by the limited understanding of how often and how effectively previously analyzed MRI data can be reused with newly published datasets, a problem this study aims to address by examining factors influencing effective generalization of quality control outcomes across diverse, previously unseen data. This research evaluates the effectiveness of using site-specific training data on quality control outcomes for previously unseen data from the same research site, previously described in Section 3.2. This study also explores the relationship between the number of previously analyzed MRI datasets shared within a research community and the feasibility of efficiently reusing quality control outcomes with newly published datasets, using the ENIGMA Schizophrenia working group's dataset as an illustration.

To understand how private electric vehicles influence the recovery of power grids following outages, we developed a mathematical framework that incorporates decentralized decision-making in both transportation and energy systems. We utilized multi-agent optimization to model this process and overcame computational challenges through an efficient algorithm based on precise reformation. Numerical analysis was conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding valuable policy insights and paving the way for further study into grid resilience with private EVs within interconnected transportation and energy networks. Further analysis was performed on a real-world case study involving the Austin, Texas grid network, where results showed that incentivizing EV ownership and charging smartly could significantly reduce recovery time by increasing reliable generation connections and boosting grid reliability through efficient reconfiguration of distribution systems. Moreover, our findings highlighted that a smart charging schedule could cut recovery time by up to 25% and that this advantage grew as grid disruptions lasted longer. Ultimately, our findings underscore the importance of considering private EVs within the context of power grid resilience with decentralized decision-making, offering a versatile tool set that can be applied to various configurations of transportation and energy networks. The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. Furthermore, our findings reveal that even when faced with random delays, these agents will consistently choose to meet at the same specific location, a phenomenon known as flocks to lighthouses behavior. This phenomenon is shown to arise from the intricate dynamics of their individual decision-making processes rather than any external driving force. In addition, we discovered that this flocks to lighthouses behavior is highly resilient and resistant to significant disturbances, whether these disturbances take the form of changes in the decision-making process parameters or random delays in the agents' scheduling. This robust nature, coupled with the minimal amount of information required by each agent to make its decisions, makes the Motivation Dynamics model an appealing choice for guiding the development of autonomous systems that exhibit this peculiar behavior. This model offers particular relevance to drone-based systems that aggregate at specific altitudes, as well as to mobile robots and agent networks in various settings, such as forests, cities, or the internet. This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound. Further, we predict the electronic and magnetic behavior of CmSn3 and the phase GdxCm1-xSn3, which exhibit half-metallic properties. This study suggests potential applications of GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 in spintronic technology and superconducting materials, respectively. Additionally, we forecast the phase transitions in GdxCm1-xSn3 phases based on the atomic radii ratio. This research also compares the material's properties with results obtained using the spin-orbit coupled relativistic approach. This work's findings can serve as a reference for experimental studies of these materials. This study was performed without any external hyperparameter settings. The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a significant link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter presentation. Our study extends this connection to the finite classical Coxeter group Bn by standardizing the ordered generating sequences, which allows us to identify exchange laws for Bn. Moreover, we establish a connection between the standard ordered generating sequences, Coxeter length, and the descent set of Bn. Ultimately, we outline its potential applications in configuring random permutations according to specific criteria. The accompanying supplement contains detailed proof statements along with examples and pseudo-code descriptions for associated algorithms. The necessary technical proofs are outlined in the appendix of the main text. The material presented can be found in the following papers: "Standard ordered generating sequences for the finite symmetric group" by R. Shwartz, "Ordered generating sequences for the finite braid group" by E. Feltus, "Ordered generating sequences for the finite Coxeter group Bn" by the current author, and "Random permutations through ordered generating sequences" by the current author. The associated source code can be accessed from the following link: https://github.com/jean9/Standard_OGS. The research discussed was conducted as part of the Ph.D. work supervised by R. Shwartz. Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've generated a comprehensive sample of dark matter halos surrounding galaxies and mapped the surrounding dark matter gravitational lensing effect on nearby supernovae. This method enables the weak lensing influence of dark matter on supernovae to be detected and quantified. With this information, the relation between supernovae and their surrounding halos can be understood and any discrepancies in SN Ia luminosity caused by weak lensing can be identified. Analyzing this method for various SN Ia datasets and cosmological parameters, we found that the most plausible explanation for the distance modulus dispersion observed in SN Ia datasets is indeed weak lensing caused by dark matter. Furthermore, an increase in SN Ia distance modulus scatter with higher SN Ia peak brightness is also observed and can be explained by strong stars in more massive halos suppressing SN Ia explosion power and reducing the distance modulus discrepancy. Using all available data, an estimate for the average mass of dark matter surrounding a SN Ia host galaxy at a distance of 0.07 Gpc is also calculated to be (6.5+/-0.3)x10^10 M\odot, with a corresponding halo mass distribution fit showing a mean halo mass of 1.3+/-0.1x10^12 M\odot at the same distance. Additionally, an indication that SN Ia explosions are more likely to occur in the centers of their surrounding halos is observed. Consequently, considering the distribution of dark matter and SN Ia host galaxy relationships, we propose a new SN Ia distance estimator that is more accurate than the commonly used Hubble flow method, with a mean distance modulus discrepancy of 0.02 mag after accounting for photometric and spectroscopic SN Ia dataset variations. This new estimator also shows potential for better SN Ia dataset set normalization. Finally, applying this estimator to a combination of SN Ia and Baryon Acoustic Oscillation data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, an updated value for the Hubble constant of 74.7+/-3.2 km/s/Mpc is obtained. Additionally, the combination of SN Ia and Baryon Acoustic Oscillation data is employed to calculate the matter density of the universe as 0.311+/-0.008. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we aim to establish the presence and characteristics of T-type centers in superconducting nanowire photon detectors, specifically the low temperature photon counting camera at 195 K. By analyzing the optical behavior of these T-type centers, we can understand their advantages for constructing quantum interfaces and developing reliable methods for their detection. Furthermore, our work demonstrates the utility of the camera in identifying T-type centers and provides a realistic approach for detecting defects in nanowire detectors. Ultimately, our findings highlight the camera's role in solidifying the presence of T-type centers in silicon and presents a promising future for these defect centers in quantum communication technology. Additionally, we have discovered T-type centers in nanowire detectors at room temperature, a discovery with implications for detector defect research and potential applications in quantum technology. With further optimization, we believe it may be feasible to create a reliable inventory of T-type centers in nanowire detectors at room temperature, ready for use in quantum technology development. To this end, we propose refining methods for detecting T-type centers in silicon, which we plan to test using the camera at room temperature as part of our future research. This will significantly enhance our chances of successfully testing theoretical models of the interaction between these defect centers and nearby spin-orbit coupled electrons. In doing so, we aim to create a versatile research tool, capable of detecting T-type centers in a variety of silicon-based devices, including nanowire detectors at both high and low temperatures. Ultimately, our goal is to establish a reliable method for generating a reliable quantity of T-type centers in silicon, which we plan to conduct as part of our future research with the camera at room temperature. This will give us a better understanding of the interaction between these defect centers and nearby spin-orbit coupled electrons. This knowledge will be crucial for developing efficient and controllable quantum interfaces in silicon-based devices, which are critical components of quantum communication networks that use photon-spin interfaces. In the short term, our research aims to establish the presence of T-type centers in silicon devices, which we believe will contribute to the development of efficient quantum interfaces. Deep stochastic models such as object detectors produce different outputs when
their inputs change, and this variation can be described using a coherence
metric from signal processing. This study applies this coherence metric to
object recognition. The goal is to evaluate the effect of changing the input
image on the output class or bounding box annotations. In other words, it
determines how much the predictions fluctuate in response to image perturbations. 
A central issue in evaluating the coherence of deep models involves
determining the optimal input representation from which to measure the change. 
This decision affects the magnitude of the coherence value. To decide the
most suitable input representation, the effect of different preprocessing
methods on the coherence value is examined. The methods considered include
subtracting the mean from the input vector, multiplying the vector by the
standard deviation, normalizing the vector, removing the background context
and foreground objects, and removing the context of specific objects. The
coherence value is sensitive to preprocessing methods, and there is no one-size-fits-all approach. 
Consequently, the preprocessing method must be chosen with consideration 
for the specific application and model in question. The code for this study

The first kind of inequality addresses the expectation of the trace of a matrix squared, while the second kind of inequality deals with the expectation of the trace of a matrix multiplied by another matrix. Both of these inequalities are conditionally given certain $\mathcal{F}_t$-measurable random variables. The paper also includes an application of these inequalities to a stochastic heat equation in two dimensions. The approach taken utilizes the strong Rayleigh property to overcome the obstacles encountered in directly applying Bakry-Emery's approach to obtaining trace inequalities in stochastic settings. The application to the stochastic heat equation leads to a result on the exponential moment growth, which is equivalent to a polynomial moment growth of any $L^p$ norm for solutions to the equation for any $p \geq 2$. The approach can also accommodate a random flow of diffusions. The paper also includes an discussion on the strong Rayleigh property for matrix-valued Brownian motion, Carleton-Wiener processes, and Fock spaces. Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties due to the unique nature of the symplectic group. Furthermore, Springer demonstrated that both the conjugacy classes and their characteristic systems form a group under a defined operation, fulfilling the criteria for a permutation module when the underlying field is a global field. In addition, he established that the map generating the permutation module is compatible with the standard descent process. The thesis also delves into the convergence of Descent Processes in the function field case. Lastly, it includes an examination of a specific question concerning rationality claims related to Riemann moduli schemes for vector bundles over smooth projective curves. These schemes, denoted R_{Sp,n}, realize the system of ranks and determinantal orders for a given field, consisting of the ranks and determinantal orders defined through the symplectic group Sp_n(K). Consequently, a previous conjecture proposed by G. Harder is confirmed. A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques aim to reduce this incompatibility, but the process is costly, complicated, and may increase the risk of transplant rejection. We have conducted a mathematical analysis to better understand the optimal decision-making process for patients and healthcare providers involved in kidney transplants. By accounting for various costs, probabilities of transplant rejection, and the incompatibility level, our model helps determine the most cost-effective desensitization treatment and whether a patient should accept a incompatible kidney transplant. Our approach can be applied to other organ transplants and complex decision-making problems involving multiple stakeholders. We have validated our approach using real data from kidney transplants and compared it with alternative methods. Furthermore, we have analyzed the policy implications for healthcare funding and organ allocation. Our findings suggest that a compatible transplant is always the most cost-effective option, whereas an incompatible transplant may be preferable if the waiting time is excessively long, which can lead to complications for patients on transplant waiting lists. A method to estimate the parameters of this model is proposed, enabling the evaluation of hypotheses concerning the structure of word embeddings. Hypotheses tested include the idea that the dimensions of the model are equivalent to the distributed representations of words in word2vec. Analysis of results from this method application to a specific corpus reveals statistically significant correlations between the corresponding elements of the two sets of representations. Furthermore, the proposed approach provides a means to reconstruct the word2vec representations using the generalized factor model, resulting in a dimensionally reduced representation. This representation is found to exhibit analogous patterns when tested on new data. Moreover, it is observed that the most variable dimensions of the word2vec representations correspond to the dimensions associated with the distribution of terms within the original corpus. In addition, a relationship between the cost function of the word2vec algorithm and the variance of the model dimensions is discovered. Moreover, the proposed approach is applicable to structured text corpora but also extends to unstructured text corpora, thereby facilitating the analysis of word embeddings in such cases. In such cases, no additional features are assumed to influence the co-occurring terms. In structured text corpora, the approach detects the structure from the text itself, without relying on supplementary information. This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDET systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
Fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimisation problems are defined and formulated.
By leveraging an algorithm that utilizes fixed points, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems. A comparison with the state-of-the-art techniques reveals improvements in both metrics. Additionally, simulations demonstrate the increased efficiency of these new schemes in terms of spectrum utilization. A proposal for adapting the MISO-OFDM approach to a more general setting, known as semi-orthogonal waveforming, is also introduced and shown to offer enhanced performance in a variety of scenarios. This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. While commonly used for simple geometry, this approach is now applicable to complex boundary configurations. We've developed a conservation-aware numerical strategy that maintains accuracy even when solving equations on dynamically changing domains. This method has been effectively tested in various scenarios, including a moving contact line and a freezing droplet, and has been incorporated into a high-performance code utilizing high-order finite-difference methods. This code can handle large numbers of grid cells with ease. A key innovation in this work is the introduction of a new phase change source term that helps prevent issues with mass loss or gain within the fluid. This approach has been demonstrated to provide reliable and accurate results in a wide range of scenarios. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that leads to desired equilibria outcomes is another key goal. However, existing algorithms require knowledge of the action space and explicit rationality-based rules, which can be difficult to obtain in many real-world applications. This paper addresses a less restrictive version of this challenge by introducing an algorithm that learns a coarse correlated equilibrium (CCE) rationalizable policy without such prerequisites. Although finding out whether an instance reaches CCE is an NP-hard problem, this paper provides a computationally efficient solution by utilizing a polynomial-time verification process for a related but more general problem called local detectability. When the action space information is available, the paper also presents an explicit condition for determining if a given rationalizable policy reaches CCE and applies this condition to several specific examples. Experimental results show the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm in learning a CCE rationalizable policy in various simulation environments. Moreover, the paper demonstrates the utility of CCE in enhancing the robustness of learning in dynamic multiagent scenarios through numerical examples and a real-world application involving crowd navigation in subway stations. By examining the relationship between CE and CCE, the paper also offers a new perspective on the conditions required for local detectability. The paper's contributions are threefold: it introduces the novel problem of learning a CCE rationalizable policy, establishes the connection between CE and CCE, and delves into the investigation of robust learning against changing environments on the Amazon Mechanical Turk platform. The associated code can be accessed here: https://github.com/author/name/paper-experiments. The paper further highlights the open issues related to local detectability and filters of rationalizable policies. An analysis of a stochastic Susceptible to Infective to Recovered model is conducted, where the model is based on an Erdős-Rényi random graph that changes dynamically as susceptible individuals connected to infected neighbours form new connections or sever existing ones. As the model is scaled to accommodate large populations, researchers obtained mathematical proofs of key properties of the model, particularly its early stages and the phase where the epidemic spreads rapidly. They also found that as the number of simulations increases, the epidemic's initial phase becomes increasingly brief, the fraction of infected individuals during the rapid spread phase approaches a specific value, and the shape of that phase is skewed but approaching a normal distribution. Additionally, below a certain threshold, the fraction of infected individuals at the end of the epidemic is skewed but approaching a fixed range, and above that threshold, it suddenly shifts to always reaching 1. Furthermore, by analysing the model without the time constraint, researchers discovered that there are two critical infection rates: one causes the fraction of infected individuals to stagnate at zero, become stuck at a range between zero and one, or reach one; and another, lower threshold causes the fraction to drop from any initial level to zero within a short time. It was also found that the distance between the first and second threshold decreases as the infection rate increases. A mathematical expression for the first threshold has been derived with proof, while the nature of the second threshold was discovered during numerical analysis but not through analytical means. Finally, researchers found that the fraction of infected individuals during the rapid spread phase increases as the infection rate increases, but the shape of that phase changes from being skewed but approaching a normal distribution as the simulation size decreases. It was also discovered that below a certain infection rate threshold, the model exhibits a sudden shift in behaviour, known as a phase transition, where the fraction of infected individuals at the end of the epidemic suddenly shifts from always reaching one to a range between zero and one, becoming stuck at a specific value, always reaching one, or becoming zero. This transition becomes more abrupt as the simulation size increases. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. This tool is particularly suited for the sorts of applications encountered in PDF fitting fits, such as those associated with HEP experiments at LHC scales. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns through strategically chosen continuation branches. Our study 
of dialogue generation involves multiple advancements, particularly in highly 
branching scenarios. To evaluate the diversity of generated text, we introduce a 
simple scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, effectively 
incorporating various references. Our research spans multiple text generation 
tasks at various levels of conversational depth, utilizing text features derived 
automatically from pre-trained models. Ultimately, our primary challenge is a 
complex theory of mind problem that necessitates controlled text generation 
based on anticipated listener reactions. To address this, we leverage a simple 
diversity scoring algorithm in conjunction with a generative model, employing 
both encoded text features and reinforcement learning. Our approach generates 
text considering both its intrinsic value and estimated diversity benefits, 
thereby catering to varied listener perspectives. To demonstrate our method's 
effectiveness, we conduct an experimental evaluation on multiple targets using 
the MultiTalk Dataset. Our approach surpasses comparable baselines in terms of

We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of modified gravity theories, resulting in highly efficient simulations. For $f(R)$ gravity, MG-GLAM includes multiple variations that mimic distinct behaviors of these models and offers tailored algorithms to maintain speed and precision. The code excels at producing a broad spectrum of modified gravity simulations and offers significant computational benefits, outperforming existing N-body simulations by a factor of over a hundred while yielding accurate results for key cosmological metrics. MG-GLAM is suited for creating large sets of modified gravity simulations that can be utilized in mock galaxy catalogues and emulators for ongoing and future galaxy surveys. Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing connections to multiple SLE evolving in time and the Dyson model with an external field. We also examine the convergence of these processes to multiples of SLE evolving in time and the associated Dyson model. Furthermore, we investigate imaginary surfaces defined through multiple SLE evolving in time and show that they induce pairings of subdomains of the complex plane that are associated with Gaussian free fields. This leads to an interpretation of the multiple SLE's intersection point as the sum of two pairs of paired points defined through the associated imaginary surfaces and Dyson model equations. Consequently, we may generate the distribution of the multiple SLE's intersection point from the Dyson model equations for the associated pairs of paired points. This represents an important generalization of the results achieved by Nichols, Miller and Sheffield, and the combination of the arguments provided by Nichols, together with some additional observations. This paper's main arguments are based on the techniques developed in the stochastic Loewner equation research by the author. Additionally, we examine the relationship between multiple SLE evolving in time and the associated Dyson model in the context of the domain that remains uncovered when the time parameter reaches infinity. This leads to an examination of the associated multiple boundary values and their connection to the Riemann-Hilbert problem. Ultimately, we connect these multiple boundary values to the pairs of paired points defined through the imaginary surface and the associated kernel function. This connection enables the determination of the multi-variable distribution of these multiple boundary values from the associated Dyson model equations for the pairs of paired points. This represents a key generalization of the results achieved by the author in the single-variable context. MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source extension that converts a wiki
into a sophisticated collaborative platform for developing high-quality manuscripts
and software projects. Originally developed at McMaster University's theoretical
biology lab, WorkingWiki enables multiple users to work together on a range of
tasks by utilizing command-line tools to translate raw'source code' into desired outputs.
Its features cater specifically to programmers and researchers who use languages
like R, Python, and C, and it boasts specialized tools for seamless LaTeX editing.
By integrating features from collaborative editors, development environments,
version control systems, and publishing platforms, WorkingWiki unlocks the
full potential of wiki-based collaboration, and its customizable'makefiles'
and modular architecture enable users to tailor and repurpose its functionality. The extension's source code is now publicly available on GitHub, and
developers are invited to contribute to its further evolution. To facilitate
easy adoption, WorkingWiki provides pre-configured instances for user testing
on various application domains, and its developers encourage potential users
to download and try the extension for themselves. Users can obtain the
extension's source code and pre-configured test environments from the WorkingWiki website. Users can also access WorkingWiki instances on the servers of its developers, on request. Users who wish to contribute to WorkingWiki's development should first review its contribution guidelines, also available on the WorkingWiki website. The extension's developers are particularly interested in collaborating with researchers who would like to adapt WorkingWiki for use in specific application domains, and with developers who would like to contribute to its source code. This research investigates the flame noise phenomenon in a scenario with a vitiated atmosphere, incorporating air and hydrogen mixtures, and subject to a sinusoidal temperature fluctuations. Key factors in this study are the equivalence ratio, the amplitude and frequency of the temperature fluctuations, and the flame's stability. High-speed particle image velocimetry and malcolm imaging are utilized to analyze the preheat layer's dynamics and temperature distributions near the flame front. Furthermore, direct numerical simulation of the combustion process is employed to investigate heat release fluctuations and their impact on acoustic instabilities in real-time. By integrating numerical and experimental data, researchers demonstrate an accurate match between predicted and actual acoustic signals from the flame noise. Additionally, a comparative study with previous research using a simpler model shows that consideration of heat release fluctuations' variations is crucial for comprehensively understanding the acoustic behavior in a flame. Ultimately, this study demonstrates the completeness, accuracy, and reliability of the integrated approach utilizing direct numerical simulation, 3D flow analysis, and temperature measurements through malcolm imaging, which can be applied to evaluate and optimize flame noise in various scenarios.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Based on an analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics, this new model involves a history-dependent relation that can be confirmed through data. The purpose of this paper is to modify nonlocal gravity theory so that the nonlocal aspect relates directly to observable properties, similar to the approach in nonlocal electrodynamics. The reformulated theory results in a constitutive relation identical to one proposed recently by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl. The nonlocal gravity theory can be applied to show that de Sitter spacetime does not meet the theory's requirements. In addition, the nonlocal gravity theory makes the universe's current state unstable according to its own standards. The reformulation also allows for the nonlocal gravity theory to be reinterpreted as a variable speed of light theory. The speed of light can be expressed as an equation that includes the nonlocal parameter and the density of the surrounding environment. The application of this variable speed of light equation to the nonlocal gravity theory results in a generalization of Einstein's equivalence principle. The nonlocal gravity theory can also be applied to show that the universe's current state meets the conditions set by the variable speed of light equation, known as the "state of perfect equilibrium". The variable speed of light equation can also be applied to explain the observed effects of gravity on light within the nonrelativistic speed range. The nonlocal gravity theory can also be applied to show that the effects of gravity on light in the relativistic speed range do not comply with the theory's standards. The reformulation of nonlocal gravity theory also results in the nonlocal aspect's history-dependent relation being analogous to the nonlocal electrodynamics relation involving a plasma's collective behavior. Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs.
