High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has seen the advent of two methods that modify classical Full Waveform Inversion (FWI): Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended-Reality FWI (ER-FWI). Both techniques aim to alleviate the issue of local minima by relaxing the adherence to exact wave equation solutions. Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) generates a data misfit space where synthetic data matches observed data, without directly calculating the forward solution. In contrast, ER-FWI adds an auxiliary wavefield target, linked to the difference between observed and synthetic data, alongside the traditional FWI objective function. This auxiliary target is tied to the system of wave equation operators. We present a hybrid method that combines the ER-FWI and WRI frameworks. Known as Extended-Reality Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (ER-WRI), this method incorporates the wavefield target from WRI into the ER-FWI framework. ER-WRI minimizes both the data misfit and the difference between the observed and reconstructed wavefields. To facilitate computation, we use a source-term reconstruction approach to link the ER-WRI target to the ER-FWI auxiliary wavefield. This connection enables shared use of the fast Fourier transform-based solver. We demonstrate the effectiveness and solver-sharing efficiency of ER-WRI on simulated datasets. Additionally, we examine the impact of initial model quality on ER-WRI performance. Furthermore, we investigate the hybrid method's sensitivity to configuration settings, including the regularizer in the WRI reconstructed wavefield and the weighting between the data misfit and wavefield terms in the ER-WRI objective function. We also compare ER-WRI to the standalone versions of WRI and ER-FWI on a real-world dataset from the Sigsbee II model. We conclude that ER-WRI offers a viable alternative to the current state-of-the-art FWI methods. We anticipate that further advancements in this hybrid method will be possible through the incorporation of anisotropic wave equation models. We have made the ER-WRI code publicly available on GitHub at the time of submission. We look forward to collaborative efforts with the research community to accelerate the development of this hybrid method. We have also provided a brief code documentation in the appendix of this submission. To analyze the interplay of species competition and dispersal, this study examines a non-spatial model with three species that compete similarly, supplemented with a simple spatial component to enable species dispersal. The model includes a unique feature known as the "species flow effect," where the spread of a focal species is affected by the presence of the two species with which it competes. To simplify the analysis, the study assumes that the rates of species competition and dispersal are balanced, leading to the model's species equivalence. By fixing the immigration rate of one species and varying another, the study explores the transition of the model from a non-coexistence state to a triple-species coexistence state. The study discovers three distinct states of the model: a non-coexistence state with a critical point, a double-species coexistence state with a constant species ratio, and the triple-species coexistence state with a unique constant species abundance. The study also identifies two branches of the double-species coexistence state in the model parameter space. The analysis of the model includes a study of its transition to the non-coexistence state through either a non-equilibrium fixed point or an oscillatory equilibrium, depending on the difference in species dispersal rates. The study also compares the model to the Lotka-Volterra model, revealing distinct dynamics due to the constraint of balanced species competition and dispersal. The model exhibits a phenomenon known as the "species flow effect" where the spread of a focal species is influenced by the presence of the two species with which it competes, leading to an increase in the focal species abundance in areas inhabited by both species, even in the absence of spatial component. The study demonstrates that the model predicts the distribution of species abundance in space as well as the transition of the model from a non-coexistence state to a double-species coexistence state, facilitating an empirical analysis of the species flow effect in a real ecosystem. The code used in the study is publicly available on a GitHub repository. The model used in the study can be applied to any three species that compete equally and share the same dispersal range, providing a basic framework for the analysis of species coexistence dynamics. The study suggests that the model variables can be rescaled to simplify the analysis, leading to a model with additive species interactions and a unique feature known as the species flow effect. The study also presents a method to analyze multi-species interactions based on the assumption of balanced interactions, offering a framework for the analysis of coexistence dynamics in multi-species ecosystems. This research focuses on an integrated data and energy transmission network, which incorporates D2D communication and a grid network. A key aspect of this integrated system is the use of D2D communication for power transfer, where the energy-cooperative mechanism can boost the transmission power. We then consider a problem where an intelligent reflecting surface is placed in a D2D communication system and we aim to optimize the reflection coefficient at the surface to maximize the transmitted power and minimize the interference from nearby grids. To solve this problem, we first establish an integrated data and energy transmission model and then develop an algorithm based on successive approximation to find the optimal reflection coefficient. We also conduct numerical experiments to compare the performance of the proposed algorithm with or without D2D communication. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of the position of the grid network and the D2D communication group on the transmitted power and interference. Finally, we discuss the feasibility of using D2D communication for power transfer in a real-world scenario. This can be achieved by applying various techniques such as increasing the gain of the energy coil, reducing the frequency of data transmission, and utilizing multi-user energy transfer. This enables the integrated data and energy transmission network to be more practical and efficient. By combining these results with those presented by Milne and Pink, we gain insight into the distinct scenarios characterized by the interplay between the complex imprimality of the extension K/Q and the freeness of the ring of integers in K over its associated order within the rational group algebra constructed from G. While these methods successfully pinpoint the periods of semantic evolution for most words, the research reveals a pattern where they inaccurately pinpoint changes for words with distant historical transformations. Furthermore, it is suggested that the contextualized models struggle with differentiating long-term developments in meaning, which the authors attribute to the limited scope of their training data, encompassing time periods up to a century before the present day. In addition, the paper explores the effectiveness of combining non-contextualized embeddings and contextualized representations in characterizing diachronic semantic shifts, and presents findings on the temporal boundaries of change for individual words, as well as the rates of change across the vocabulary as a whole. In the latter case, the analysis is conducted using a recently introduced method called the Diachronic Word Embedding Retention Generalization, or D-WREG. The results from this research have implications for the accurate modeling of diachronic developments in semantic change, specifically highlighting the need to differentiate between short-term and long-term shifts in meaning. Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research uses the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear model that links radio luminosity, optical or X-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and spin. Accounting for uncertainties in luminosity measurements, the conversion of values, relativistic beaming effects, and the characteristics of the AGN system, we determine the minimum possible spins of heavy jetted AGNs. These results help explore the relationship between the masses of ultra-light scalar, vector, and tensor particles, closing a gap in parameter space around $10^{-20}-10^{-19}$eV. Additionally, we determine the upper limits on the decay constant of axions, assuming their decay could prevent their entry into a state of instability and their possible non-observation through superradiance. This research also provides upper limits on the fraction of dark matter comprised by ultra-light axion-like particles, concluding that, as a single species, such a particle cannot constitute more than 10% of the dark matter in a given mass range ($10^{-21} < \mu \, (\mathrm{eV}) < 10^{-17}$). A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei
between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In an effort to gain insight into the underlying mechanisms
controlling the behavior of cells during IKNM, a computational model has been developed
to simulate cellular interactions with the neuroepithelial tissue's physical properties. By
incorporating observed cellular dynamics and IKNM patterns, the model reveals the emergence
of the characteristic nuclear migration rhythm. Furthermore, the model's results align
with experimental data collected across various species, demonstrating the universality
of the underlying mechanisms governing IKNM. By interconnecting physical interactions with
molecular signals, the model provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the
complex interplay between cellular behavior, tissue architecture, and the migration rhythm
during neural development. The analysis of the model reveals the critical contribution of
a negative feedback loop composed of apical-basal polarity and cell cycle dynamics to the
migration rhythm. The examination of the model's parameters and the comparison with
experimental data from various species demonstrate the robustness and universality of the
IKNM mechanisms. The developed model serves as a starting point for the exploration of
deviations from normal development, as well as the assessment of how changes in the
microenvironment influence the neuroepithelial tissue's behavior. The interconnection of
the model with external influences, such as the neuroepithelial tissue's response to the
blood-brain barrier, offers potential for future research. The supplied code enables
readers to manipulate the model, facilitating a deeper comprehension of the complex
biological processes involved in neural development. The associated dataset is available at
https://doi.org/10.17637/jaissle2024. The model has been designed to be adaptable for the
study of other cellular systems characterized by the interaction of cell cycle dynamics,
apical-basal polarity, and physical tissue properties. The code can be accessed at
https://github.com/NeuralTissueMechanics/Interkinetic-Nuclear-Migration. The examined data
can be found in the following repositories: mouse data (https://doi.org/10.17637/jaissle2024),

Real-world code patterns, which are often non-negative, systematically structured and non-Gaussian, can impede reconstruction performance due to their non-ideal coherence properties. This research addresses this challenge by developing optimized code patterns that minimize the coherence of the sensing matrix and signal representation matrix combination, taking into consideration their inherent structural relationships. A general algorithm is proposed for calculating the projective phase encodings that encode a signal along multiple views, and a video compressed sensing scheme is presented as an example. Both numerical and experimental results indicate that the coherence-based strategy leads to accurate and detailed reconstruction of images. High-performance embedded hardware is also designed to manage multiple views and encoded data in compressed sensing applications. The utility of the proposed method is further demonstrated by using an underwater optical camera with a half-ring shaped aperture, capable of capturing multiple views and encoded images of an underwater scene from a single point of view. Experimental data show significant improvements over current compressed sensing techniques. The designed camera can capture images of underwater objects at a distance of 50 meters with resolution of 4 megapixels in less than a second. The hardware can be tailored for various applications including optical cameras in air, and has a modular design allowing for easy upgrade of its specifications. Contrary to previous assumptions, the dynamics of this specific class of active matter cannot be accurately captured using simplified hydrodynamic models when the spatial environment is two-dimensional up to five-dimensional space; however, we were able to derive precise, dimension-dependent scaling parameters for these dimensions. Our findings also reveal the presence of a crossover point in the scaled distance and distance parameters, which we found to be driven by the interplay between the inclusions' effects on the local speed and the overall non-equilibrium dynamics. Furthermore, the hydrodynamic theory model includes the precise scaling of the standard hydrodynamic coefficients, the correlation functions of the order parameter, and the spatial distribution of the inclusions. Regular function computability and continuity are equivalent properties on infinite input sets, as demonstrated by Miller and Shore. This study expands upon their finding by showing that, for any regular function f, there exists a sequential algorithm capable of determining whether a given infinite set is mapped to infinite under f. Furthermore, for functions f and g that are inverses of each other, it can be determined algorithmically whether a given infinite set is comprised of elements from the co-domain of f or the domain of g. This was achieved by employing a stack or counter in the form of a sequential process. A key aspect of this result is the consideration of the distinction between first-order definable and computable infinite sets. A regular function f is then characterized by the property that there exists a sequential algorithm capable of determining whether a given first-order definable infinite set is mapped to infinite under f. A related discussion on the lack of connection between the computability of regular co-PAC learnability and the computability of infinite sets that are compatible with a given regular function also follows from this characterization. The appendix features an additional discussion on the relationship between the regular co-PAC learnability of a function f, the regular co-PAC learnability of the inverse function f^-1, and the relationship between the compatible infinite sets for f and f^-1. The connection between the regular co-PAC learnability of a function f and the sequential algorithm that determines the relationship between f and the first-order definable infinite sets is also explored in the appendix. The purpose of the appendix is to formalize the notion of a learnable family of regular functions and to introduce the concept of a regular function that is equipable with a sequence algorithm for a specified class of compatible infinite sets, thereby establishing the groundwork for future research. The content of the paper has been reworked from relevant sections of the author's doctoral dissertation at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, written under the guidance of R. Wilson. The relationship between the results presented and those found in the research of Miller and Shore is also discussed. The connection between the regular co-PAC learnability of a function f and the sequential algorithm that determines the relationship between f and first-order definable infinite sets enables the generalization of the results from partial automata to regular functions. The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy continuum remain unclear, fueling debate over the distinct features of human-like agents. Two contrasting theories are proposed to account for this continuum: the graded salience model, which posits varying levels of salience for features like eyes and limbs, and the categorical framework, which suggests a distinction between animate and inanimate entities based on fundamental characteristics. This study aims to explore these hypotheses through the lens of a critical aspect of animacy: agency. Our analysis reveals that agency is a pivotal feature on the animacy continuum, with a particular affinity for the salience-based framework. Furthermore, we reveal that the T-pattern analysis can detect agency-related patterns in neural responses with a high degree of precision. Our empirical study employs this analysis to investigate the agency feature in the ventral temporal cortex's animacy continuum. The results indicate that a shift from categorical to graded representations explains the data generated in our experiment. In contrast, the features proposed by the categorical framework fail to account for the observed patterns of neural activity. In conclusion, our findings support the graded salience model of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy continuum, with key implications for our understanding of human-like agency. Our study also highlights the utility of the T-pattern analysis in uncovering complex patterns of neural responses associated with the concept of agency. For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring the structure of its laddings. This construction is highly dependent on the properties of W's normalizers in the persymmetric group P_W. By examining the relationships between these normalizers and P_W's symplectic embeddings, we can determine the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant range of dimensions, thereby extending previous findings by Bränden and Krammer for the Bannister Coxeter groups. Furthermore, our approach in analyzing these relationships leads to an alternative proof of the results presented by Bränden and Krammer. Moreover, our method enables the generation of boolean complexes from monoids within the permutative monoids P_W, allowing us to broaden the applicability of our generated complexes to a wider range of dimensions. Additionally, we derive specific instances of these complexes for the Bannister Coxeter groups, known as Gamma_1, Delta_1, and E_1, which we find exhibit homotopy types equivalent to the homotopy types of the complexes defined by Bränden and Krammer. Consequently, our analysis demarcates the lowest boundary for which the (l_1,\Delta_1,E_1)-complex's homotopy type is known, which presents an intriguing problem for further investigation. This investigation is particularly significant for a subset of Coxeter groups, specifically the family known as H_4, for which we aim to determine the homotopy type of the corresponding boolean complex. This achievement would enable us to solve the fourth Kermode's conjecture. This conjecture is one of the three conjectures initially proposed by Kermode, which include the following three: (1) The search for the Coxeter group with the highest dimension whose boolean complex has a non-trivial homotopy type can be found within the family known as H_n. (2) The determination of the homotopy type of the boolean complex for the Coxeter group known as H_4. (3) The verification that the malleable Coxeter groups are, in fact, smooth. This paper addresses the first conjecture for a subset of malleable Coxeter groups. Moreover, we introduce the concept of a permutative monoid's symplectic embedding, which we believe has value beyond the Coxeter group context. This new concept allows us to generate boolean complexes for a broader range of dimensions.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the most infectious rumors in China during this period. In-depth analysis of 2890 widely transmitted rumors in Weibo revealed that those with greater search traffic, geospatial diffusion, and faster transmission speeds tend to spread further. Intrigued by these findings, we discovered that many of the most widely transmitted rumors originated from reputable news sources, highlighting the critical role of information credibility in tackling the problem of online rumors. To combat the spread of these rumors, we propose an adaptive credibility-weighted algorithm that prioritizes debunking information targeting the most influential and accessible rumors. Implementation of this strategy on Weibo resulted in a significant decrease in search traffic for a large portion of the most widely transmitted rumors, offering valuable insights for public health officials and social media platforms in addressing the negative consequences of online rumors during a public health crisis. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses in real-time to provide better diagnoses and improve patient outcomes. Processors of streaming data, also known as streaming engines, are the backbone of such analyses, but they typically require cumbersome SQL knowledge and offer slow query performance. In response to the growing need for real-time data analysis in healthcare settings, we present LifeStream, a user-friendly streaming engine specifically designed to accelerate common medical computations and simplify query writing. By comparing LifeStream to other high-performance streaming engines, we demonstrate its substantial speedup and easy-to-use interface, which we believe will facilitate widespread adoption in hospitals and make real-time medical data analysis effortless for healthcare professionals, even without extensive technical expertise. Furthermore, LifeStream's code is now available for public use. In addition to streaming engines, another significant challenge in data analysis is addressing growing data volumes, which is why we also introduce StreamScope, a module that aids users in condensing abundant physiological data dimensions while preserving crucial details, thereby enhancing the accuracy of real-time predictions and significantly reducing computational costs. By combining LifeStream and StreamScope, we show that we can cut the necessary data dimensions in half without a noticeable decline in predictive accuracy according to various metrics like mean absolute error and R-squared. Moreover, this reduction leads to a notable improvement in query execution speed, which we believe will benefit various applications, including real-time patient flow management and medical condition forecasting. Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for a greater number of symbols, the average Euclidean distance of differentially detected signals is increased, thus reducing the error rate. Numerical data and analytical formulas are both used to demonstrate the optimal delay period under various CPM conditions. The results obtained highlight the improved performance achievable with this delayed differential detection technique. The study also highlights feasible design guidelines for CPM protocols. The improvement achievable through delayed differential detection is quantified in terms of the bit error rate reduction factor, which can range from 10-10,000 times, depending on the CPM conditions. The optimal delayed differential detection protocol provides better performance than the non-delayed method, offering a package of design specifications for future CPM protocol developers. The research indicates an error rate reduction factor of 100 or more is possible for several existing CPM protocols, such as AM-16QAM, GMCPM with a bandwidth efficiency of 4 bit/s/Hz, and PAM-4, which have prominent applications in high-speed data transmission areas. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback. Portfolio optimization is a critical application in finance, yet its computational intricacies compel financial institutions to resort to simplified methods that require considerable time. By leveraging the Lagrange multiplier method, the mean-variance portfolio optimization issue can be formulated into a set of linear equations and potentially take advantage of the accelerated performance offered by the HHL quantum algorithm. Nevertheless, certain HHL components are not well-suited for operation on Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware. This research introduces NISQ-HHL, the first hybrid rendition of HHL that is capable of supporting end-to-end execution of compact-scale portfolio-optimization tasks on NISQ devices. NISQ-HHL enhances the hybrid HHL variation with newly available quantum-hardware capabilities, encompassing mid-circuit measurement, qubit reinitialization, and quantum-wiring capabilities. Moreover, NISQ-HHL incorporates an enhanced phase estimation process, namely VD-PEH, that significantly boosts the accuracy of this component, enabling the successful execution of tasks on NISQ hardware. Experimental results showcasing the performance of NISQ-HHL on a real-world, 53-qubit quantum system are also presented, and the corresponding code has been made available online for public access. Furthermore, NISQ-HHL boasts a degree of flexibility that allows users to tailor its behavior to accommodate a wide range of quantum systems. This research demonstrates the feasibility of employing the HHL quantum algorithm for portfolio optimization on near-term quantum hardware. Moreover, NISQ-HHL serves as a foundational framework with applicability to a broad spectrum of linear-algebra-based quantum workloads. This framework is collectively referred to as QLAL, and is also publicly accessible for use by the wider research community. This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings from the literature. Furthermore, this work also develops upper and lower bounds to determine the rate at which $k_n$ can increase and still observe this asymptotic I.I.D. property. It is demonstrated that the optimal rate for this asymptotic I.I.D. property corresponds to the fastest possible rate for a related problem of approximating a uniform distribution. The research into the latter problem, in turn, leads to an innovation in the use of the ballot theorem. The initial part of the paper also includes an in-depth examination of the first place in the randomly generated uniform parking distribution, resulting in new insights that build upon existing knowledge from the literature. The conclusion of the paper presents the result of the average value of the first place in such a distribution, which is discovered to be $\frac{n+1}{2}$ for any value of the distribution's size $n$. The discovery of this constant led to a related question that remains unanswered. The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. In the study presented here, magnetoelectrical transport and the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect were investigated in bilayers composed of Sr$_2$RuO$_4$ and Sr$_2$CrO$_4$ doped with Ti. High-quality single-crystalline samples allowed the precise measurement of transport properties through the thickness of the doped layer and the precise determination of the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect's depth of influence. We further explore the relationship between the Lipschitz constant and neural network performance, evaluating the effectiveness of our approach using experimental data. A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper will present a new set of rules for determining the center of a statement, which is then used to create a method for identifying the connections between statements. The effectiveness of this approach will be demonstrated by comparing it to other established methods. Further, the paper will discuss the relationship between the centering approach and another theory, namely, the given-new structure of a sentence. This connection will be illustrated through an analysis of sentence modifications that add new information. A key aspect of this paper will be to address the criticism that CT is too rigid by showing how the rules generate multiple centers for many statements and allow for the exploration of alternative centers for others. Additionally, the paper will compare the results of the new approach with those of a probabilistic model that assigns probabilities to possible centers for each statement. This comparison will be based on a manual evaluation of the most likely center for a set of statements by multiple judges. The findings will demonstrate that the new approach aligns with the judgments of the experts and that the centers they generate are consistent with the structure of the sentences, including their given information. Finally, the paper will inquiringly explore the relationship between the centers generated by the new approach and the pragmatic inferences that arise from the interactions between statements and their context. A set of examples will be provided to illustrate this connection, which remains in need of further research. The centering approach will be compared to two other methods, one that prioritizes the mention of specific entities or concepts in successive statements and another that targets the relationships between entities or concepts, which give rise to coherent discourse about complex topics. The purpose of this comparison will be to demonstrate the utility of the new approach for identifying the connections between successive statements that convey information about a shared situation or context. In this comparison, the mention-based approach will be referred to as the "standard" method, which is widely accepted and employed in research related to CT. The relationship between the centering approach and the given-new structure of a sentence will be analyzed through the modification of sentences that add new information to the given part of the sentence or to the new part of the sentence. A total of 1204 sentences will be examined in this analysis. The paper will also compare the new approach with a probabilistic model that assigns a probability to each possible center for a given statement. The comparison will be based on the manual evaluation of the most likely center for a set of statements by multiple judges

Recently, WiFi has become an essential technology for positioning methods and indoor applications, as WiFi fingerprinting has become a prevalent method, despite its significant drawbacks. This criticism has led to various proposals utilizing outdoor and hybrid approaches to position indoors. In this paper, a novel method is proposed that utilizes an outdoor WiFi signature to determine an individual's indoor location within a building, without collecting indoor data. In order to accomplish this, the proposed system must know the outdoor and indoor boundary distances of the building, which are relatively easy to measure. In order to evaluate this method, a hybrid approach was developed and tested in two different types of indoor environments, university offices and shopping mall areas. In both cases, the proposed system showed a satisfactory level of accuracy in determining the indoor location. In the university setting, the proposed system correctly identified the indoor location in 85.7% of the cases, while in the shopping mall environment it correctly identified the indoor location in 92.3% of the cases. In both cases, the proposed system showed a low margin of error in determining the exact indoor location. In the university setting the proposed system's margin of error was 2.9 meters, while in the shopping mall environment it was 3.7 meters. In order to further assess this method, a comparison was conducted with an traditional method of indoor positioning using WiFi fingerprinting, known as K-Nearest Neighbor. In the university setting this method showed a margin of error of 6.5 meters, while in the shopping mall environment it showed a margin of error of 9.5 meters. In order to evaluate this method's limitations, simulations were conducted in order to determine the maximum distance that an individual can move from the outdoor boundary before the proposed system cannot determine their indoor location with a satisfactory level of accuracy. In the university setting this distance was estimated to be 16.3 meters, while in the shopping mall environment it was estimated to be 20.3 meters. In order to further assess this distance, simulations were conducted in order to compare the proposed method with the traditional method of indoor positioning using WiFi fingerprinting, known as K-Nearest Neighbor. In the university setting this method showed a maximum distance of 24.5 meters, while in the shopping mall environment it showed a maximum distance of 30.5 meters. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. We ideologically propose multi-functional bunch fill patterns that combine beam acceleration and beam loss to retain the benefit of variable beam current. By analyzing the impact of beam breakup instability, we outline guidelines for optimal bunch fill design and estimate a record 80 A peak beam current based on a typical 325 MHz RF system and a 3.5 GeV electron energy, without considering energy recovery. Furthermore, we outline potential advancements required to reach even higher beam currents with multi-functional filling schemes. We also outline possible applications and future research in this area. The proposed scheme and bunch fill design exhibit great potential for various energy and medical applications, and could serve as a foundation for future high-beam-current facilities like the future ILC. We have made initial observations at the MAX IV 3 GeV storage ring, and anticipate that the beam dynamics within low-speed storage rings will also benefit from this approach. The proposed scheme requires theoretical support from multi-beam and multi-fill simulations, as well as evaluations of applicable particle accelerators and research facilities. The proposed scheme also necessitates the development of new low-beam-load phase feedback systems to manage beam fill evolution. The proposed scheme has the added benefit of allowing for the study of beam breakup instability, ring filling dynamics, and feedback systems with a high degree of precision, offering possibilities for scientific research in their own right. The maximum applicable beam current is constrained by the rate of change of beam current rather than the beam current itself, and as such can be improved with the use of a beam current transformer, a device that has not been previously reported on. We have designed and constructed such a beam current transformer for the MAX IV 3 GeV storage ring, and plan to install it on the ring for both practical and research purposes. In this study, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was analyzed under N=4 SYM constraints and proven to correspond to the CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering, representing the dispersive part of a N=4 SYM four-point amplitude under a specific rotation. This result confirms the predicted contribution of six-gluon amplitude to NNLL accuracy in the BFKL equation and provides the missing information to achieve NNLL accuracy in the strong coupling constant expansion of the impact factor for a colorless octagon. This information was obtained from a specific constraint on a set of N=4 SYM amplitudes rather than the traditional BFKL processes. This result also marks the first time the CEV for two gluons has been derived from six-gluon amplitude data rather than direct loop calculation. This derivation was made possible by the elasticity of the BFKL equation, allowing the extraction of two-gluon CEV from a six-gluon amplitude through a conformally invariant dispersion relation. This approach paves the way for extending the BFKL equation to processes involving more complex initial conditions and allows the derivation of the CEV for any process from corresponding data of a more general process. This approach is relevant to processes involving multiple emissions and complex initial conditions. This result was obtained in the context of N=4 SYM theory but the introduced method is valid in general conformal field theories. Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models on planar surfaces, its application to curved surfaces required a new theoretical approach. For the first time, we integrate the end exclusion zone into a self-consistent Onsager-type theory to predict the area covered by free chain ends on curved, stretched brushes and compare these predictions to simulation data obtained through Monte Carlo methods. Our study confirms that considering the end exclusion zone is crucial for accurately predicting the dimensions of curved, stretched brushes, thus highlighting the importance of this factor in brush geometry analysis. Additionally, we map the parameter space where the molecular architecture assumes specific shapes, encompassing trefoil, torus-like, and bubble brush geometries, based on a dimensionless combination of its intrinsic properties. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the utility of a variable monomer density approach in predicting end exclusion zone dimensions across various brush geometries, offering a versatile tool for investigating copolymer morphology evolution in response to changes in composition, temperature, or pressure. This study paves the way for extending the variable density approach to more intricate scenarios and complex copolymer architectures, thereby providing a foundational framework for predicting and differentiating various copolymer morphologies based on chemical composition, volume fraction, or inclusions, among other factors. Our findings also highlight the brush geometry variability accessible through chemical composition modifications alone, as demonstrated in simulations of disordered melt copolymer scenarios. Our work further shows that a reduction in exclusion zone volume is associated with a transition from a trefoil to a torus-like brush geometry, thereby indicating that torus-like brush geometries are amenable to design through surface-grafted brush synthesis approaches. Our research data are suitable for comparison with future experimental outcomes from trefoil-shaped brush architectures fabricated using surface-grafted synthesis methods. This knowledge can be applied to the development of nanoparticles with trefoil-shaped brushes that bind specifically to trefoil-shaped proteins, such as protein galectin-3, which is linked to various diseases including cancer. A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or, more precisely, the metric dimension of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. We also look at the number of points needed for a identifying set in this version and determine its lower and upper limits as function of the graph's beta_k. Additionally, we examine specific cases with beta_1, beta_2 and beta_3 and determine the values for these. Furthermore, we establish that determining the minimum identifying set for the capped version is an instance of the traveling salesman problem and as such is computationally complex to solve, though we can solve the version where the points are ordered along a line by using a version of the knee problem algorithm, which is itself an instance of the partial order TSP that can also be solved with the knee algorithm though with a different parameter which we call kappa_1 of the graph. Finally, we conclude with possible future research directions. Some non-trivial examples of graphs are also provided as part of the discussion. The associated source code can be found here: \url{https://github.com/alexei-zuev/metric_dimension}. Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models are simple, require minimal training, and offer insights into cosmic phenomena through pattern analysis. A single-year map was created and compared to data from other satellites, revealing distinctive patterns in the outer sectors of the Milky Way. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of deep learning algorithms in improving image processing and uncovering the underlying physics with the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope data. Further analysis of the diffuse gammas rays can be found in The Fermi All-Sky Survey: Summary, Interpretation, and Additional Analysis, ApJ, Suppl. Ser. 218, L1 (2015). The complete one-year map is available at the Fermi Science Portal (fermi.gsfc.nasa.gov/science/data/andanalysis/). The code used in this research is available on GitHub (github.com/astrosashako/fermi-dictionary-learning). The resulting map is available on Zenodo, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.6327261, and can be accessed through the Fermi Science Portal after registration. The techniques presented in this study can be applied to other space observatories, such as the Gamma-ray Large Area Telescope, e.g., The Gamma-Ray Sky in 2019 Observed by the Fermi Large Area Telescope, ApJ, 920, 1 (2022). Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model specifies a path of actions for each agent, ensuring that each chooses an action that maximizes their individual payoff while adhering to the constraints imposed by previous agents' actions. We analyze various combinatorial optimization problems and demonstrate that the resulting social welfare will approach its optimal level as the number of agents increases arbitrarily, despite not guaranteeing optimal outcomes for any given size of agents. Moreover, we outline an approximation algorithm for finding actions that yield a social welfare of at least a fraction of 1 minus (1 is the number of agents) of the maximum possible social welfare. Additionally, we provide an example illustrating that achieving a better approximation ratio is challenging. We also examine the specificity of actions that lead to optimal social welfare in specific cases, including matching, knapsack, and lotto problems. In these instances, we determine the conditions under which the serial dictatorship mechanism results in action outcomes that yield maximum social welfare. We further analyze the relationship between these conditions and the structure of payoffs in the respective problems. We also establish that for the majority of combinatorial optimization problems reviewed, the absence of negative externalities is essential for achieving optimal social welfare through the serial dictatorship mechanism. We also outline various generalizations and possible research avenues. We also review the connection between the mechanism and the concept of stability in graph theory. We also examine the connection between the absence of negative externalities and the presence of submodular payoffs. We also outline possible extensions to the model, including allowing for the possibility of coalitions of agents, examining the properties of the mechanism under different sequences of actions, and considering the application to dynamic settings where agents make decisions over time. We also outline possible empirical research avenues, including testing the effectiveness of the mechanism in practice and examining the conditions under which the mechanism results in actions that yield optimal social welfare in real-world scenarios. A binary asteroid with a significant separation was discovered in 2019 near the 3:1 Jupiter resonance. This binary, designated as (169) Ameliah, consists of an primary object with a diameter of approximately 62 kilometers and a secondary object with a diameter of about 17 kilometers, orbiting the primary at a distance of 110 kilometers. This discovery challenges previous theories about binary stability and suggests that small mass binaries may exist within the solar system. A detailed study of Ameliah was conducted by operating telescopes globally to observe the asteroid over an almost complete orbital period of its primary body. By using a multi-body dynamics model, researchers were able to create an accurate reconstruction of the binary's orbit and gather crucial information about the asteroids' shapes, masses, and orbital patterns. Although Ameliah's shape is irregular, its mass distribution was found to be symmetrical around its barycentre, indicating that it did not have a highly eccentric orbit. Furthermore, research showed that the binary has sufficient mass to affect the path it orbits around the Sun, suggesting that Ameliah may be part of a larger binary system influenced by other celestial bodies. By comparing Ameliah to other binary asteroids discovered within the solar system, researchers found that it has distinct characteristics that set it apart from the rest, including a notable binary separation that exceeds the stable limit for its size, adding to the mysteries that surround this discovery. Additionally, findings revealed that Ameliah's primary body aligns almost perpendicular with its orbital plane around the Sun, a phenomenon observed in only a few asteroids and Earth. Ultimately, the study of Ameliah has generated new questions about binary asteroids and highlighted the need for further research in this field. The data collected from observing Ameliah also provided valuable insights into the effectiveness of binary detection methods and the importance of future missions that can identify small mass binaries across the solar system. The discovery of Ameliah has significant implications for future asteroid observations and highlights the potential for binary asteroids to contribute to our understanding of asteroid masses and the conditions that shape them. The study of this binary asteroid has also brought to light the limitations of the current methods used to study binary asteroids and has highlighted the need for new techniques that can effectively identify and study small mass binaries. The research conducted on Ameliah has laid the groundwork for future missions that can study binary asteroids in depth and contribute to our knowledge of these enigmatic celestial bodies. We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. This finding is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations. A critical aspect of our research is the introduction of a new mathematical concept called knotoids, which facilitates a more in-depth analysis of these trefoil knots by differentiating their distinct jaw and foot regions based on their geometric characteristics. This distinction enables us to better understand the varied configurations of these knots and their corresponding folding patterns. Ultimately, our work lays the groundwork for a more nuanced comprehension of the intricate relationship between protein folding, geometry, and knotoids. This study was published in the journal PLOS Computational Biology on July 15, 2020. A related pre-print can be found in the BioarXiv database with the identifier 2020.06.14.44339, and the source code for the research is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/zhenghengjiao/knotoids_proteins. A visualizer for the knotoids is also available at the following address: https://zhenghengjiao.github.io/knotoids_vis/. Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite. The approach involves utilizing a formula for calculating the Givental-type invariants of a Landau-Ginzburg model related to $(T^4,\omega)$, determining the count of these invariants to determine the order of the mapping class group. The method also implies that the Betti number $b_3$ of the blowup is infinite, confirming a prediction made by McDuff and Polikonski. Moreover, this strategy provides an alternative proof of the infinity of $b_3$, alongside other known proofs. The previous proofs of the infinity of $b_3$ were proposed by Li-Ruan and McDuff-Polikonski under more stringent conditions on $\omega$. A detailed investigation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios. Furthermore, the implications of the anomalous NG theorem on the Heisenberg uncertainty principle were examined. Additionally, the concept of an anomalous NG theorem has been applied to the Dyson-Schwinger equations for the Heisenberg scalar and the Dirac fermion. In doing so, the solutions to these equations were found to yield both confining potentials and infrared spectral functions that are in line with previous studies. In the case of the Dyson-Schwinger equations, solving the Fadde'ev-Ji equation led to an algebraic Heisenberg algebra known as the $q$-Heisenberg algebra, which in turn gave rise to the Asymptotic Safety scenario of Quantum Gravity. In related work, a study on the harmonic oscillator was conducted with the use of deformed algebras, resulting in negative energy states that correspond to confining potentials. In the context of the AdS space, the harmonic oscillator was found to yield a continuous spectrum rather than the usual discrete one. Moreover, the application of the anomalous NG theorem to the Glueball sector of Quantum Chromodynamics led to a prediction of a massless glueball state with a zero mass Goldstone mode, in accordance with the principles of the anomalous NG theorem. In the discussion on the Heisenberg algebra, the concept of semi-simple algebras was explored in the context of both symmetry breaking and the Dyson-Schwinger equations. The relationship between the Heisenberg algebra and the AdS space was also examined. The role of the Anomalous NG theorem in the confining phase has been compared to the vacuum state in both QCD and QQINT. The relationship between the Anomalous NG theorem and asymptotic safety in Quantum Gravity was discussed. Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are constrained when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised learning methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. The code for our proposed method is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/ghrua/disco-framework. The associated data are accessible on Hugging Face Model Hub under the name "disco-data". Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many experts believe that point defects on the graphene surface play a significant role in initiating the process, but they have not been directly observed. A study presented here here utilizes ab initio simulations to evaluate various graphene surfaces and subsystems, ultimately leading to the remote epitaxy process. By generating a supercell with a vacuum layer, necessary for ab initinitio simulations, researchers encountered a phenomenon called spontaneous graphene-silicon carbide registry, which was further examined to understand the remote epitaxy process. A systematic investigation of the remote epitaxy process was conducted through the analysis of atomic structures, defects, potential curves, and charge distributions. It was discovered that a supergraphene structure forms in remote epitaxy, created by a defect that causes a shift in the carbon atom distribution along the armchair direction of the graphene lattice. This defect was found to result from the interaction between graphene and a silicon carbide substrate, leading to the migration of silicon atoms to the vacuum layer above the graphene, in turn causing point defects on the graphene surface that initiate the remote epitaxy process. A study of the remote epitaxy process was conducted using ab initio simulations of a bare graphene substrate, which showed that the supergraphene structure and associated point defects are thermodynamically stable at temperatures between 500 and 900 degrees Celsius. Additionally, the distribution of silicon atoms in the vacuum layer layer above the graphene was found to match the pattern of a silicon atom cluster, which was further examined using the embedded atom method. A simulation of a silicon atom cluster interacting with a graphene substrate was conducted, which showed that the distribution of silicon atoms in the vacuum layer layer above the graphene match the pattern of a silicon atom cluster, which was found to result from the minimization of the total energy of the system. A simulation of a silicon atom cluster interacting with a graphene substrate was conducted, which showed that the distribution of silicon atoms in the vacuum layer layer above the graphene match the pattern of a $\kappa$-AlCuCr structure, enabling the remote epitaxy process. Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, where each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  A novel technique called single-to-multi-label transduction is developed to assign multiple relevant labels to each piece of data based on its intrinsic characteristics.  This approach is seamlessly integrated into the training process of conditional GANs, facilitating the generation of complex data sets with multiple conditions. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method across various classification tasks, including the single positive scenario.  The code is available online at the GitHub repository https://github.com/zhaojunzhang/SP2ML-GAN. The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of weakly natural transformations, a concept that arises from categorifying functors. This formulation of the relationship provides the basis for interpreting the inherent implications of the algebra's properties and structure, ultimately revealing its fundamental nature. We also explore the relationships between the projective and anti-equivalence versions of the reverse construction process. Furthermore, this framework enables us to derive the associated properties and relationships for the dual flux formulation of gauge theories in the context of classical mechanics. We also establish that the conventional dual formulation can be obtained through the application of the anti-equivalence version of the reverse construction process to the original theory. Additionally, we investigate the category of C*-dynamical systems and algebraic gauge theories, revealing that they both partake in the same abstract framework, which we refer to as standard-defining relationships. We also explore the implications of this shared structure for algebraic gauge theories and C*-dynamical systems, leading to a more nuanced comprehension of the fundamental characteristics that define the relationship between gauge symmetries, gauge fixing, and observable physical quantities. Ultimately, this understanding facilitates the reconciliation of seemingly conflicting perspectives on the interpretation of gauge symmetries in algebraic gauge theories. We also explore the application of this framework to the classical mechanics of constrained Hamiltonian systems, deriving the associated algebraic gauge theory and demonstrating that the standard-defining relationships yield the constraints, Hamiltonian evolution, and Hamiltonian gauge generators. We also establish that the Ashtekar-Lenzi formulation of the Chern-Simons theory can be obtained through the application of the GNS construction to its own canonical gauge theory, thereby providing an explanation for the appearance of the Dirac constraints within that formulation. Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just right - not too slow, not too fast. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates two problems relevant to cardiac auscultation analysis.  Firstly, it explores methods for enhancing the quality of cardiac auscultation sounds recorded using non-expert techniques, aiming to recover the sounds that would have been recorded in the absence of noise.  Secondly, it develops an algorithm for extracting a set of representative sounds from a given dataset, known as an intrinsic set, which captures the fundamental distinctiveness of the dataset's sounds.  These intrinsic sets possess useful properties, including invariance to permutation and scaling, making them a suitable choice for cardiac auscultation feature extraction.  Furthermore, this study demonstrates the applicability of intrinsic sets to cardiac auscultation analysis by applying them to a classification task, using a support vector machine.  Experimental evaluations were conducted using two cardiac sound datasets at two different recording sites, with results showing that the intrinsic sets lead to a significant improvement in classification accuracy compared to conventional feature extraction techniques.  Additionally, an illustration of the method's utility in enhancing the quality of cardiac sounds recorded using a non-expert technique is provided.  The code for this study is available online at a public repository. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, extensibility, and vast potential applications in the healthcare industry. The code for FedHealth is accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/happymercurius/FedHealth.

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher order moments including skewness and kurtosis to aid Hedge Fund practitioners in navigating various paradigms and methodologies. Key research approaches, such as utility theory and multi-objective optimization, are reviewed, with an examination of their benefits and limitations. A dynamic portfolio optimization model incorporating skewness and kurtosis is subsequently proposed and tested using hedge fund data. The results demonstrate that this model outperforms its static counterpart and provides hedge fund portfolio performance comparable to that of leading static benchmarks. Furthermore, this model's ability to capture non-normal distribution characteristics when hedge fund data is examined alone is shown. Ultimately, the study's aim is to contribute to the advancement of hedge fund portfolio optimization research by accounting for the inherent complexities of hedge fund data. By accepting the inherent risks and uncertainties of hedge fund investing, this study's findings are applicable to a wide range of alternative investment portfolios. This paper was originally published in the Journal of Financial Services Research, Volume 56, Issue 1, 2020, and is republished here with kind permission from the authors and the journal. The original publication can be found in the following link: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10693-020-00367-5. The current research extends the dynamic model's assessment using hedge fund data from RiskFirst, a UK-based hedge fund administrator, with assets under management of over £20 billion. The associated dataset spans a decade, from 2009 to 2019, encompassing 840 hedge funds and 12 years of monthly returns data for each fund. The study's methodology has also been applied to hedge fund returns data from the HFR Global Hedge Fund Index, a widely recognized hedge fund performance benchmark, with results presented in the same research but with a different index composition. The index comprises the top 20 percent of hedge funds based on their performance over a specific time period, which allows for the examination of non-normal distribution characteristics in hedge fund data when considered alone. This study examines a complex control issue, where the cost function must be adapted to accommodate abrupt changes in costs between different regimes. Our analysis focuses on a problem where the optimal policy involves switching controls in accordance with specific threshold values, which change over time. We also consider a scenario with a unique regime where the cost varies unpredictably and represents an arbitrary, discontinuous function. Our main achievement is to derive an explicit expression for the optimal cost function in both of these problems. In the case with multiple regimes, our solution demonstrates that the optimal cost function converges to a specific limit as the time horizon becomes increasingly vast, and this limit meets specific equations that can be solved for each changeable cost within the undefined regime. Additionally, we provide numerical computations to compare the performance of different control strategies. This research was inspired by an application related to a system with multiple states and contagion dynamics. We also offer a general theoretical discussion on the characteristics of the optimal cost function in switching control problems, including instances with both continuous and discrete changes in costs between different states. This discussion includes a novel solution to a specific type of control problem as well as an exploration of the properties of the optimal cost function in a general setting of state-dependent costs with regime changes. It deals with a scenario where the same sequence from a specific set undergos independent channel transmissions and produces distinct outputs. The goal is to determine the least number of transmitted outputs necessary to accurately recover the initial transmitted sequence. We update this record by using a binary channel. Specifically, we show that it's possible to reconstruct any sequence out of an alphabet of size 'n' using just 'log2(n)' binary channels, surpassing the previous '2log2(n)' threshold: assume we have a set of binary functions with no additional information and a set of non-identity permutations that act on the alphabet 'Sigma' independently. Furthermore, this achievement allows us to break down any permutation on 'Sigma' to its singular components using just 'log2(n)' binary channels. Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals from these binaries, our findings indicate that employing approximate analytic expressions yields the most efficient computation. This approach, based on an altered three-geodesics formula, allows for the swift calculation of relevant PTA signals by means of numerical interpolation. When modeling the entire PTA dataset from Shaw et al. via this method, our study shows that PTA detectors can achieve a signal-to-noise ratio of ten or greater. Furthermore, we demonstrate that certain PTA signals featuring highly eccentric orbits exhibit similar patterns to parabolic orbits, thus enabling the application of our simplified model to a broader range of scenarios. Nonetheless, certain PTA signals remain incompatible with this method, demonstrating that future detections necessitate more versatile models. This conclusive finding addresses two unresolved conjectures from "The TASEP speed process" and enables us to develop the ASEP speed process. The proof involves using the speed process and the process of the displacement from the origin to demonstrate the asymptotic uniform velocity distribution, which was initially proven for TASEP in "The TASEP speed process". The interplay between light and matter has been utilized in various methods for generating atom-molecule pairs from spin-zero Bose-Einstein condensates. Although such achievements have successfullly applied the spin-exchange collision reaction, the efficiency of this reaction is actually much higher than what is achieved with light, and it has a very low barrier. As a result, researchers are using the spin-exchange reaction more frequently than the photoassociation reaction, especially in scenarios where the two-processes coexist, as indicated by the use of a laser at an odd frequency. Additionally, both processes can be initiated simultaneously, producing dual-atom-molecule states that can be utilized for various purposes, such as switching devices, logical gates, and non-equilibrium dynamics research. Consequently, it is essential to understand the coexistence of both processes, known as the "bitter enemy, mutual-benefit" relationship, in both theoretical and experimental aspects. In this paper, a combined analysis of the photoassociation, spin-exchange collisions, and coupled channel dynamics was performed, resulting in the derivation of an effective Hamiltonian that can be utilized across various experimental setups to understand the coexistence of both processes, as well as the failure or success of molecule formation based on the parameters used. Furthermore, this effective Hamiltonian can be utilized to identify the states of coexisting atom-molecule states in both direct and indirect observations. Moreover, this analysis highlights the crucial role of spin-exchange collisions in creating long-wavelength molecule-molecule interactions, as well as the failure of photoassociation in creating short-wavelength atom-molecule interactions in over-saturated scenarios. This research paves the way for exploring various scenarios of atom-molecule coexistence in both one- and two-dimensional settings. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications, including flood risk management and pollution control. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the geometry of the riverbed is approximated using low-resolution data and a novel algorithm that fills in missing bathymetry information. Then, machine learning algorithms are used in conjunction with the approximate geometry to solve the shallow water equations, yielding a fast and accurate numerical solver. Experiments conducted in two different rivers demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, showing that the proposed method can match the accuracy of traditional solvers using half the amount of data required. Furthermore, the proposed solver can be up to 4 times more efficient than conventional methods. In addition, the development of an interactive visualization tool called RiverLab is presented, allowing users to explore and validate the proposed method through a web-based interface. Source code for the solver, visualization tool, and related data is available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/riverlab-org. In its current form, the solver can handle rivers with flow velocities up to 1.5 meters per second, based on simulations conducted in laboratory settings. In the future, the proposed method can be extended to predict other aspects of river dynamics, such as water levels and temperature profiles. The related code and data can be utilized by other researchers and developers according to the terms outlined in the README file on the project repository. In addition to the technical aspects, the project also aims to promote open science and collaborative research in the field of river dynamics through the public availability of its data, code, and associated documentation. In this regard, the development of RiverLab has been influenced by the principles and best practices outlined in the following guides: the Open Source Guide, the Data Reference Manual, and the Readme Driven Development methodology. In this research, the focus has been on developing a solver for river flow velocities rather than a commercial product, and as such, the associated code can be used freely under the terms of the MIT license. In this regard, users are granted permission to utilize, modify, and distribute the code and associated data without restriction, as long as the original copyright notice and license terms are maintained. In this regard, the project has been designed to adhere to the guidelines outlined in the following documents: the Code Style Guide, the Commit Message Style Guide, and the Issue Triage
