Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continuous learning scenarios. In this thesis, we delve into two prominent open-world problems: robotic task learning and game level learning. In robotic task learning, our primary objective is to enable a single robot to master multiple tasks and learn from experience encountered on the job. In game level learning, we aim to empower a game agent to adapt to an infinite number of unknown levels, based on limited training in a tiny subset of levels similar to the types it will encounter in the wild. To tackle these challenges, we developed two novel reinforcement learning frameworks. The first framework, codenamed TADQL, leverages a unique combination of intrinsic and extrinsic motivation to encourage exploration and learning about new tasks. It also employs a distinct neural memory module to combine insights from both the intrinsic and extrinsic components. The second framework, known as LevelNet, utilizes a hierarchical neural network structure to differentiate between general level knowledge and specific instance-level data. Additionally, it incorporates a novel form of intrinsic motivation called intrinsic hierarchy learning to facilitate discovery of new level characteristics. Our experimental results demonstrate notable improvements in performance across both robotic task learning and game level learning, as well as the validity of our model's internal hypotheses through reverse design tests. In conclusion, our innovative approaches to addressing two critical open-world problems have been successfully tested and show considerable promise for further exploration. Our approach develops an algorithm to identify processes from event flows, represented as Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs, providing temporal process data and subsequently declarative process models. To explore this question, we examined a sample of 22 star-forming main sequence galaxies with central stellar masses greater than ten times that of the Milky Way, drawn from the z=0.87 observed galaxy population with extensive data. This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content of news headlines using both few-shot and zero-shot learning
techniques. The primary objective is to categorize Croatian news headlines as
positive, negative, or neutral in relation to selected COVID-19 policy
measurements. A multi-class sentiment analysis model is developed and tested
using a small dataset of translated Croatian headlines. The model's effectiveness
is further assessed using both English and Croatian headlines, showcasing its
ability to adapt across languages. The findings indicate that the model excels in
zero-shot learning scenarios but requires significant improvements in addressing
linguistic nuances. The research also delves into a political trust theory to
better comprehend the underlying sentiments associated with selected COVID-19
policies. The analysis uncovers distinct sentiment patterns based on different
social group affiliations and highlights the model's limitations in accounting
for these variations. The study recommends further development of the model to
enhance its linguistic flexibility and encourage policymakers to prioritize
building trust with their constituents. The sentiment analysis model proves
particularly valuable in examining the emotional impact of policies on specific
social groups, uncovering in the current study the varying levels of positive
or negative sentiment associated with different policy measurements among
Croats, further highlighting the significance of considering the underlying
social identity of the population being studied. The research presented in this
paper is part of a larger project examining policy attitudes and trust in
institutions among Croatian citizens during the COVID-19 pandemic as well as
post-conflict social dynamics in Croatia. The data collected comprises 720
online news headlines and 1,920 survey responses. The research was conducted
between 2020 and 2022 in Croatia. The primary policy measurements examined in
the study pertain to health measures, economic support, and border controls
implemented during the pandemic, making the findings relevant to ongoing
pandemic research as well as post-conflict policy analysis in Croatia. The
sentiment analysis model used in the study can be applied across languages and
formats, making it a valuable tool for tracking media discourse and public
opinions worldwide. The research presented in this paper was supported by a grant
from the Croatian Science Foundation within the project no. PRZ-PR-2017-4-1068. X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that highlight the most important image details contributing to admission decisions. By applying this method to six public datasets consisting of over 7,500 COVID-19 images, previously unseen datasets consisting of 1,500 training and 1,500 testing images were created. Interestingly, the features most critical for predicting ICU admission are not always the most visually apparent lung abnormalities. Furthermore, machine learning models trained on these features demonstrate strong predictive performance on unseen data, surpassing the effectiveness of several comparative models. Lastly, the proposed framework is shown to facilitate interpretable predictions by highlighting the specific image regions influencing model decisions. To facilitate reproducibility and advance research in feature extraction from medical images, the proposed method and associated datasets are made publicly available. With potential applications in various clinical scenarios beyond COVID-19, the proposed framework provides a versatile tool capable of enhancing the understanding of medical images by highlighting the most relevant features for specific patient outcomes. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, the relationship classification head encounters a class imbalance issue due to the massive number of background classes. To address this imbalance, the authors propose Balanced Anchor Sampling, a technique that adapts anchor classes based on precision scores. This approach dynamically filters the most relevant anchor classes and reduces the effective number of classes, thereby improving the precision of the relationship classification. Experimental evaluations on the Visual Relationship Detection dataset demonstrate a significant precision boost of 10.4% for the standard Visual Relationship Detection task and 13.3% for the large-scale Visual Relationship Detection dataset. The proposed method also exhibits compelling performance on the human pose estimation task, achieving a 13.6% boost in precision. The code for this research has been made available open-source.

We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores with imbalanced stellar disks, specifically focusing on three notable galaxies: NGC 4594, NGC 2681, and NGC 812. These galaxies exhibit significantly slowed star formation, and we set out to determine the key factor responsible for this inhibition. Both galaxies with balanced and unbalanced disk structures typically experience star formation suppression due to central black holes. However, we discovered that the lopsided disk feature itself is sufficient to impede star formation, likely as a result of the disks absorbing and distributing the energy from stellar encounters, thereby reducing their mass density and the likelihood of star-forming mergers. Additionally, these lopsided galaxies often host massive dark matter halos that can prevent minor mergers and starbursts, further contributing to their low mass density and continued inaction. Ultimately, we found that their core characteristics are more closely related to the properties of their dark matter halos than their actual disk masses. We propose a revised hypothesis: even massive galaxies with balanced disk structures will experience suppressed star formation if their dark matter halos are extensive enough, similar to the galaxies we studied with lopsided disks. We've developed a simplified model that successfully replicates the core mass relation observed in a balanced galaxy population, and it suggests that dark matter halos exert a linear influence on core mass while the effect of the disk is offset. We've also discovered that the distribution of mass fractions within the cores of galaxies are remarkably similar, regardless of their mass or assembly time, and we believe this pattern holds significant analytical value on its own. We've dubbed this distinctive distribution the 'Core Mass Profile'. We've further analyzed the unique characteristics of the three individual galaxies. NGC 4594 exhibits a distinct Tidal Tilted Disk feature, characterized by a nearly edge-to-edge misalignment between its central bulge and the plane of its disk. NGC 2681 displays a prominent dust lane that starts in the core but quickly gives way to an evenly spread disk. NGC 812, on the other hand, shows a more ambiguous case of disk asymmetry but is distinguished by extremely low levels of both starburst and AGN activity for a galaxy of its mass. We've explored possible explanations for the Tidal Tilted Disk phenomenon, including major mergers, minor mergers, interaction with companion galaxies, satellite galaxies, tidal tails, gas accretion, and the Tidal Tilted Disk feature itself. Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to defy scalings of this quantum phenomenon in the solid-state. Investigating electron-spin interactions in silicon is crucial, as it enables us to explore quantum tunneling effects within a quantum solid while minimizing Coulomb interactions. However, accurately measuring the distribution of individual phosphorus dopants is necessary to determine the precise location of electrons and thus determine the effective quantum tunneling distance. A study has been conducted using scanning tunneling microscopy and coherent quantum interference phenomena observed in a silicon surface. It allows for mapping the distribution of individual phosphorus dopants and directly measures the distribution of electrons in silicon crystal lattice. By knowing the precise location of electrons and their corresponding tunneling patterns, researchers can better understand the interplay between quantum tunneling, Coulomb interactions, and electron distribution. Furthermore, this knowledge can aid in the development of robust and noise-immune superconducting quantum processors. Moreover, this discovery paves the way for studying zero-point fluctuations in silicon, which can provide a direct comparison with theoretical predictions. Ultimately, this work shows that electron distribution can be precisely controlled in silicon by employing coherent quantum interference and tuning the distance between dopants. Consequently, this discovery can lead to a significant improvement in the robustness and efficiency of quantum processors powered by zero-point fluctuations in silicon. Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Recent advancements in graph neural networks have made it possible to replicate these intricate patterns of interaction through learning-based methods. This study aims to achieve a full understanding of graph neural networks by inspecting their internal functioning and comparing them to the fundamental principles of complex dynamics. By viewing networks and functions as interconnected entities within a unified framework known as the network function dynamics diagram, this study provides a clear, general mechanism for reconstructing the underlying architecture of networks from observed data and function relationships. This approach is accompanied by a specific instance of network architecture reversal applied to a case study of a brain region that exhibits highly intricate connectivity. This study demonstrates a versatile methodology for exploring the relationship between the internal functioning of graph neural networks and the underlying architecture of the systems they replicate. This relationship holds particular significance for neuroscience given the frequent occurrence of looped dynamics in brain networks. This leads to a promising line of inquiry: what information about the structure of a network can be gleaned from the observed dynamics when the network operates in a stochastic, noisy environment. This question is further explored using a combination of numerical data and a synthetic neural network consisting of a hundred neurons with varying connection patterns, and is illustrated to be effective at recovering precise details of a network architecture even in the presence of significant noise. We also establish a connection between these counts and the coefficients in the expansion of certain symmetric functions, ultimately deriving formulas for average values and standard congruence properties. Building on the work of Guy, we use these formulas to prove an unbounded increase in the gap between consecutive prime numbers in the infinite sequence defined by $P_n - p_{f(n)}$, where $P_n$ represents the $n$th prime number, and $f(n)$ is a function that, for a given set of initial values, maps the natural numbers to their respective prime indices. We also demonstrate the existence of an infinite number of pairs of natural numbers, $(a,b)$, for which the difference $a\cdot b$ exhibits an infinitely great ratio of gaps, and for which both $a$ and $b$ are products of an identical number of distinct prime factors. Furthermore, we show that the difference between the largest and smallest of an infinite sequence of prime numbers, proportional to the index of these primes, also exhibits an infinitely great ratio. A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which involves accurately defining the treated region. Although this task has become more efficient with the help of stereotactic electrophysiological data and imaging, accurately defining the area treated during LITT procedure remains a challenge. A novel approach is proposed to address this issue by using a type of machine learning called Gaussian Mixture Models to map the temperature distribution created during the LITT procedure to a probability map of the treated area, and then uses this map to define the area treated. Evaluating this approach on data from seven epilepsy patients shows that it can efficiently determine the area treated with less dependence on expert opinion compared to other methods used in research, and produces comparable results to more complex machine learning methods while being more computationally efficient. Furthermore, this approach can forecast the shape of the treated area with sufficient accuracy to be applicable in surgical procedures guided by real-time feedback, and even accurately predicts the development of new brain lesions in four out of seven patients studied. In summary, this research presents a practical solution for predicting the outcome of LITT procedure, which can be employed in a variety of applications including guiding the procedure in real-time, predicting the outcome for individual patients, and conducting theoretical research on the relationship between the geometry of the brain and the procedure for a specific medical condition called temporal lobe epilepsy. GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. We further developed three specific methods: an unsupervised contrastive learning technique and two supervised contrastive learning approaches. Our framework's applicability across various applications is demonstrated by incorporating it into deep neural networks and conducting experiments on five different datasets. Experimentation confirms the framework's efficacy in reducing data dimensionality while preserving classification performance. We establish an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into two distinct orbits while exhibiting quasiprimativity on just one orbit, specifically within a class of twisted wreath structures. Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples classified under the star normal quotient twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs. Furthermore, our contributions update the record of twisted wreath structures with multiple distinct orbits that exhibit quasiprimativity. The twisted wreath structures in this category include twisted wreath structures with a single non-trivial quasiprimitive orbit described as P$\Delta$-actions on infinite set partitions, as well as a infinite generation of twisted wreath structures characterized by multiple quasiprimitive orbits described as O$_n$-actions on ordered sequences of length n. The latter include an infinite number of twisted wreath structures for which there is no established name, while the former include an infinite number of twisted wreath structures for which there is no established name, theta and Permutation-like actions, and a collection known as Anti-regular twisted wreath structures. The latter include anti-regular twisted wreath structures, theta actions, and Permutation-like actions, often referred to as A, $\Theta$, and P actions respectively. The A, $\Theta$, and P actions were first introduced in a 2016 study by Giudici, Li, and Praeger who also established the classification of twisted wreath structures within the star normal quotient twisted wreath category as including all A, $\Theta$, and P actions with multiple quasiprimitive orbits. The contribution of our research is the addition of a collection known as Permutation actions on ordered sequences of infinite length, described as O$_\infty$-actions. The generation of the sequence is demonstrated to be crucial for our approach, as attempting to use a single finite length would result in a twisted wreath structure characterized as P$_n$-actions on ordered sequences of length n, for which there is no established name in the literature. The P$_n$-actions are, however, referred to in the twisted wreath structure subcategory known as diagonal normal quotient twisted wreath structures, as well as in the collection known as twisted wreath structures with a single quasiprimitive orbit described as D$\Delta$-actions on infinite set partitions. Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for continuous data, the Group Lasso often fails to produce sparse solutions for categorical features, especially when they're irrelevant. This study presents an algorithm called Generalized Category Lasso to achieve both model selection and sparse solutions when features have categorical definitions, building on the success of Group Lasso. By redefining the lasso penalty in a way that encourages category consolidation, the algorithm generates a interpretable model with a small number of consolidated categories for each feature. This is equivalent to assigning a small penalty to all but one category for each feature. This leads to a computational problem that combines category consolidation with automatic model selection through cross-validation, solvable using an interior point method. Experimental results show that GCL outperforms multiple comparisons, both in terms of accuracy and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, when compared to competing sparse models for categorical data. Additionally, GCL is applicable to high-dimensional data with only a slight increase in computational time when compared to lower-dimensional data. This is further illustrated by applying GCL to a real-world genomic cancer diagnosis problem. This is accompanied by a code repository for reproducibility purposes. This code is available on GitHub at this link https://github.com/ali-khassidoun/Generalized_Category_Lasso. Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the limitation of these models lies in their ability to leverage structured information effectively. We investigate how knowledge graphs, with their well-defined structure and precise relationships, can benefit the models. In comparison to using natural language sentences, we find that structured knowledge poses less ambiguity for the models and is more beneficial for their performance. Based on these findings, we introduce a simple approach to incorporate knowledge graphs, training the models on statements rather than sentences. The results show significant improvements in LAMA-based knowledge testing and vast gains in natural language inference, with effect sizes 1.4 times larger than the controls. The proposed method also demonstrates considerable success in generating correct logical forms from unstructured text, with an 8.5% increase in the exact match score over the baseline T5 model. In conclusion, infusing structured knowledge in the form of knowledge graphs into large language models proves to be a valuable resource with numerous applications, and our research serves as a starting point for further exploration. To improve the effectiveness of the dual-path RNN architecture in modeling lengthy sequences for speech separation, a modified version of the model has been proposed. Initially introduced in [1] to reduce computational requirements, the dual-path RNN was characterized by a short RNN that processed input sequences of any length and a lengthy RNN that handled only long sequences. The model's authors noted that the RNN components had different capabilities and suggested using them separately for tasks like speech separation, where the input is a sequence of varying lengths. However, [1] used the same RNN components without modification and didn't account for the distinct time scales present in the target sequences. Based on the principle of the Dual Path RNN described in [1], a revised model has been developed for speech separation, termed the Time Domain Dual Path RNN (TDDPRNN). The TDDPRNN consists of two RNNs with different time scales, one with a short time scale that repeats frequently and another with a long time scale that operates less often. The model includes separate RNN components for the encoder and decoder processes. Evaluations conducted using the wideband speech separation dataset demonstrated the TDDPRNN's effectiveness, as it achieved an average source signal-to-noise ratio (SSNR) of 27.9 dB, surpassing the Dual Path RNN's performance of 26.5 dB [1]. The proposed model also showed its potential for narrowband speech separation, as it was able to reconstruct wideband speech signals from the separated narrowband signals. The reconstruction process involved passing the narrowband speech signals through the decoder RNN component of the TDDPRNN, followed by post-processing. The results showed that the TDDPRNN could reconstruct a significant portion of the frequency band loss, as the average SSNR improvement was 2.4 dB. The proposed model has a potential application in scenarios like mobile data transmission, where the available bandwidth varies over time. The code for the TDDPRNN model has been made available online at [2]. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Furthermore, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. Additionally, we find that the shadow radius radius does not influence the heat capacity's sign change, yet it affects the heat capacity's peak value, in turn affecting the heat flux in a linear response model. Our research demonstrates that the shadow radius can serve as an external probe for investigating thermodynamic phase transitions in black holes. In doing so, this investigation validates previous findings made with Einstein-Maxwell-Dilaton gravity. In the EPYM case, we discover that the shadow radius reaches its critical point at the same temperature as the horizon radius. By the Einstein power law, this occurs at $\Gamma = 5/3$, confirming the results obtained with Einstein-Maxwell-Dilaton gravity. In the Einstein-Power-Yang-Mills scenario, we discover that the phase transition temperatures differ when considering either the shadow or horizon radius when $\Gamma$ equals either $3/2$ or $4$, respectively. In both instances, we observe that the phase transition is of the laser-enveloppe type, with the solid line representing the condition $d r_{s}/d T|_{H}=0$ when applying the definition from Bardeen et al.. In addition, we discover that the heat capacity curve's peak value shifts with the shadow radius, which affects the heat flux in a linear response model. In the process, we graph the heat capacity curve, the event horizon radius, the heat flux, and the temperature as functions of the dimensionless coupling constant in the Einstein-Power-Yang-Mills framework. Our research provides the phase diagram, heat capacity curve, and heat flux diagrams for nonlinear, charged AdS black holes within the EPYM gravity context. In doing so, we establish the connection between the shadow radius and an observable, heat capacity, which can be investigated externally without interfering with the black hole itself. Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field requires both complete knowledge of an infinite number of optical intensity and correlation measurements and a mathematical function that transforms the state, known as the inverse Radon transform. Unlike discrete-variable systems, the process of state reconstruction is tied to the use of the Wigner-Weyl transform, which, in an ideal scenario, allows a unique determination of the state from its optical tomogram. While the Wigner-Weyl transform provides an accurate solution for this problem, the inverse process, which gives the optical tomogram from the Wigner-Weyl transform, is not defined uniquely in the case of continuous-variable systems. A possible approach to resolve this ambiguity involves employing additional information about the state or a non-unique inverse transformation. On the other hand, a distinct approach is one that bypasses the use of the Wigner-Weyl transform by directly addressing the reconstruction of the state from its optical tomogram, without referencing the Wigner operator. In fact, such a state-reconstruction approach can be applied to both discrete and continuous-variable systems. In our work, we outline the procedure for state reconstruction through the use of the Radon transform inverse, which is applicable to both continuous- and discrete-variable systems, and we also outline the systems and scenarios for which this approach holds true, including any conditions on the state and the types of measurements used. Additionally, we outline the approach's connection to the Wigner-Weyl transform, which is only relevant for continuous-variable systems. Furthermore, we outline the approach's extensions to the reconstruction of multiple systems and scenarios, such as the reconstruction of joint states of continuous-variable systems and their coupling systems, as well as the reconstruction of continuous-variable systems from partial knowledge of the state. Moreover, we outline the approach's applications in the context of various experimental setups, such as the reconstruction of a state of one mode of light based on the measurement of another non-interacting mode of light, as well as the reconstruction of continuous-variable systems from partial or incomplete measurements. Finally, we outline the scope and limitations of this approach, as well as any necessary modifications required for the reconstruction of systems with unique invariant operators that are different from the Wigner-Weyl transform. On the other hand, for the case of discrete-variable systems, we outline the conditions under which the Wigner-Weyl transform becomes the unique invariant transform, as well as the conditions under which the Wigner-Weyl transform becomes the only invariant transform that is connected to the state reconstruction

However, these techniques faced a critical challenge as their algorithms generally necessitated a small bond dimension at sufficiently low temperatures or time points, despite a fundamental requirement for approximating thermal states and time-evolved systems where the bond dimension is directly related to system size. In our research, we introduced a novel application of a thermodynamic-like inequality to efficiently combine two nearby tensor network descriptions and acquired a precise understanding of the conditions under which the hybrid construction achieves significant improvements in reducing the bond dimension while maintaining high accuracy. Our findings were illustrated through sample approximations of locally equilibrium situations within the one-dimensional XXZ quantum ferromagnet. Additionally, we introduced a new class of geometrical decimation techniques tailored to solve a sample transfer problem where our results showed that in some cases, we could achieve a bond dimension that decreased polynomially with distance, in contrast to the exponential increase typically observed. Our developed methods and associated analysis were further showcased within the same XXZ quantum ferromagnet model. Our research demonstrated that through careful re-arrangement of the same set of local Hilbert spaces, we could derive a series of distinct approximations, each corresponding to a specific level of the nested Hilbert space structure, allowing us to tackle a variety of decimation-related problems within the context of local equilibrium situations. Ultimately, our novel approach provided a framework with which we could assess, compare and customize various tensor network descriptions and associated algorithms, based on a unified nested Hilbert space framework. This was further utilized to approximate a reference local equilibrium state, with results showing the effectiveness of our hybrid construction approach for reducing bond dimension. Furthermore, our developed framework and associated algorithms are highly versatile, with our code capable of being easily adapted for application to a wide range of other scenarios. Researchers are focusing on extremely thin alloys made of rare earth and transition metals, with controlled composition and unique magnetic properties, to create advanced photonic applications that operate rapidly. Despite the potential, it is very difficult to achieve small scale dimensions, which are essential for scaling down devices, while maintaining the necessary functionality and maintaining the unique magnetic properties. This study demonstrates a breakthrough by integrating minute amounts of ferrimagnetic alloys within a gold nanoarray to create a highly complex crystal that reacts differently to light and controlled magnetic fields, resulting in clear and adjustable features in the spectral patterns. This discovery enables the development of precise light-sensing tools and provides a foundation for innovative technology that could manipulate magnetic properties with light in rare earth and transition metal alloys. This approach can be further improved to include multiple elements and more sophisticated patterns, potentially leading to groundbreaking advancements in magnetophotonic technology. This discovery was made possible by using a precise technique called molecular beam epitaxy and a pre-curated alloy source to achieve unprecedented control over the composition and thickness of the alloys. This level of precision has not been previously achievable through other methods, allowing for an in-depth analysis of the interaction between light, magnetic fields and the alloys' unique properties at the atomic level. This knowledge can be applied to create more complex crystals with adjustable reactions to light and magnetic fields, opening up possibilities for innovative technology that could manipulate magnetic properties with light in rare earth and transition metal alloys. This study was conducted under the guidance of Xianghua Wu and Xingyu Gao, and co-first authors Hua Zhang and Xiang Zhang also contributed significantly to the research. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. By analysing the relationship between the network's inputs and its decisions, it's possible to determine the model's underlying distribution, which can then be used to train a more efficient model that matches the original's performance. Experimental evaluations on MNIST, ResNet-50, and MobileNet V2 demonstrate the effectiveness of this novel distillation approach. Source code is available at https://github.com/ghruen/b3kd-kd.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. We also compare our scheme with conventional PAC code decoding and sequential decoding, demonstrating comparable computation costs and significantly better error-correction performance. Furthermore, our proposed metric exhibits a linear relationship with computation computations, facilitating a simple trade-off between computation and error-correction performance. We validate our scheme using 1024-bit sequences and simulation results from the UCI Mobile Channel Simulator. We emphasize the low computational cost and error-free transmission priority in our scheme, which is particularly suitable for resource-constrained devices used in scenarios like Internet of Things. We also propose a progressive decoding strategy for larger sequences, which can be applicable to various PAC code decoders. In this strategy, the decoder first determines the number of computation reductions required to determine the sequence's correctness, then allocates the remaining computations to identify the exact error pattern. We anticipate our scheme to benefit a wide range of applications, including device testing and simulation scenarios with complex channel conditions, protocol testing with delayed feedback, and cybersecurity testing with embedded systems. Neural machine translation systems often require massive vocabularies, yet reinforcement learning can be less efficient due to the numerous out-of-vocabulary words that can delay training. Our research confirms that reducing the vocabulary has a positive impact on reinforcement learning, with a specific finding that limiting the range of translation targets can significantly improve performance. We developed a method to automatically categorize words into target types based on their frequencies in source and target texts, effectively creating a compressed vocabulary. Our approach achieved notable improvements in metrics for English-German translation tasks, surpassing the results of previous reinforcement learning methods even when using full vocabularies. Our findings also highlight the importance of intensional control over vocabulary constraints, demonstrating that restrained target types can lead to better translations when the reference texts describe common objects, whereas unrestricted target types yield better results when the references describe unusual objects. Our models and data are available for public use.

A rational number p/q represents the basis for a numbering system. Words composed of digits 0 through p-1 in base p/q correspond to unique rational numbers, represented as the sum of multiples of p/q by each digit. This study examines the set of words that, when interpreted in base p/q, result in nonnegative integers. The authors classify the language comprised of these words as context-free for certain rational bases, p/q. Additionally, the study identifies patterns for generating the set of words evaluated to positive integers, or the set of words evaluated to nonnegative integers in base p/q, for specific types of rational bases, including those with a specific prime factorization structure. The work also compares the set of words evaluated to nonnegative integers in base p/q with the co-Beta language, showing that they are equivalent for certain rational bases, p/q. The study concludes with the non-context-freeness proof for the set of words evaluated to nonnegative integers in base p/q, a result achieved using a Cayley graph-based approach. The method is distinct from previous proofs and provides a more direct connection to the non-regularity of the co-Beta language. The work further extends the previous result, demonstrating that the set of words evaluated to nonnegative integers in base p/q has a context-sensitive grammar with a linearly bounded stack for all rational bases, p/q. The study also presents an example highlighting the context-freeness challenges for specific quadratic bases, p/q. The task of determining the context-freeness of the set of words evaluated to nonnegative integers in base p/q, for a given rational base, p/q, is shown to be equivalent to solving a reachability problem in a Petri net system, whose net structure can be arbitrarily complex for certain bases, p/q. The study concludes by outlining directions for future research and discussing the relationship between the set of words evaluated to nonnegative integers in base p/q and the first-order logic with the order property. The connection between the order property and the context-freeness of a language was previously established in a related study. The work presented in this paper is an extension of the research described in the paper "Deciding Monadic Second-Order Definability for Unary Counting Classes" which was recently published. The earlier study focused on the case when p and q are relatively prime. The current work builds upon that foundation by addressing the scenario where p and q share a common factor, p/q = p'/q', p' being a divisor of p

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. Furthermore, our approach can be adapted for efficient checking of similar variants of snapshot isolation in other distributed database systems. Our approach was demonstrated on examples of TPC-C and YCSB workloads for sharded MongoDB deployments. Our results show that the checks are efficient, taking milliseconds rather than seconds. Our approach, the MongOSI toolchain, is available online at https://github.com/angelakereddy/MongOSI/. With the increasing use of transactions in NoSQL databases, our approach addresses the growing need for efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by these databases. In our discussion, we also examined the limitations of our approach and the challenges of checking variants of snapshot isolation that support multi-document transactions with last-winner-wins conflict resolution. Our results and toolchain are relevant to the development and testing of distributed database systems, particularly NoSQL databases like MongoDB. Our approach can be valuable for database practitioners and developers who work with such systems. Our approach can be seen as an extension of the approach presented in the previous work of Drasey, Hemanth, and Vijayshankar on Cassandra's transaction protocol. Our approach differs from their work in several key aspects, including the databases with which they worked, the variants of snapshot isolation they checked, and the efficiency of their tools. Our approach also provides an empirical study of the performance of MongOSI on examples of TPC-C and YCSB workloads, and our toolchain is available online at https://github.com/angelakereddy/MongOSI/. Research on intricate systems from the human brain to social connections has uncovered a hidden pattern - a universal level of complexity lies just before systems become overly complicated and collapse. This threshold is particularly evident in geometrically frustrated structures that can exist on multiple levels and have captivating implications for understanding and predicting the behavior and eventual downfall of these systems. This study reveals the precise threshold of geometric frustration in random graphs and presents a theoretical framework to track a system's progression from simplicity to collapse. Furthermore, the research reveals that this threshold serves as a catalyst for the sudden onset of extreme chaos in dynamics and the abrupt shift from cooperation to selfish behavior in game theory. The findings and proposed framework also offer insights into the eventual failure of societies and the collapse of cities. The study's methodology can be applied to any geometrically frustrated system, making it a promising tool for condensed matter physics, biology, sociology, and other related fields. This discovery was made possible by combining the study of complex systems with the principles of geometry and random processes. The research's primary innovation lies in its introduction of a novel dynamics-based approach to defining the threshold of geometric frustration, a concept initially introduced by physicist Philip W. Anderson. This study was inspired by the questions posed by renowned mathematician and physicist Stephen Hawking in his book A Briefer History of Time. The research was conducted within the interdisciplinary Condensed Matter Physics and Complex Systems group at the University of Liege, Belgium, in association with the University of Cambridge, England, and the University of Geneva, Switzerland. The work was driven by the memory of physicist Jean-Philippe Bouchaud and was supported by the Belgian National Fund for Scientific Research, the European Research Council, the National Fund for Scientific Research, the Swiss National Science Foundation, the University of Liege, and the Fund for Scientific Research - Flanders. The study's results were validated through numerical simulations and experimental data collected from the research of other scientists and academics. The research on random fractional structures and networks was conducted in collaboration with physicist Hau Lee from the University of California, Berkeley, and mathematician Vito Squartini from the University of Milan, Italy. The study's theoretical framework was tested on realistic models of the brain, cities, and financial systems, drawn from previous research by other scientists and academics. The research also explored connections with other complex phenomena, including the spread of diseases, earthquakes, sandpiles, traffic flow, population dynamics, genetic regulatory networks, power grids, hydrodynamics, quantum mechanics, Viana-Jaeger curves, percolation

Researchers studying strong shock waves in an expanding universe have found similar results using both approximate analytical and exact numerical methods to solve self-similar equations. When the adiabatic index lies between one and two, these shock waves exhibit an intricate, multi-shock-layer structure. This structure forms when the pressure drop inside the radial direction is greater than the pressure increase along the longitudinal direction. A recent paper provides an analysis of advancements made in categorizing monodromy-free Schrödinger operators with rational potential properties. A specific subset of potentials, characterized by a potential ratio of the form $V(x)/((x^2+1)/\pi^2)\cdot r(x)$, where $r(x)$ is a defined ratio function with polynomial roots at $x=0$ and $x=\infty$, with vertical asymptotes at $x=0$ and $x=\infty$, is examined. The study introduces generalized Hermite polynomials to restructure the kernel of the scattering matrix, ultimately leading to a determination of the sign of the monodromy under specific conditions. A distinction is drawn between two distinct cases based on the distance between the polynomial roots and the location of the asymptotes, both measured in the complex plane. The analysis involves applying the Selberg-Zagier type formula to calculate the monodromy, which is found to be non-zero for the 1-dimensional problem under study. The study also compares its results with existing data for the harmonic oscillator, Airy functions, and the Bessel operator. Furthermore, the research implies that the monodromy can serve as a measure of the operator's non-integrability within a specific parameter range. The paper's conclusions include the potential applicability of its methods to study other operators with discrete spectra and rational potentials, as well as its potential to facilitate the analysis of random Schrödinger operators. The study also highlights the generalized Hermite polynomials' unique properties and their affiliation with the harmonic oscillator operator within the space of the Wiener algebra. The paper ultimately highlights the limitations of its results and the need for further research, specifically addressing the integration of its method with other approaches that can provide more comprehensive data about the monodromy. The research setting includes a discussion of its connections to multiple related topics, such as the analysis of random Schrödinger operators, the application of its methods to study the harmonic oscillator operator, the analysis of Bessel operator, the investigation of the monodromy for the Airy function, and the comparison of its results with existing data for these specific cases. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, yielding precise insights into long-range beam-beam effects, as predicted by the improved TRAIN code. Furthermore, the data revealed significant beam emittance fluctuations, with a minimum emittance as low as 2.8 picobarns observed. The results from the emittance scans have significant implications for future high-intensity hadron colliders, like the Future Circular Hadron Collider, where beam-beam effects are expected to significantly impact collider performance, and accurate modeling is crucial. The methodology presented can be adapted for other colliders and experiments experiencing intense beam interactions. The emittance scans also highlight the importance of proper modeling of beam emittance distribution and closed orbits for an ideal collider scenario. The TRAIN code, along with the newly developed Beam-Beam Tuning Scan Simulator, are valuable tools for simulating beam interactions and closed orbits in future hadron colliders. The necessary modifications to improve the TRAIN code are also outlined, and the code is available upon request from the authors. The data from the emittance scans have been utilized in the FCNH and FCC-he studies conducted by CERN. The methodology introduced can be applied to other hadron colliders, such as the 20 TeV Compact Linear Collider, and the techniques described can be employed on other particle beam devices. This paper explores the optimization challenges in multi-agent systems that involve agents behaving maliciously, which leads to a misdirection away from optimal solutions through the spread of false information and significant communication costs. To address this issue, we develop a distributed optimization algorithm based on gradient updates, where trustworthy agents share quantized data with each other. Theoretical proof of solution convergence near the optimal solution is provided, along with the effects of communication constraints and malicious behavior on solution accuracy. This is further illustrated through numerical experiments presented in the study. Our findings can be applied to a broad range of distributed optimization problems, including the reduction of the multi-asset lot size problem and the optimal flow problem through linear programs. The impact of the attack on solutions is demonstrated in scenarios involving both a single attack and multiple attacks from different agents. The code for the experiments is available on GitHub at the time of submission, awaiting peer review. This code allows for easy replication of the experiments shown in the study. 

In the context of linear programs, our approach can be modified to tackle problems like the optimal flow problem and the multi-asset lot size problem by employing mixed integer programming. Our results indicate that the effects of the attack become more pronounced as the communication constraint intensifies, leading to solutions farther from the optimal solution. This is true for both linear and mixed integer programs, and it is demonstrated that the impact of the attack diminishes when the level of communication constraint is reduced, or the amount of perturbed data shared is decreased. The code for the experiments described in the paper can be accessed at https://github.com/AustinJJump/adversarial_distributed_optimization. 

Finally, our approach can be adapted to address issues in two other problems: the consensus problem and the distributed optimization problem with individual linear constraints. The solution to the consensus problem is shown near the end of the paper, along with the formula for the convergence rate. The formula for the convergence rate is derived through the analysis of the eigenvalues of the operator that arises from the protocol, providing further insight into the impact of the communication protocol on the convergence of the consensus algorithm. This insight is demonstrated through an example involving a non-homogeneous multi-agent system on a circle, resulting in a range of values for the operator's eigenvalues that can be determined graphically. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects rather than statistical errors. The most significant challenge is likely to be instrumental polarisation systematic effects, which can take multiple complex forms and mimic polarisation signals. This paper outlines a three-step process to evaluate instrumental polarisation systematic effects: characterising individual effect components, combining them into a vector form that affects observed polarisation patterns, and comparing them against actual observations. Furthermore, the paper presents a novel approach, the Polarisation Systematic Effect Separator, that leverages machine learning and optimisation techniques to distinguish overlapping systematic effect components and accurately calculate their individual contributions. This method is applied to the QUaD experiment data and its results are presented. The code developed for this research is available online. This study is pertinent to current and future cosmic microwave background experiments that employ polarisation sensitivity, including the CMB-S4. The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset. Furthermore, our proposed MD-CSDNetwork exhibits a substantial decrease in computational requirements, making it a highly efficient deepfake detection solution. Our code has been made available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/zhengzhong114 MD-CSDNetwork.

Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Furthermore, our study provides a detailed breakdown of Forsage's earnings and sheds light on the numerous pseudonyms used by its key administrators. Our research on Forsage highlights the need for investors to be cautious and for regulatory bodies to scrutinize financial products built into blockchain smart contracts. With the increasing popularity of blockchain technology, a thorough examination of its applications, particularly in finance, is crucial in uncovering the truth behind its implementations. Our Forsage dataset is available for other researchers to explore. In this context, we explore certain classes of holographic tensor networks, which can efficiently simulate various systems using the principle of minimization, serve as quantum codes to prevent information loss, and accurately describe phenomena exhibiting power-law behaviors. A key finding reveals that networks comprising a single type of tensor and characterized by a universal geometric structure can effectively combat quantum errors and withstand significant distortions before becoming unreliable. Furthermore, their ability to smoothly transition between different phases of matter also facilitates the seamless integration of quantum phases with gapless and lattice-like characteristics, thereby bridging the quantum crossover region. A significant discovery has been made indicating that the combination of a specific tensor network architecture and a particular choice of variational ansatz, known as the brute force method, fulfills the requirements for error correction and crossover phase compatibility. Additionally, this approach provides a sophisticated means of analyzing tensor networks through the decomposition of a single type of tensor into a combination of a matrix and a scalar, accompanied by an explicit expression for the renormalized tensor. This achievement also enables the efficient simulation of the dynamics of quantum systems on a local level. A detailed examination of a representative system, the Kitaev honeycomb model at its crossover point, reveals that its complex dynamics are accurately captured by the simple renormalization of a single type of tensor, or more specifically, the fidelity of the system's state is reproducible with a high degree of precision using just three tensors. This accomplishment paves the way for a deeper understanding of the intricate relationship between holographic tensor networks, the bra-ket algebra, and the dynamics of local physics. This knowledge can, in turn, contribute to the development of robust quantum codes capable of seamlessly bridging quantum crossovers. This research is an extension of previous findings discussed in arXiv:2007.04369, arXiv:2012.08858, and arXiv:2109.01394. Deep-learning techniques such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent
Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results for various
predictive tasks. Our research expands on existing knowledge by testing five
different variants of deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks and
Multi-layer Perceptron with dropout, for predicting the characteristics and
occurrence time of subsequent process events. Uniquely, we assess these models
at multiple stages of a process, determined by event quantities and case
completion times, thereby providing valuable insights into their behavior under
different process conditions. Empirically, the results reveal that the usage of
process data pre-processing holds critical importance for successful predictions.
Furthermore, the findings offer guidelines on selecting suitable deep learning
models for specific process scenarios, showing that, in certain cases, a single
model outperforms the others for a wide range of processes, whereas in other
cases, no significant difference is observed between the models. Consequently,
this research contributes new knowledge on the behavior of deep learning models
in real processes, demonstrating the potential for further exploration and
potential applications in the process-mining field. Our methodology is
available online for the reproducibility of results. This research is an initial
step towards the complex goal of automatically designing deep learning models
for predicting future process events based solely on process definitions. Our
aim is to lay the groundwork for future research aimed at integrating process data
with deep learning models and, ultimately, employing this integrated approach
to automatically design models for predicting future process events based solely
on process definitions. Our research and methodology are publicly accessible
online. Our code is available at: https://github.com/andersonsantos/deeppredise

open-source initiative developed in collaboration with IBM Research, UT Austin,

We investigate key properties of several types of Cantor spaces that have been recently introduced, including spaces defined as ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}$ with ${\sigma}$-invariant measures, and show that these spaces are essentially equivalent to conventional Cantor spaces except in specific, ${\Delta}$-defined instances where they possess nontrivial, one-sided components. Furthermore, we establish an algorithm for determining the exact structure of these spaces and prove that they are homeomorphic to a combination of two Cantor spaces in a specific, ${\Delta}$-dependent manner. Additionally, we examine the relationship between these spaces and the concept of symbolic dynamics associated with irrational rotations on the circle. Moreover, we demonstrate that the topological entropy of the rotation dynamical system is directly proportional to the measure of the nontrivial component of the associated Cantor space. Moreover, we establish that this entropy measure can be determined through the study of the irrational rotation system itself, without requiring an examination of the associated Cantor space structure. Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this progress, a critical limitation remains - the absence of detailed spectral energy distributions (SEDs) for many of these flare events. A new comprehensive library of energy distributions has been created for white-light stellar flares on low-mass stars based on data from several space telescopes including ULISSES, Kepler, and K2, along with ground-based spectroscopic observations from MuSCOTA and MuSCOB at the South African Astronomical Observatory. This energy distribution dataset was obtained for 2495 superflares and 1415 smaller flare events detected on several target stars. A statistical model was developed to generate a large set of randomly selected energy distributions (REDS) comprising 10,000 flares each on several types of low-mass stars. Each star in the sample has a corresponding REDS set of 10,000 flares. This allows for accurate flare predictions for unobserved flare events on similar stars. Moreover, empirical relationships have been established between flare energy distributions and various stellar and planetary parameters including the orbital period of planets surrounding these stars. Consequently, a tool has been created to generate precise energy distributions for individual flare events on low-mass stars based on their spectral types, the energy of their flares, and the orbital periods of their surrounding planets. This information is crucial for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Additionally, this energy distribution dataset can be beneficial for modeling stellar flares in spectroscopic, photometric, and biosignature data. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this vulnerability, our research introduces a novel metric that assesss a model's robustness to typical three-dimensional transformations: translation, rotation, and scaling. This metric utilizes a proxy that compares the predicted points from a neural network with actual points based on their spatial relationships, and it evaluates the consistency of these predictions under various transformations applied to a point cloud. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this metric on multiple models by analyzing the discrepancy between their predictions and the ground truth points, and also the discrepancy of these predictions with each other in scenarios of single and combined transformations. Furthermore, our results show that robust models perform better in both scenarios. This research provides a foundation for further study on the robustness of point cloud models by offering a quantifiable method of analysis. Experimental code is available online at the following repository: https://github.com/zhongyurui/pointcloud-robustness.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest. Furthermore, the proposed approach is compared to non-linear PCA and a nonlinear neural network, showcasing its clustering performance. This work's framework is adaptable and provides a foundation for incorporating additional factors like constraints, anomalies, and varying time horizons into the clustering analysis. This approach is available through the ClustMD Python package on GitHub. This research paves the way for addressing clustering challenges in more intricate scenarios and dynamic data, with the code readily accessible for the community. Developing neural text generation models through Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task due to the slow training speed and the difficulty in stabilizing the generator. To address this challenge, we draw upon the slow-learning theory and propose the Slow Learning Generator, which reduces the generator's parameter updates in each iteration. We further introduce the Slow Learning Discriminator, implementing a waiting strategy for parameter updates based on the similarity between the sample and the generated text. To evaluate our model, we conducted experiments on the text generation datasets CMU and IUL, and our results showed significant improvements in terms of both generative quality and speed compared to state-of-the-art methods. To ensure reproducibility, our model has been trained using a limited number of samples, specifically 15,000 and 30,000 for CMU and IUL respectively. Our code has been made available online for public access.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a mathematical model is developed which takes into consideration various factors including how long microbial life forms can survive, the speed of stars dispersing, and how ejected material scatters across space, all to assess the likelihood of discovering evidence for interstellar panspermia. By examining statistical relationships between pairs of life-bearing planetary systems, a new function is derived which considers the time it takes for microbial life to travel between the two systems. This function is compared with observed patterns in the movements of star systems and planetary material, both in our own galaxy and in distant galaxies. As the search continues for signs of life beyond Earth, this study provides a framework for interpreting future observations and puts the possibility of detecting interstellar panspermia within our galaxy's reach. Moreover, the model offers clues about possible manifestations of interstellar panspermia among extraterrestrial life forms, offering a basis for a panpsychic perspective on the subject. The statistical relationships derived in this study also offer insights into the dispersal of planetary material, a phenomenon known as stellar archeology, and provides a foundation for future research in this field. The mathematical framework developed in this study has been made available online at www.interstellarpanspermia.com. The relationships between pairs of planetary systems are analyzed based on the movements of specific stars and planetary material observed in the Milky Way and other galaxies, and are compared with the predictions of the model. The most promising candidates for detecting interstellar panspermia are discussed, together with the results of applying the model to these cases. The study concludes with a panpsychic interpretation of the relationships between pairs of planetary systems, and the implications of this for our understanding of life and the universe. Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from multiple sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at the same time.  This new method results in enhanced precision when estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters.  When applied to real data from black bears, it reveals increased precision in estimating population density and provides more precise space usage information, captured through the use of beta shape parameter estimates.  This parameter measures the skewness of the probability distribution used to model encounter probabilities in relation to distance, which can be interpreted directly.  This new method offers valuable tools for future research in the field of capture-recapture studies. This will be particularly important for applying this method to studies involving complex species configurations, such as multi-sex or multi-age analyses. The integration of formal verification and testing techniques aims to provide improvements in creating and testing dependable software, as well as its ongoing development. Our geometric testing theory is designed to be a blueprint for a testing environment that can be part of a toolchain used by software developers, including professionals and academics in computer science. This environment features a sophisticated automated tool that can identify mistakes found during testing and help fix them by visually presenting the underlying causes in a graphical format on a screen. This format can be easily navigated to pinpoint areas of the code that need adjustment to resolve the issue. Once modified, the software can be retested with ease. Our approach is unique in its use of a verification technique called predicate abstraction, combined with testing, that was previously only applicable to small programs. We have applied our testing method to a broader range of programs, specifically those written in the C language, and incorporating features of embedded software. Our results show that this approach can efficiently detect and fix various types of errors, including subtle timing-related issues, in realistic program examples. Our testing environment is an automated program that can be accessed from anywhere on the internet through a simple text command, at the address: http://www.cs.columbia.edu/~sedwards/predtest/. Our program testing methodology has been published in a paper that can be accessed from the website of the Computer Science department at Columbia University, at the address: http://www.cs.columbia.edu/techreports/. We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a network's size accurately, especially in the context of wireless ad-hoc networks. Our investigation considers a scenario where up to one-third of the network's nodes can act maliciously and have complete knowledge of the network. Under these conditions, we develop an algorithm called "CountStream" that enables a node to estimate the network's size by sending data packets at random intervals. This algorithm allows for a large number of nodes to estimate the network size with a high degree of accuracy. Furthermore, we analyze the performance of CountStream under various network conditions and different levels of malicious activity. Our findings show that CountStream can effectively resist manipulation of its data and accurately estimate the network size, even in the presence of a significant number of malicious nodes. In addition, we discuss the potential drawbacks of CountStream and propose possible enhancements to improve its performance. Our analysis includes an evaluation of the algorithm's overhead, its resistance to manipulation, its precision in estimating the network size, and the conditions under which it performs optimally. We also compare CountStream with another widely used algorithm, called "Counting Quorum" or CQ, and highlight the advantages of using CountStream in networks with mobile nodes. Our research further delves into possible modifications of the CountStream algorithm to improve its performance in certain network conditions. We also examine the potential applications of accurate network size estimation, discuss the difficulties associated with achieving this goal, and propose possible solutions. Our research in this area has far-reaching implications for various network management tasks, including network scaling, node ranking, and distributed voting systems. We believe that our algorithm, CountStream, can serve as a starting point for the development of future scalable algorithms in wireless ad-hoc networks. Our research assumes a scenario with up to n Byzantine nodes in a network of size N, where n is equal to one-third of N. We also consider a scenario with mobile nodes, where our algorithm requires the time it takes for a message to propagate across the network, known as the network diameter, to be significantly shorter than the time required for a node to rejoin the network following node failure or departure. We also examine a scenario with node failure or departure, where our algorithm ensures accurate estimation in the presence of up to n deleted entries in a hash table of size N. We use the terms "Byzantine nodes" and "malicious nodes" interchangeably to describe nodes that can act deceitfully in the network.
