Accurate traffic management heavily relies on reliable traffic state estimation.
This study introduces a novel nonparametric approach to estimate short-term
queue lengths without assuming random arrivals or estimating specific parameters.
The method, which uses simple mathematical expressions based solely on traffic
signal timing, estimates conditional queue lengths for an approach lane at an
intersection. Specifically, a Negative Hypergeometric distribution models these
estimates, which are compared to existing parametric methods using real-world data
from probe vehicles. The findings suggest that the proposed nonparametric
methodology matches the accuracy of traditional methods used in the field study. 
This method offers a computationally lightweight alternative for real-time
traffic state estimation applications. 
It is crucial to note that the proposed method is aimed at estimating queue
lengths for an approach lane at an intersection, not a crossroad. Also, the
estimations are based on average values and do not provide information about
queue length variations throughout the time period under consideration. 
This preliminary research opens up possibilities for further investigation into
traffic state estimation at signalized intersections, especially those with loop
detectors or similar devices that can supply necessary data for better queue
length estimates. 
In the current form, the proposed method is suitable for developing simple
traffic simulation models or estimating queue lengths in urban intersections for
short periods of time (15-30 minutes). 
In contrast, scenarios requiring more complex traffic models or longer time
frames may necessitate additional data or more sophisticated methods to ensure
accuracy. 
The code and data associated with this research are available at [1] or can be
accessed using the reprex package [2] as demonstrated in the appendix. 
Future research aims to extend the proposed nonparametric approach for
estimating traffic state variables at stops signs or midblock signals, or within
roundabouts, or in tunnels, or on bridges, or in areas with variable speed
limits, or in construction zones. 
Also, possible future directions include using machine learning algorithms to
combine the nonparametric method with other traffic state estimation techniques
or incorporating simulation tools like SUMO or AIMSUN for more complex scenarios. 
In addition, incorporating loop detector data or other direct measurement
technologies with the nonparametric method can enhance accuracy even further. 
In conclusion, this study presents an innovative nonparametric solution for a
specific estimation problem and provides the code, data, and necessary details
for replication, all of which can be found in the accompanying documentation at

In numerical relativity simulations, solving the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints is crucial for accurately predicting the evolution of gravitational waves in complex matter scenarios. However, solving the Hamiltonian constraint analytically can be impractical due to the concavity issues with the elliptical projection operator, especially when employing finite-dimensional subspaces, which are a standard method of approximating solutions. This study presents a novel approach utilizing the Dyham quadratic formula to find an expression for the inverse of the elliptical projection operator, enabling the efficient solution of the Hamiltonian constraint via an iterative multigrid method. Successfully tested on a range of nonlinear geometries and waveforms, this method shows a substantial improvement in solution accuracy and convergence speed compared to existing techniques. The code developed in this research is available online. The project also highlights the constraints' solution's impact on the subsequent evolution of the gravitational waves. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. Ultimately, our research reveals an explicit relationship between the anomalous Nernst and Hall effects in these materials, thereby offering a simplified pathway for the study and characterization of the anomalous Nernst effect in even the most intricately structured materials. Moreover, our findings indicate that the anomalous Nernst coefficient can be minimized by optimizing the lattice parameter and electronic structure of these materials. Ultimately, our study demonstrates the anomalous Nernst effect can be managed and even eliminated in materials with carefully designed point defects, presenting a promising avenue for the reduction of the anomalous Nernst effect in these cutting-edge materials.

We have derived improved differentiability properties for solutions to a non-autonomous obstacle problem, formulated as
  \begin{equation*}
  \min \left\{\int_{\Omega}f\left(x, Dv(x)\right)dx\,:\, v\in
  \mathcal{K}_\psi(\Omega)\right\}.
  \end{equation*} Given that $f$ satisfies growth conditions with respect to both the spatial and gradient variables, assuming $f\in
  \mathcal{C}^{\alpha}(\overline{\Sigma})$ for some non-degenerate convex set $\Sigma$, we demonstrate the following differentiability result: if the spatial domain $\Omega$ has a Lipschitz boundary, then a solution $v$ derives differentiability from its map $x\mapsto a(x)$. If the boundary of $\Omega$ is smooth, then $v$ derives differentiability from the map $x\mapsto a(x)$. These differentiability properties are achieved under the condition that the angle between the inner and outer normals to the obstacle $\psi$ is bounded away from zero. These results are an enhancement to earlier differentiability outcomes in both the autonomous and non-autonomous settings. The approach used in the derivation leverages variational inequalities, the differentiability of tangential mappings, and the properties of Sobolev spaces. Moreover, we outline an illustrative application to the setting of the double obstacle problem. The principal innovation offered by this research becomes apparent when addressing the non-autonomous setting, where differentiability outcomes are obtained through the application of classical H\"older continuity properties to the obstacle function, coupled with the utilization of Montag-Sims's outcomes on differentiable tangential mappings. The resulting outcomes are analogous to, yet more comprehensive than those achieved in the autonomous context, thereby extending the array of function growth conditions under which differentiability is guaranteed. The research outcomes achieved within this study also encompass the outcomes achieved in the paper by Gil, Gwinn, and Novaga following the current direction of research. The approach used in the derivation of differentiability outcomes in the non-autonomous setting presented in the current research can be applied to the setting of the double obstacle problem. The principal challenge encountered in extending the outcomes achieved in the paper by Gil, Gwinn, and Novaga to the non-autonomous setting becomes apparent through the failure of the integration by parts formula in the Sobolev space $H^1_0(\Omega)$.

Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, accurately detecting deformation is crucial for predicting and preventing catastrophic failures.
This research aims to address this issue by using a coupled electromechanical and electrical analysis to correlate mechanical deformations with electrical conductivity changes in CF-PEEK composites, and ultimately develop a self-sensing damage detection method based on accurate information about the shape and size of defects obtained through electrical impedance tomography. Numerical models of a plate with a circular hole or a crack are compared to experimental results, and the effectiveness of using different search algorithm options with the Gol'dshtein-Kaipianetzki method is evaluated. Additionally, detection tests on actual self-sensing samples are conducted using real EIT data. The findings highlight the importance of accurately defining search intervals, utilizing real data instead of reference shapes, and employing the Gol'dshtein-Kaipianetzki method with accurate intervals to achieve precise detection results. The research presented demonstrates the feasibility of using a tomographic technique and the Gol'dshtein-Kaipianetzki method for detecting defects in self-sensing composites based on real-time electrical conductivity measurements. The developed approach is shown to be highly accurate even for complicated defects like cracks, and has significant implications for enhancing safety in critical engineering projects that utilize composite materials by enabling real-time monitoring of material integrity. The most compelling aspect of this method is its ability to detect defects in real-time, thus preventing incidents of material failure and reducing project costs associated with damage occurrence. The positive outcomes of this research motivate further studies on the utilization of tomographic techniques and the Gol'dshtein-Kaipianetzki method for detecting various types of defects in different types of self-sensing composites, and exploring more efficient search algorithm options. This work proposes a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces centered on geometric vector techniques and illustrates the method's efficacy through a variety of vector integrand identities proved using this framework. Within this context, Euclidean spaces are viewed as part of affine spaces defined by their algebraic structure, and variations are expressed using covariant and contravariant derivatives. A central aspect of this tensor framework is the derivation of a gradient operator for scalar functions, resulting in a vector expression that incorporates both derivatives and the space's metric tensor. Furthermore, this framework has been applied to establish a variety of vector integrand identities, several of which have been validated through explicit numerical examples and others through comparisons with existing analytical proofs. Additionally, this approach has been demonstrated to provide a suitable foundation for the derivation of both local and global conservation equations for vector fields within both fixed and variable Euclidean spaces. In an appraisal of this tensor framework, it is observed that it offers a suitable foundation for the stabilization of vectors in fixed Euclidean spaces, as shown in the results presented. However, the proposed approach requires the satisfaction of a key stability criterion known as the "geodesic stability criterion", which this work also seeks to address. In sum, this tensor framework has the potential to serve as a basic foundation for the stabilization of various quantities in both fixed and variable Euclidean spaces. In its current form, it succeeds in deriving a set of conservation equations for vector fields in both fixed and variable Euclidean spaces, and offers a suitable framework for stabilizing vectors in fixed Euclidean spaces, but requires further development if it is to be applicable in a broader sense of variable Euclidean spaces. In such scenarios, additional modifications to the approach become necessary. This work was initially presented at the 2020 Virtual Journées Statistiques conference. In this role, it is compared to three alternative approaches, and through numerical examples, is found to offer a comparable performance. In this capacity, it was compared to an alternative method known as the Taylor expansion technique, through a set of numerical tests, and was found to offer a superior performance. All Toda conformal field theories serve as comprehensive expansions of Liouville conformal field theory and exhibit a heightened level of symmetry. Within Toda conformal field theories, this higher-spin symmetry is made apparent by a Lie algebra based path integral formulation. This document is intended to outline the means through which this higher level of symmetry is manifested within a probabilistic framework that was rigorously introduced by Rhodes, Vargas, and the first author. A distinguishing aspect of this framework is the presence of holomorphic currents, which are derived through the precise identification of a conserved quantity within the field theory itself. This has implications for the solution of the Knizhnik-Zamolodchikov-Bellman equation and contributes to a deeper comprehension of the interconnection between Toda and Liouville conformal field theories. Furthermore, this framework facilitates the derivation of a novel character formula, which can be applied to calculate certain correlation functions within Toda conformal field theories as well as the spectrum of the Knizhnik-Zamolodchikov-Bellman operator. This latter achievement provides a clear picture of the discrete spectrum that emerges from the combination of the Laplacian and holomorphic Hamiltonian operators within Liouville conformal field theory. This analysis also highlights the presence of a continuous component to the spectrum, which was previously unidentified. This component is found to be comprised of a singular component along an imaginary axis that is defined by a parameterized family of Bessel operators, which are derived through a application of the Paley-Wiener theorem to the inverse scattering problem of the Knizhnik-Zamolodchikov-Bellman operator. This achievement also affords an enhanced understanding of the relationship between the Liouville conformal field theory and a family of entire functions that are defined by the combination of their zeros and asymptotic behavior. This analysis demonstrates that these functions are invariant under specific transformations that characterize the symmetry of the dilaton grain interface, which is a solution to the Knizhnik-Zamolodchikov-Bellman equation. This allows for an explicit derivation of the correlation functions of these functions within the Liouville conformal field theory, which in turn facilitates the calculation of the correlation functions of the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ characters. This achievement is accompanied by a discussion of the relationship between the continuum spectrum of the Knizhnik-Zamolodchikov-Bellman operator and the Witten Laplacian along the grassmannian.

We demonstrate that Coxeter groups possess biautomatic properties, resulting from which we derive that uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings also exhibit biautomatic structures. This further implies that these lattices have equivalent nitay complexity to their parent group. This achievement represents an enhancement of Horbeck's findings on Coxeter groups and presents a preliminary case study towards proving a broader theory involving discrete group actions on buildings. This paper's key results are then applied to address several specific questions and generalize known facts about specific Coxeter groups and associated lattices. A notable example is the successful classification of countable Coxeter groups with a specific growth rate, achieving a goal initially sought by Milnor in the context of unknot decomposition. Additionally, this paper demonstrates that the nitay complexity of certain Coxeter groups and associated lattices can be compared to the nitay complexity of their parent group, leading to an easier solution for the nitay version of Rips' question. This achievement also enables the proof of a generalisation of the nitay version of the Strong Markoff-Lagrange Conjecture for nilpotent groups of a specific class, which in turn results in the nitay version of the Anagnostopoulos-Kalaidziej Question being affirmatively answered for certain Coxeter groups and associated lattices. This paper also delves into the investigation of a question initially posed by Milnor by proving that among Coxeter groups with a specific growth rate, the symplectic and orthogonal groups cannot be infinite. This achievement is obtained through the use of Grigorchuk's corona construction, dynamic systems, and the study of group growth. This paper also provides an example of a group with a specific growth rate that cannot be factored using the corona construction, addressing another question initially posed by Milnor. This example is based on an analysis of the relationship between the nitay complexity and group growth of Coxeter groups, leading to an innovative application of the method for detecting impossibility of constructions, which is a general-purpose tool also used in the solution of the nitay version of Rips' question. Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation level (>0.9) between predicted and actual step rates, indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of more complex aspects of walking. Overall, the high level of precision achieved in this study using high-level sensory information from the motor cortices through chronic ECoG recordings supports the feasibility of utilizing this type of signal for accurate walking state decoding, paving the way for its use in the development of invasive BCIs for gait rehabilitation in individuals with spinal cord injuries. To facilitate the clinical application of this technology, the study's findings are made available on Figshare, a public data repository, in the hope that researchers working towards similar goals may find them useful by building upon this foundation. The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception structure to guarantee convergence. Theoretical analysis has revealed that NN meets the conditions for fast convergence, specifically achieving a rate of convergence of O(ε^2) when utilizing an iterative solver of O(ε) complexity for the preconditioning matrix. Furthermore, we establish that NN possesses the capability for near-linear scaling when employed on massive linear systems with sparse matrices and implicit preconditioning. To demonstrate the practical efficacy of NN, we present detailed experiments across various domains and linear systems, showcasing its performance on increasingly large data sets. Our results reveal that NN excels in a broad range of applications, from the solution of nonlinear partial differential equations to the computation of graph Laplace operators, consistently delivering the fastest known approximate matrix inversion when employing moderate amounts of computational resources. Our code has been made available online for the community. With its impressive performance and easy-to-maintain structure, we believe that NN presents a valuable solution for the widespread issue of efficient matrix inversion in the scientific computing community. By convention, we have titled it 'Nested Neumann' to honor the legacy of its namesake, who pioneered groundbreaking work in the field of linear algebra with his innovative application of Neumann Series, subsequently known as the Neumann model. In honor of this achievement, we have also contributed a detailed mathematical reconstruction of his original work, previously inaccessible due to the limitations of ancient documents. In this reconstruction, we have uncovered new insights, confirming that the Neumann model, in fact, conforms to the intricate pattern of inception structures, thereby guaranteeing its own convergence. This explicit confirmation was previously unknown and has been contributed to the linear algebra community as part of this research. In this process, we discovered an error in a preceding research claim related to the convergence of the Neumann algorithm, which we have publicly addressed and provided a corrected version for the benefit of the scientific community. Our study investigates outcomes of the Event Shape Engineering method implemented in lead-lead collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy.  Events with the same level of centrality but varied average flow are used to investigate initial state conditions.  Results reveal that the event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient is unaffected by transverse momentum.  Also found is that charged hadron distributions are steeper for events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, indicating interactions between radial and elliptic flow phenomena.  Consequences of the Event Shape Engineering approach on radial and elliptic flow decays with transverse kinetic energy are also studied.  Calculated results show that initial state condition fluctuations influence both radial and elliptic flow decays.  Furthermore, influenced by the same fluctuations, both phenomena exhibit similar cross-section densities of fluctuations.  Consequently, their proportional contributions to radial and elliptic flow remain constant throughout the centrality spectrum examined.  Calculated results also show that the proportion of radial to elliptic flow remains largely unaffected by event-shape selection.  However, due to the Event Shape Engineering method's ability to target initial state condition fluctuations, charged hadron distributions and corresponding distributions of charged particles with transverse kinetic energy exhibit differences with centrality levels varying from 30-50%.  In such cases, the proportion of radial to elliptic flow becomes affected, exhibiting increases of 10-20% with corresponding charged hadron distribution increases of 10-15%.  Also found is that charged hadron distributions exhibiting steeper slopes display proportional increases in cross-density fluctuations of radial and elliptic flow, indicating that the event-shape selection's influence on initial state condition fluctuations becomes non-trivial in mid-central nuclear collisions. This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and extremal network theory to examine the extremal gain resulting from optimal power control in contrast to binary (on/off) power control in large interference networks, focusing on uncovering new theoretical insights. Numerical studies have shown that in many real-world applications, binary power control is near optimal, however the extremal analysis indicates there are settings where the gain from optimal power control can be substantial, also offering bounds on extremal gain values from a GDoF perspective. As its primary contribution, this research precisely defines the extremal GDoF gain of optimal over binary power control as proportional to $\sqrt{K}$, where $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ represents the ratio, for any number $K$. It's worth noting that this gain can vary between the minimum $\lfloor \sqrt{K}\rfloor$ and a maximum of $2.5\sqrt{K}$, for any number of $K$. Further investigation into networks that reach the extremal gain reveal they could potentially be described as multi-tiered, heterogeneous networks. A note is made that due to its focus on long-term analysis, this gain characterizations hold value primarily in theoretical contexts rather than as practical design guidelines for heterogeneous network implementations. In such a scenario, other factors like backhaul technology, user eligibility, base station site costs, and power consumption become more crucial for optimal design. In spite of this, the characterization of the extremal gain can still be beneficial in understanding the limits of current practices and can serve as a benchmark for future innovations in base station design and network planning. A suggestion is made for practitioners and industry leaders to consider the potential implications on heterogeneous network design and consider possible variations of the characterized gain in future work. A proposal for future research involves exploring the extremal gain in binary power control in small, non-scalable networks, also examining the gain in hybrid scenarios that combine features of both large and small networks. A final proposal made involves studying the policy-making perspective of base station sleep duration with an emphasis on dynamic pricing and revenue maximization, particularly in the context of heterogeneous networks. A suggestion is made to consider both non-cooperative and cooperative game theoretical approaches to achieve a deeper understanding of base station sleep duration in relation to revenue and other relevant factors. A proposal for future research also involves examining the base station sleep duration from a cooperative perspective with an emphasis on designing robust mechanisms that are resistant to non-cooperative behavior from individual base stations. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flow simulations. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations. In multiple-step simulations, this limitation can be bypassed to enhance efficiency, but it introduces inaccuracy because the collision process is artificially lengthened. Our new algorithm uses a variable time step that can be stretched during particle collisions without deviating from the second-order accuracy required for numerical solutions. This allows for realistic short collision times in multiple-step simulations. Our tests showed that artificially prolongating collision time, even if not necessary, can lead to particle sediment entrainment and increased turbulence. Nonetheless, our research found that stretching collision time for too long causes numerical instability. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. A key factor in solving this dilemma is accurate terrain perception, which can be achieved through a dual-camera system set up on the sole of a robot's foot. By capturing high-resolution images of the sole's surface and inferring terrain information from them, a dual-camera setup provides detailed data about the deformation of the sole and surrounding terrain. Furthermore, an image-based method has been created to measure displacement fields on the sole and surrounding terrain with a high degree of precision. Experimental testing has demonstrated the effectiveness of this technique in accurately capturing sole and surrounding terrain deformation with a mean absolute error of $1.6 \pm 0.3$ mm in a $19.6 \times 19.6$ cm field of view. A dual-camera setup set up on a seven-legged robot successfully captured data during testing on a variety of surfaces, ranging from a hard, smooth floor to sandy ground with pebbles. The technique has also been applied to a CMOS camera and a real-world sole design, demonstrating its versatility. A study of the dual-camera setup's resolution optimization revealed a direct relationship between image resolution and the precision of terrain measurement, with the latter increasing in proportion to the square of the former. Ultimately, a framework has been established for estimating terrain deformation, sole impedance, and command forces for a sole-equipped robot based on a dual-camera-based deformation measurement system. Experimental testing validated the effectiveness of this approach, demonstrating successful estimation of command forces, sole impedance, and terrain deformation in a variety of environments. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. These results demonstrate a significant improvement over existing methods in terms of topic coherence and hierarchy stability. Our approach is intended to serve as a foundational technique rather than a standalone solution, as seen in our experiments using document embeddings and hierarchical neural networks, which can further refine generated hierarchies. Our code is available online for public use.

Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study delves into the distinction between these two processes through the dynamics of interlinked bosons and a spinless fermion in periodically-varying potential environments. We contrast quenching and annealing's complementary dynamics in the same system and demonstrate how reversing the direction of time affects the annealing/quenching trajectories. Furthermore, we derive accurate solutions to previously reported numerical data on quantum annealing algorithms. The analysis across multiple scenarios highlights the inverse relationship between the duration of annealing/quenching and the duration of revivals in the coherent dynamics. The generality of these findings is ensured by the parameter-neutral character of the involved variables. The developed solution framework is applicable to a broad spectrum of quantum systems. The recently introduced variable called the quantum annealing trajectory in the variable space of the Hamiltonian is examined in depth. This involves the discussion of the variables' inter-relationships, the identifiable patterns, and the distinct boundaries in the annealing/quenching process' trajectory. The investigation across various scenarios reveals the common features of the trajectories in the time domain. The analysis of these trajectories in the time domain reveals the intertwined relationship between the coherent dynamics' revivals and the annealing/quenching time constants. The distinctive boundaries in the trajectory are found to be indicative of the onset of the dissipation-dominated regime in the annealing/quenching process. This occurs when the annealing/quenching time constant approximates the inverse of the average Hamiltonian level spacing. The investigation of the trajectory in the variable space is accompanied by the discussion of the recently introduced quantum annealing landscape and mountain pass theorem. To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for question answering. To address this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware model, which evaluates the necessity of using external knowledge on a case-by-case basis for each question. This model differentiates between three types of knowledge: (1) necessary but not readily available, (2) available but not necessary, and (3) both available and necessary. It then leverages a knowledge-aware mechanism to draw upon relevant external knowledge for the appropriate questions. Experimental evaluations using the CommonsenseQA dataset demonstrate superior performance compared to various baseline models. In addition, an in-depth analysis of the knowledge awareness mechanism through both numerical and textual outcomes is provided. Moreover, the efficacy of individual model components is proved through ablation testing. Our proposed model exhibits comparable performance to high-end pre-trained models but with significantly reduced parameters, making it a promising solution for future development.

Astronomical environments, particularly in comets, are rich in molecular cations whose exceptional brightness under UV to visible light can facilitate the detection of cometary activity. Although molecular cations generally exhibit stronger spectral features when bound to electrons, some isolated cations like C2+ and N2+ have distinctive emission lines that could be used for mapping cometary areas. For the sake of completeness, additional cations like CN+, CO+, and O2+ that have been observed in cometary spectra are also included in our analysis. We have also considered alternative formation mechanisms for these cations such as solar wind interactions with interplanetary mediums, but cometary environments remain their most observable and studied context. By examining existing spectroscopic observations and simulations, we outline possible emission features associated with these cations and discuss potential scientific inquiries that could be addressed with the Europa Clipper Telescope, a proposed NASA spacecraft. Based on the sensitivity of the instrument, we project that the number of detectable cometary electrons could be as low as 10 to the power 45 over a period of two weeks, or in other words, a single Earth-sized comet with average brightness. Furthermore, the emission spectra of these cations would allow the determination of cometary electron distributions and also provide constraints on the composition of cometary material, including the absence of carbon monoxide in the outer Solar System. In addition, the study of these cations could also offer valuable insights into the geometry of the cometary magnetosphere and the extent to which solar wind can interact with cometary electrons, in turn, influencing our understanding of the Earth's magnetic environment and potential effects on the Europa Clipper Telescope observations. Additionally, the proposed telescope could also study other Earth-like gas-rich small bodies like Saturn's moon, Rhea, and other cometary bodies like Giacobini-Zhang and 67P, provided that appropriate observation techniques are employed to detect the weaker emission features of these molecules. Ultimately, the direct observation of cometary electron distributions could also be achieved with a space-based telescope in a closer orbit around the comet but would require a more sophisticated mission design. A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. This approach belongs to the category of adaptive data regularization techniques that reduce overfitting when working with highly confident labelled data. The method has several advantages over alternative techniques such as adversarial and generative models, primarily due to its minimal computational requirements. Evaluations using publicly available MRI datasets - specifically ACDC and MMWHS - demonstrate that this proposed technique outperforms existing semi-supervised models, with source code available on GitHub.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study particularly considers settings with varying communication schedules between devices. Theoretical convergence rate analysis for smooth loss functions is provided, and the robustness of the FedBuff algorithm is demonstrated through numerical experiments. Additionally, the feasibility and effectiveness of using the FedBuff algorithm are shown in two real-world applications, including a large-scale image classification task using MobileNet and a sentiment analysis task using BERT. The code for the experiments is available on GitHub at https://github.com/linguster/FedBuff. The MobileNet experiment can be found at https://github.com/linguster/MobileNet-FedBuff. The BERT code is available at https://github.com/linguster/BERT-FedBuff. The term "buffing" in the algorithm's name is an informal expression for synchronizing updates and refers to the practice of hitting a character or target repeatedly to damage them in video games. The character performing this action is called a "buff character". The FedBuff algorithm was thusly named as it efficiently hits the character of loss function regularly. Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example, transferring knowledge from a trained English model to recognize Slovenian speech. This study explores the concept of "bridge alphabets" in ASR, which represents an intermediate, pseudo-native phonetic representation of a target language's phonology, based on an existing alphabet, and is utilized to train an ASR model on a related, but easier-to-acquire dataset. We successfully applied this idea to recognize Slovenian speech using a trained English ASR model and Slovenian phonetic alphabet, and our results show a significant improvement over a direct transfer learning approach. Additionally, our findings indicate that the Slovenian phonetic alphabet requires modification to serve as a bridge alphabet for Slovenian ASR. In the process, we discovered that the PHOENIX 2014 dataset contains recorded Slovenian speech along with its transcriptions in the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA), which has not been utilized in previous Slovenian ASR research, thus offering a valuable resource for the community. In the course of this research, we converted the Slovenian pronunciation dictionary from the Slovenian National and University Library to IPA format to be able to employ the data from the PHOENIX 2014 dataset set. This dictionary was not previously accessible in IPA format, thus we are making it available for others to use. This study was carried out within the framework of the Slovenian Research Agency project No. J1-2610. The ASR model training data used in this research is available at https://www.dropbox.com/s/clhpxq6pkv5q2td/slovenian_asr_data.zip?dl=0. The dictionary converted by the authors can be found at https://dl.dropbox.com/s/2xv6q5x5q5q5q5q/slovenian_pronunciation_dictionary.zip. The PHOENIX 2014 dataset can be obtained from the website of the organizers at http://www.ph4nix.com/. The source code used in this research is available at https://github.com/Aleksander79/bridges. The trained ASR models are available at https://www.dropbox.com/s/clhpxq6pkv5q2td/slovenian_asr_models.zip?dl=0. The research reported in this paper was conducted under the ausp

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA: a new algorithm for offline policy evaluation.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being demonstrated in underwater navigation.  Our approach also has a model-based variant known as SPGP-TD, and with minimal modifications, this variant is obtainable.  Our findings are backed by extensive simulations and actual underwater robot learning experiments.  The code for our project is available online at https://github.com/igorcortesb/SPGP-SARSA.  Future work will concentrate on integrating our method with other promising TD learning techniques such as priority replay and distributed learning.  Our project was supported by the National Science Foundation under grant IIS-2033494 and also benefited from the advice of Dr. Andrew Gordon Wilson from the University of Cambridge.  Our SPGP-SARSA implementation was inspired by the GPyTorch library developed by the University of Cambridge, the University of Edinburgh, and the University of Malaga.  Our SPGP-TD implementation was inspired by the GPyTorch library developed by the University of Cambridge, the University of Edinburgh, and the University of Malaga.  Our project also includes data collected from actual underwater robot learning experiments conducted at the Florida Institute of Technology.  Future underwater robot learning experiments will concentrate on tasks such as object recognition and manipulation of marine life.  With the current code, it is feasible to train a robot to recognize a specific marine animal just by showing it to the robot within an underwater environment.  With the SPGP-SARSA algorithm, it is feasible to train a robot to navigate an underwater environment for 500 seconds or approximately 8 and a half minutes, which is a notable achievement given the uncertainty associated with underwater sensor data.  Additionally, our findings demonstrate how our approach overcomes the limitations associated with the range of action exploration in TD learning.  Our approach also includes two novel sparse approximations techniques known as Frobenuis and Structured, which were not previously known in the literature. By direct resolution and reconstruction, new exact solutions for this two-fluid case are found. Additionally, three theorems applicable to the single-fluid scenario can be adapted to yield two-fluid solutions from their single-fluid counterparts. Furthermore, three-fluid solutions may also be obtained by a similar adaptation. Lastly, three theorems for the single-fluid case can be used to generate solutions for specific single-fluid cases. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel multi-task meta-learning model, consisting of a primary GEC encoder and two auxiliary modules: a domain indicator generator and a task-specific mask generator. The model generates a shared code for GEC and a domain-specific indicator for each sentence. To facilitate cross-domain learning, the model generates a random mask for a portion of sentences, enabling both intra- and inter-domain GEC through reinforcement learning. To enhance robustness and tackle domain shift, the model employs a multi-domain training dataset and pseudo data from various domains. Experimental results indicate that the proposed model achieves significant improvements in eight domains with either 10-shot or 20-shot learning, outperforming the baseline multi-task GEC model by 8% in terms of F-score. Furthermore, the model compares favorably to a strong single-domain GEC baseline with 400 pseudo data, demonstrating its effectiveness in large-scale learning settings. In addition, an ablation study and qualitative analysis are conducted to facilitate understanding of the model's performance. This paper's code and models are available online at https://github.com/zhanglei1997/adversarial-metareg.

The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents requires ensuring that the allocated items are fairly distributed. Envy-free up to one good (EF1) is a prominent standard for fairness, where no agent prefers another agent's allocation over their own. To achieve this level of fairness using indirect mechanisms, designers must gather sufficient information about agents' valuations. In the process, many existing studies have demonstrated the feasibility of this goal in various settings, often utilizing a broad spectrum of information including upper and lower bounds of valuations. However, the question remains whether such a high level of fairness is attainable when designers have limited information about the structure of agents' preferences. In this research, we investigate the viability of achieving EF1 through truthful mechanisms in a scenario where designers have only the minimal required information about upper and lower valuation limits. To address this challenge, we develop an innovative auction design based on a new type of randomised allocation protocols, and in the process, our solution includes an original analysis of the probability distributions of protocols to ensure the truthfulness of our mechanism. Furthermore, our design incorporates an unique cut-off strategy to prevent inflationary bids. The resulting mechanism meets the standards of efficiency, fairness, and selflessness, and can be implemented with only a polynomial scale of computations. Additionally, our design includes a derivation of an existing result as well as a new theorem on the expected value of the most expensive item in a uniform distribution within a hypercube space. This expected value is further found to be linear with respect to the dimension of the hypercube. The accompanying benchmark involves an interesting comparison with the distribution of the most expensive item in a uniform range within a one-dimensional space. The comparison is made possible by an interesting extension of an existing result on the concentration of the distribution of the maximum value in a uniform range within a one-dimensional space. The original result on the concentration was proven by chance process inequalities. The extension to hypercube space requires new chance process inequalities as well as the use of the rotation matrix to rotate the hypercube. The derivation of these inequalities involves the application of an operator theorem. The operator theorem involves an interpretation as the expected value of a function of a random rotation matrix. The expectation is taken over two distinct sets of random rotation matrices, each with a distinct probability distribution. The distinction in the probability distributions arises from the opportunity to choose either one or the other after rolling a die. The connection to the original question about the expected value of the most expensive item also involves the application of the rotation matrix to a vector

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system. A comparative study with Malin 1 reveals several similarities, including a similar specific star formation rate in the outer radii and a preference for distant radii for its HII regions. The isolated, grand-design spiral galaxy, NGC 6240, is also considered in the study as a possible third instance of this rare galaxy phenomenon. The research suggests that galaxies with dark matter-dominated, stable disks may infrequently exhibit unusual, off-axis star formation, fueled by the slow migration of a small, long-lived stellar "ghost" cluster that forms as a result of a rare, three-body interaction. This phenomenon could be an extremely rare phase of galaxy evolution, observable only when viewed edge-on and with minimal internal star formation. The presence of such galaxies may have been underreported due to the edge-on requirement and biased sampling of bright HII regions. The study proposes a new mechanism linked to three-body interactions that could explain the observed star formation in these galaxies and suggests future observational and simulation efforts are necessary for a deeper understanding. The unique case of UGC 8839 also highlights the importance of comprehensive, wide-field observations of galaxies with dark matter-dominated disks. The 2000 NTT ultraviolet study that discovered UGC 8839 is particularly notable as it provides a long baseline to compare the distribution of its UV emission with the previously known HII regions and reveal any changes over nearly two decades. The research opportunities presented by UGC 8839 are further enhanced by the existing observational data available for the galaxy. The study acknowledges the existing ultraviolet, infrared, and radio data for UGC 883

Using lattice QCD, a study has been conducted to examine the correlations between quark currents and pion properties at small quark masses. A novel approach was taken to directly measure the two-point function of a quark operating within a quark current and a quark within a pion, enabling the investigation of correlated fluctuations between quarks and allowing for the accurate determination of the pion's electromagnetic form factor. This form factor's determination was achieved at multiple pion momentum values, spanning 0.6 to 3.9 GeV, through a simultaneous lattice fit of quark-connected two-point functions with light quarks. Key findings include a form factor scale of approximately 0.024, a dimensionless pion charge that increases with the pion's momentum but is dimensionless, and the confirmation of a linear relationship between the pion's charge and radius, exhibited through data analyzed at three lattice spacing values: 0.47 to 0.61 times the native lattice spacing. Additionally, the research demonstrated that the pion's electromagnetic form factor exhibits a trustworthy interpretation of the quark current's distribution across the pion, exhibiting a reliable sensitivity to the choice of local quark current, and showcasing no notable variations when utilizing either a point or a clover quark action for the quark current. Furthermore, the dimensionless pion charge was discovered to be extremely sensitive to the quark mass, exhibiting a near-exponential increase with diminishing quark masses, and was found to be remarkably robust when employing either valence or sea quarks. The most comprehensive analysis to date, this research has made significant breakthroughs in accurately determining the pion's electromagnetic form factor through the direct observation of quark currents within the quantum chromodynamics framework. This achievement has paved the way for a deeper comprehension of the intricate relationships between quark currents, pion properties, and the fundamental forces governing the behavior of subatomic particles. This study has been conducted utilizing a state-of-the-art lattice QCD simulation of quark quanta, commonly denoted as quarks, at a level of precision that mimics the characteristics of the native quarks found within the quantum chromodynamics framework. This research has been carried out through a complex numerical method known as lattice discretization, cast across a vast array of possible quark configurations, spanning various distances, momenta, and quark masses, and has been executed at multiple lattice spacings, a dimensionless unit of length that is native to lattice simulations. Evaluating protoplanetary disk evolution is closely tied to understanding how mass migration and accretion rates are influenced by the interplay between stars, disks, and planetary systems. As a key indicator of disk evolution, mass accretion rates are affected by several factors, including magnetic field activity, X-ray irradiation, and the distribution of accretion hot spots. Researchers have made significant progress in determining mass accretion rates using spectroscopic techniques, particularly through the use of $e$-folding lengths in the Paschen-alpha line profile, which provides a direct measurement of mass accretion rates with a lower limit of about 0.01 $M_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$. By analyzing the relationship between $e$-folding lengths and other relevant factors, scientists can further refine mass accretion rate estimates and gain a deeper understanding of the complex interactions in protoplanetary disks. Additionally, studying the shape of the Paschen-alpha line profile can reveal details about the geometry of accretion hot spots and the distribution of gas in protoplanetary disks. Furthermore, comparing mass accretion rates derived from Paschen-alpha line profiles with those from other techniques, such as the H$\alpha$ line, helps evaluate the limitations and variability of these methods and establish precise conversion factors for both techniques. Ultimately, this research enables more accurate retrospective analysis of disk evolution and provides valuable constraints for theoretical disk evolution models. Furthermore, the direct measurement of mass accretion rates from Paschen-alpha line profiles has implications for the study of supercritical H II regions in the nuclei of galaxies. This study was originally published in 2009, and there have been significant advancements in the field since then. Nonetheless, the techniques and methods presented are still relevant for investigating the physics of narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies. This work lays the groundwork for a subsequent study that includes a larger sample of narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often faces issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. Moreover, the benefits of SIT are further highlighted through a module-based exploration of its innovative components. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghrua/SIT.

We developed a novel approach for registering MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they fall short for low-quality megavoltage images and have limited capture ranges. To overcome these challenges, we employed a Convolutional Neural Network, resulting in a dataset-based comparison using 50 brain images, which demonstrated improved results relative to conventional methods. The difference in target intensity levels, a critical factor affecting capture range, was also investigated and showed to impact the effectiveness of our network. Furthermore, a practical application for registering pre-treatment and actual treatment images during radiation therapy was explored with promising outcomes. A code version of this work is available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/RTRegistration/MV-Image-Registration. With further refinement, this method shows promise for enhancing radiation therapy treatment.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. The core of his argument centered on instantaneous non-local phenomena implied by the $EPR$ scenario, which sparked significant debate. To better understand the implications of Einstein's experiment, we explore the concept of non-local instantaneity through the lens of the ever-present effects of measurement decoherence. By examining the interplay between the geographical spread of a quantum system and its surroundings, we reveal how the non-local nature of instantaneous effects becomes apparent when analyzing the trajectory of a lost particle in relation to its accompanying photon within the context of the $EPR$ experiment. By doing so, we gain a more intuitive understanding of the significance of Einstein's experiment, which he used to argue the need for a more comprehensive, deterministic framework of quantum mechanics. Ultimately, our analysis serves as a stepping stone for examining the implications of the $EPR$ scenario on the topic of quantum holism. Additionally, we also discuss the experiment's potential applications in testing the concept of quantum non-locality through the use of scattering phenomena with photons and particles such as atoms or electrons. The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and addressing concerns about security and privacy, whereas Blockchain technology presents possibilities for secure and verifiable data management. This paper conducts an in-depth review of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs, exploring potential problems, viable solutions, and future directions. This comprehensive survey can serve as a foundation for developing novel BC-Enabled FL solutions to address various IoVs data privacy challenges and scenarios. Moreover, two specific IoVs data privacy scenarios are outlined alongside code implementations for easy reproduction by interested researchers. This study is relevant to various IoVs applications such as traffic management, intelligent navigation, and vehicular social networks. Further research is needed to address key challenges including data confidentiality, trust issues, and scalability in BEFL protocols. This survey is aimed at stimulating innovative ideas for homogenous BEFL protocols and secure code development for open-source platforms. This is an extended version of a paper that was previously presented at the 2022 International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Blockchain. V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose extreme evolution over nearly three years has been closely observed.  V392 Persei, which rapidly shrank from 2 days, exhibited early spectral characteristics pointing towards several massive ejections interacting and causing both gamma-ray and optical illumination through shock waves.  V392 Persei entered its deep minimum phase in 2020, with a quiescent magnitude of 37.3 for optical observations, and a quiescent X-ray output that was extremely low.  The extensive study discovered evidence for both a residual hot white dwarf and a disc/flows system during its minimum phase.  V392 Persei's extreme behaviour is very similar to that seen in the well-known objects U Sco, U Sge, and RS Oph, which all exhibit both nova and DN characteristics and exhibit both short periods and large luminosity excesses during their minimum phases.  V392 Persei's decline from its pre-nova state to its post-nova state over nearly three years is the quickest observed to date, with the optical and X-ray outputs declining by 99.9 per cent within two and a half years from its pre-nova levels.  V392 Persei's extensive study also includes observations of both the pre and post-nova phases with both the Hubble Space Telescope, as well as numerous ground-based optical and near-infrared telescopes.  V392 Persei's unique trajectory, which is the most extreme observed to date, offers a unique opportunity to study both the pre and post-nova phases of a single object with the same level of detail applied. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach aims to enhance limited feedback transmission. Initially, a precoder codebook is created with Gaussian mixture models (GMMs), which are used to define clustering and determine the best codewords. A subset of the codebook is selected and transmitted to the base station in a limited feedback phase. The approach results in improved performance, especially in scenarios with restricted feedback, but requires increased initial information to be transmitted. Experiments using real data demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique. The codebook design process involves selecting the number of GMM components, the codebook size, and the clustering criterion, which are explored in relation to system performance. A modular framework is also provided for incorporating this codebook in existing systems. The code is offered for use in research purposes. The most suitable parameters for this codebook are presented, and it is suggested that further research is necessary to improve this codebook in various aspects. The code is publicly available on GitHub at the specified link. The work described in this letter was conducted as part of the MACSAD EU project, which aimed to enhance multimedia transmission over next-generation wireless networks. The research presented was influenced by collaboration with project partners, particularly ST-Ericsson and Samsung, and also drew from discussions held during technical meetings with other partners like Intel, Nokia-Siemens Networks, and T-Mobile. The approach described was tested using data obtained from the T-Mobile network in the city of Munich, Germany. The project's broader goals and methodology are outlined in detail within the MACSAD EU project document. The GMM-based codebook design process addresses several key issues faced in current codebook designs. The precoder codebook is constructed from a limited dataset, which leads to codebook gaps due to underrepresentation. A proposed solution utilizes GMMs to model codebook entries based on provided training data, producing a codebook through a nearest neighbor approach. The codebook's effectiveness is analyzed through simulation, varying the codebook size, GMM component count, and clustering criterion, which affects performance in terms of eigenvalue ratio. The optimal GMM parameter settings were determined through simulation, yielding a codebook with performance comparable to a full dataset codebook. A type of genuine two-dimensional crosscurrent that flows counter to its direction has been lacking in scientific knowledge since its one-dimensional counterpart was discovered. A setup for realizing these currents on a three-dimensional cubic lattice has been devised by coupling a Hofstadter model to two separate heatbath Hubbard models through cross-dressing, demonstrating robust directed crosscurrents that persist over a wide temperature range. Theoretical calculations indicate that the system's stability is significantly enhanced by its three-dimensional structure, offering robustness against various imperfections and boundaries. Numerical simulations on both exact diagonalization and iDMFT configurations demonstrate the presence of directed crosscurrents, along with the distinct temperature dependencies observed in their amplitude. The system also exhibits the self-regulating capability to maintain the exact symmetry of any disorder or boundary, displaying the robustness of its fundamental characteristics. The novel mechanism of robust crosscurrents presented in the research might be applicable to a wide range of non-equilibrium many-body systems. The system's unique ability to maintain the exact symmetry of any disorder or boundary, along with the distinct temperature dependencies observed in its amplitude, were investigated through numerical simulations on both exact diagonalization and iDMFT configurations. The distinct temperature dependencies observed in its amplitude are as follows: in the low temperature range, the amplitude of the directed crosscurrent increases exponentially with a specific temperature coefficient that is the same in all configurations; with a further increase in temperature, the amplitude reaches a plateau stage before finally decreasing in the high temperature range; the distinct temperature dependencies observed in its amplitude also exhibit distinct pre-exponential factors that differ based on the configuration used. We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework begins with the formation of the first nuclear star clusters at redshift 12-15, where Population III binary remnants are located within their centers. These remnants then interact with their surroundings and other stars, eventually merging with each other or with lower-mass partners. Our model tracks the distribution of these remnants as they move through the cluster, moving from the center in a manner consistent with simulations. Combining this with their individual masses and spins, we predict the future gravitational wave signals from the remaining Population III binary remnants. Our predictions show that about 10% of these binaries will produce gravitational waves in the mwdetector band, with future observations potentially revealing this signature. Our model also predicts the formation of extremely massive stars and supermassive black holes in the centers of galaxies. We find that about 10% of these supermassive black holes form in the earliest clusters, with masses between 4.10^4 and 2.10^5 solar masses. These black holes will shine brightly when the universe cools enough and can form quasars, with about 10% of these quasars being powered by binaries with masses between 10^4 and 10^5 solar masses. Our model also predicts the formation of smaller mass binary black holes in the mdfilter band, with formation rates that match current detections. We anticipate future discoveries in the mdfilter band and the direct detection of supermassive binary black holes in the mwdetector band. Our predictions for the distribution of Population III binary remnants in nuclear star clusters can be tested with near-infrared spectroscopy of the oldest stars in the Milky Way's bulge. Our model shows that about 10% of the most metal-poor stars in the bulge's globular cluster populations should have formed from Population III progenitors. Our predictions for future gravitational wave signals rely on specific assumptions about the distribution of Population III binary remnants in the centers of galaxies. We anticipate that this assumption can be tested with near-infrared spectroscopy of the most metal-poor stars in the Milky Way's bulge, specifically once a survey of this type yields at least one confirmed Population III star formation signature. In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. By utilizing high signal-to-noise ratio approximations and optimization techniques, we can develop effective power allocation methods that prioritize system security while minimizing interference from power consumption at transmitting nodes. Furthermore, a dual decomposition framework enables us to employ convex optimization to find efficient power loading solutions. We also investigate several suboptimal schemes for various configurations and present simulation results to validate the efficacy of these methods in real-world applications. Evaluations of two scenarios, one with and one without a relay, demonstrate the advantages of our proposed techniques. Moreover, we outline potential research directions for extending this work to more complex system paradigms. The simulation results for a system with a single user show that our method can increase the secure throughput rate by up to 57% when employing a single relay, and by up to 20% when using multiple relays, in comparison to conventional power loading strategies. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. Our studies reveal that faster simulations produce more reliable and accurate results in evaluating agent performance. Our data show that the current state-of-the-art agent requires roughly three times as long to reach the same level of solution quality in our revised tests. Additionally, TextWorldExpress offers a modernized API, a newly created example agent written in PyTorch, and comprehensive testing guidelines to ensure the integrity of future research. Our code is available online at the TextWorldExpress website.

Deep learning models have excelled in various natural language processing tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to extensive computational requirements and memory usage. A common technique used to address this challenge is efficient long-short term memory network architecture design. This study reviews LSTM models with a reduced footprint, starting with one-layer LSTM variants, then moves on to compressed methods, and finally explores current advancements in multi-layer LSTM architectures. Evaluations on four text-related datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of these efficient models. Furthermore, the study highlights potential research directions and presents a comparative analysis of the best models tested so far. The research and code are accessible via the repository at https://github.com/yingtang16/Efficient_LSTM. The model has been deployed in real-world applications, including a conversational agent for a well-known automobile brand, as evidenced by user feedback available at https://aip.awapp.cn/. The model's code has been used in a natural language processing competition hosted by Alibaba, where the winning submission ranked first in the leaderboard with a score of 92.50%. Another approach posits its fundamental expression is tied to the self-repulsive properties of a specific particle in long-range interactions. A new, closely related formulation suggests it could be formulated in terms of a particle's self-binding energy, which must remain non-negative. This new interpretation becomes particularly insightful within anti-de Sitter space due to its association with a conformal field theory, where a relationship involving the dimension of a quantum field exists. This connection allows for an exploration of the Charge Convexity Conjecture's implications on the spectral distribution of a set of quantum fields. Through the application of a mathematical principle known as the convexity of entropy, it can be proven that the spectrum of charges must be positioned in such a way as to prevent any overlap between a set of scalar fields and their gauge-invariant combinations. This conviction can be visually represented on a diagram known as a renormalization group flow landscape, which illustrates the distribution of the mass of a particle, the charge of that particle, and the binding energy of that particle in a specific configuration. This representation demonstrates the charges of the particle fields become increasingly fragmented as the distribution shifts towards the right. This phenomenon is further shown to occur across various scenarios, including different temperatures, different amounts of particle generation, and different ratios of particle generation to temperature. This analysis can be generalized to include both scalar and vector fields, as well as fields of either positive or negative charges, and even to fields that are either bound to themselves or to other fields. This exploration of the Charge Convexity Conjecture through the lens of a conformal field theory within anti-de Sitter space provides a framework that can be utilized in the investigation of other theories. This can be achieved by mapping the existing theory to one that has already been proven to satisfy the Charge Convexity Conjecture, effectively "analytically continuing" the corresponding conformal field theory. This approach has been successfully applied in the examination of certain extensions of the standard model of particle physics, specifically in scenarios involving additional scalar or vector fields that could potentially be found in a future particle accelerator, such as a Future Circular Collider.
