Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated a comprehensive study of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex through the application of infrared spectroscopy. By analyzing this phenomenon, researchers were able to identify the rates of formation and dissolution of these polar vortices in both hemispheres. The vortex in the north began forming in the late spring, and it took the entire Saturnian season to fully develop. The rapid formation of this vortex corresponds with the timing of the equinox, when the direct sunlight hits the equatorial regions of Saturn, and a specific wave pattern begins to interact with the polar air. This interaction causes a decrease in the temperature difference between the equator and the poles during the equinox, leading to a dissolution of the vortex in the southern hemisphere. The unique geometry of Saturn means that the polar air is drawn towards the equator due to the pressure gradient, causing the vortex to shrink. The vortex's core, with its warmer temperatures, is marked by the presence of ethane and methane at specific levels in the atmosphere. The search for similar phenomena on Jupiter revealed no direct equivalents, although the researchers suggest this could be due to a lack of suitable viewing angles or the presence of different atmospheric circulation patterns. The study of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex on Saturn also shed light on the formation of polar vortices in general, and how they are influenced by the interaction between the planet's rotation, the speed of the winds, and the temperature differences within the atmosphere. The unique seasonal variations in the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex on Saturn provide a valuable opportunity for comparing and contrasting the formation of these vortices with those found in the Earth's atmosphere. The application of infrared spectroscopy also enabled the creation of detailed maps of the atmospheric composition within the vortex, showing how the presence of certain gases varies with the distance from the core. The study of these variations will contribute to a better understanding of the global circulation patterns of the Saturnian system. The extensive data collected from the Cassini spacecraft will facilitate further research into the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex on Saturn, and may also shed light on the formation of similar phenomena on other planets and moons within the Saturnian system. This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. A previously established approach, derived by Glassey through the concavity of variance, is not applicable in this context due to the appearance of boundary terms of undesirable sign in the second derivative of variance. Our primary argument introduces a new, modified variance measure, bounded from below and concave in a way that is relevant for solutions in this particular scenario. This allows us to draw conclusions about the behavior of solutions based on their variance rather than energy. We also establish some relevant estimates for boundary terms that arise during this analysis. This approach can be viewed as a variation of techniques originally presented by Glassey. We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over the integers have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for nearly all prime numbers. This conclusion is true under the assumption that the variety possesses a specific property called "geometrically irreducible" in a particular context of three dimensions. The approach we take involves utilizing the local semi-parametric embeddings in an attempt to reconstruct the variety's initial definition, and in doing so, we gain insight into the nature of those definitions. A separate examination is then made into the instances where the varieties with specific dimensions fail to meet the "geometrically irreducible" standard. The main arguments presented are accompanied by an illustrative example based on a particular class of varieties known as Hatcher's subgroups. The underlying theory that drives these results is grounded in the principles outlined in the local monodromy theorem as well as the combination of topological and arithmetic properties of fundamental groups. The study that this paper draws from also includes an examination of the relationships between the geometric non-degeneracy of local semi-parametric embeddings and the conditions necessary for the existence of free resolutions in the context of defined varieties over the integers. The non-regularity of local semi-parametric embeddings near a specific geometric feature are used to demonstrate the existence of varieties with delta-invariant dimensions that range from one to the N-1, where N represents the total dimension of those varieties. The paper also delves into the discussion of the distinct differences between delta-invariant dimensions and the regular dimensions of local semi-parametric embeddings. The non-regularity of those embeddings is further shown to be a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of non-trivial free resolutions in varieties defined over the integers. The examination of free resolutions is demonstrated through the use of a sample variety known as Hatcher's subgroups. The paper that this proof is based on draws from the earlier work conducted by its authors as well as the research of Comboux-Duquesne, Guiraud, Poulshpan, and Vincent. The same topics and study that this proof is based on have been presented in the form of lectures at the 2019 Paris-Saclay Mathematics Graduate School, the aim of which was to provide a comprehensive understanding of the theoretical framework that local monodromy theorem is based on. We create a linearisation functor for full linearisation that transforms a graded bundle of degree k into a k-fold vector bundle. To do this, we define a full linearisation functor for single graded bundles and show it generates the full linearisation functor for k-fold vector bundles through a process of folding. Along the way, we establish a relationship between graded bundles of degree k and collections of graded bundles of degree one (i.e., vector bundles). This relationship involves a fibre product in the context of bundles, leading to the conclusion that the full linearisation of a k-fold vector bundle results from taking the fibre product of a collection of one-fold vector bundles with a particular bundle that contains indices, effectively reassembling the original k-fold vector bundle. This process is the opposite of the process of obtaining a collection of one-fold vector bundles from a k-fold vector bundle, which is called folding. Hence, we name the full linearisation process the fibre product functor for bundles, or the fibre product structure on the category of k-fold vector bundles, or the Bismut-Shi structure. This connection also allows us to reconfirm the fibre product structure on k-fold vector bundles in the context of graded algebras. Additionally, we introduce the concept of homotopy k-fold vector bundles, defined as homotopy graded bundles of degree k, and establish that they are equivalent to homotopy vector bundles equipped with k-linearisations as homotopy properties. This, in turn, leads to the discovery that the fibre product structure on homotopy k-fold vector bundles results from the fibre product structure on homotopy vector bundles. A key part of the discussion surrounds the explanation of Tamagawa numbers and their role in this example. Next, we examine the situation where the base field is local and non-archimedean, and we explore the relationship between orbital integrals and the volume of the group in question. Finally, we conclude by considering a situation with a global base field, and we discuss the connection to the concept of trace formulas. Along the way, we touch on various important issues, including those related to Haar measure, the relationship between the geodesic measure on the set of conjugacy classes of a reductive group and the Chern measure on the associated Grassmannian, as well as the connection to the work of Yang-Zagier. The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, atomic, or nuclear components. Although scattered light conveys both amplitude and phase information, this phase information is frequently lost during standard intensity measurements, yet it is crucial for reconstructing essential details of a target, as evident from applications like coherent x-ray imaging. A new algorithm is introduced that allows for retrieving phase information from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra, a feature we demonstrate with x-ray scattering off M\"ossbauer nuclei using a synchrotron radiation source. The knowledge gained through phase information also leads to improved amplitude analysis. Furthermore, the use of pre-knowledge about a system's dynamics enhances both phase and amplitude interpretations of data. The success of x-ray M\"ossbauer spectroscopy with phase information is shown to be superior to conventional methods, as validated by comparing the two approaches based on both simulated and experimental evidence. The proposed method's capabilities are versatile and can be adapted for other x-ray techniques, such as x-ray absorption spectroscopy or diffraction, by simply adjusting relevant parameters according to a system's specifics. In addition to x-ray spectroscopy, the developed technique has the potential to enhance other phase-sensitive techniques and scattering processes off nuclei, like inelastic light scattering, by re-analyzing previous data collected with a new level of accuracy. In doing so, previously unresolvable nuclear dynamics can be made visible across a broader spectral range, as proven by re-analyzing inelastic light scattering off $^{57}$Fe in a yttrium iron garnet sample and uncovering additional scattering peaks that were initially overlooked. In the case of x-ray M\"ossbauer spectroscopy, reducing the energy width of measured spectra allows for resolving nuclear components with shorter lifetimes, thus increasing the range of accessible nuclei by an order of magnitude, compared to conventional methods. This advancement makes possible the direct investigation of nuclear dynamics in materials with complex structures, like granular metals, and provides a more precise determination of nuclear relaxation processes in liquids and fluids. The development of x-ray M\"ossbauer spectroscopy also paves the way for combining this technique with temperature control, magnetic fields, or pressures to study the interplay between these conditions and nuclear dynamics in atoms. The technique's versatility is further highlighted by applying it to investigate free atoms, where it reveals a new mechanism of coherent nuclear dynamics, along with a parameterized model of the related process. We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. A major advancement of our approach, the pressure variable is shown to be single-valued across each fracture interface. This pressing issue is addressed by employing a mixture of continuous and discontinuous functions to represent pressure within our finite element framework. Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as even minor errors can result from incorrect coding and have significant implications for model comparison. A check function has been developed to help researchers verify the appropriateness of Bayes factor estimation approaches by ensuring that the methods used align with established standards and produce expected results in familiar scenarios. This check list comprises three primary components: the first ensures that the posterior distribution obtained is equivalent to the desired prior distribution in the absence of data, the second checks for consistency with prior specifications in cases where parameter constraints are present, and the third component validates the accuracy of estimated Bayes factors in multiple predefined situations. If the results from these checks are positive, it is highly likely that the Bayes factor estimation approach is accurate and free from errors. A step-by-step coding guide is also provided to facilitate easy implementation. This check function can be accessed using the Rfrancheck command in the Sensus package. In the appendix, a dummy code file is offered for download at the following link: <https://osf.io/7n5bd/>>. This code file can be employed for checking Bayes factor estimation approaches described in the paper by Dzielski, 1985, as well as for conducting typical Bayes factor analysis. In the context of Dzielski's research, the check function was utilized to validate the Bayes factor estimation approaches for the Gricean symmetry test of the representativeness bias, based on the data presented by Dzielski, 1985, as well as the data collected by Nisbett and Wilson, 1977, and Wilson and Keil, 1995. The R code for the Bayes factor estimation used in the symmetry test of the representativeness bias can be found in the following link: <https://osf.io/5y8j8/>. This code has been thoroughly checked using the developed framework and found to be free from errors. Consequently, the representativity bias hypothesis is supported by the available data. The check function as well as the code for the Bayes factor estimation used in the symmetry test of the representativeness bias are available for public use and can be accessed from the following links: <https://osf.io/7n5bd/> and <https://osf.io/5y8j8

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using predicted indicators between sentences to create enriched sentence representations that facilitate the identification of semantic relationships in language, as demonstrated through an upgrade to the classification performance of the BERT model on the Discourse Bank dataset. In addition to this dataset, a larger, previously unexploited resource called Discourse-Search, comprising search discussions annotated with indicators of semantic relationships, is also presented. Enriched sentence representations produced using the predicted indicators enhance the classification performance on both the Discourse Bank and Discourse-Search datasets, showcasing the versatility of this approach. Furthermore, an analysis of the predicted indicators is provided for a deeper comprehension of the relationship between discourse indicators and the semantics of sentences. The codes and datasets are available at this link https://github.com/zhuhengshang/DiscSearch.

We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. To achieve these results, we analyze a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, providing a critical connection, and also establish an independent result regarding the convexity of geodesic balls under the Riemannian quotient geometry. We further show that the Riemannian quotient geometry is geodesically equivalent to the standard Euclidean geometry within these geodesic balls. To facilitate our analysis, we outline an algorithm for approximating the geodesic distance under the Riemannian quotient geometry. We support our theoretical findings with numerical experiments conducted on realistic optimization problems arising from the sum-ratio criterion in multiuser MIMO communications. A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a bipartite graph of high enough girth and a specific degree constraint could be colored using a certain number of colors, but in 2021 this was disputed. Now, another example is given which also disputes the conjecture originally presented by those authors. This example is particularly notable as it provides the smallest known number of colors required for a certain type of star hyperbolic graph, compared to the previous record held by linear hyperbolic graphs. 

Furthermore, it is demonstrated that for a particular range of large enough 'n', the number of colors needed for a certain type of star hyperbolic graph with 'n' vertices, a specific large enough 'd' degree, and a particular small enough 'p' proportion, is less than the square root of 'd' plus the square root of 'p', but this is done without proving the stronger claim that this particular lower bound applies to all star hyperbolic graphs meeting the defined criteria. Additionally, the investigation into this topic reveals several interesting subcases and related results.

Introducing "social-learning" variations of two algorithms led to successful attainment of Nash Equilibrium, unlike "individual learning" counterparts which consistently failed to converge to the desired outcome. Utilizing simulation outcomes with a specific framework as a benchmark, we found that social-learning algorithms at a minimum match the performance of their individual learning counterparts, and in many instances surpass it, resulting in a higher success rate in reaching the Nash Equilibrium and achieving greater profit in the simulations. Additionally, we discovered that some social-learning algorithms exhibit a peculiar tendency: they initially distance themselves from the Nash Equilibrium before eventually converging towards it. We term this phenomenon "the big detour". We also observed that the most efficient algorithm in our study, MOGA using a tournament selector, is immune to the "big detour" effect, as it directly converges towards the Nash Equilibrium without first moving away from it. We conclude that the capacity of Cournot models to converge to a Nash Equilibrium is significantly enhanced through the employment of social-learning algorithms. Furthermore, we found that the magnitude of this improvement is directly proportional to the size of the market model in question. We recommend social-learning algorithms as suitable alternatives to traditional econometric methods used in empirical research settings. We also propose possible modifications to the MOGA algorithm that could further boost its performance in the future. We suggest incorporating elements of the "neural network" model into the algorithm, as well as leveraging machine learning techniques such as "deep learning". Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Real-world deployments of these systems require ensuring the reliability of their underlying hardware, shielding them against faulty memory caused by hardware errors. Following the successful use of activation clipping, this study explores efficient methods for convolutional neural networks. The proposed technique, known as Efficient Resilient ConvNet, utilizes low-cost hardware interventions to prevent faulty memory-caused incorrect data retrievals during network processing. The Efficient Resilient ConvNet achieves this through a combination of activation clipping and precise data manipulation techniques. As a result, the network is capable of automatically detecting and correcting input data affected by memory malfunctions. The experiments conducted on MNIST, Fashion-SGNIST, and MobileNet V3 demonstrate the effectiveness of ERCNet in both performance and reliability, surpassing comparable solutions currently available. The ERCNet also exhibits a highly competitive performance on a self-driving assistance task, namely lane detection. Additionally, we have encountered relationships between this generalized version and the Philips-Stern twist, along with connections to the Philsips-Stern twist's image under an adjoint operation. A combination of the generalized version and the Philips-Stern twist results in another modified version, which also fulfills the 2-cocycle criteria. This new version is equivalent to the Philips-Stern twist's adjoint transformation, revealing a form of cocycle-like symmetry. Moreover, we have discovered that the Philips-Stern twist undergoes an adjoint transformation that is analogous to the 2-cocycle's defining equation, when both twists are considered in a combined structure. Consequently, we propose that this cocycle-like symmetry be referred to as "cocyclic" symmetry. We have also explored applications of these generalized twists to the obfuscation process of the Jacobi identity for the standard Lie algebra commutator, resulting in a "twisted" structure often called the Jordanian structure. Nevertheless, due to cocyclic symmetry, we can equivalently describe this twisted structure using either the left-twist or the right-twist version, despite them being distinct in non-symmetric contexts. We have also compared our generalized version with other, similar constructs proposed by other researchers, demonstrating distinct differences between them. We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words, part-of-speech tags, and lexical characteristics; combining two methods to achieve clustering: Non Negative Matrix Factorization and hierarchical clustering. Our results show that we can boost the accuracy of machine learning models operating in a language of limited resources by training them on data from a more linguistically similar language. Our data is now available, featuring 4000 vocabulary words from 8 languages, embedded in a unified space of 20 dimensions. We believe this an intriguing starting point for future research in cross-lingual knowledge sharing. Our code and data can be accessed at https://github.com/JoostRijpma/multilingual-semantics. The benefits of this approach are particularly notable for languages with limited data, where we observe a 6.4% increase in the accuracy of a text classification model after incorporating information from a more linguistically similar language with a larger dataset. The same approach also yields a 5.8% improvement in the F-score of a machine learning model operating in a language with limited data, after training on that larger dataset, incorporating the shared knowledge space we constructed. The code and data for this project are available on GitHub at https://github.com/JoostRijpma/multilingual-semantics. The project webpage is located at https://joostrijpma.nl/multilingual-semantics/. In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. Consequently, this project proposes a modified model that integrates a diffusion process reflecting the influx of external participants essential for disorders to occur in specific subway station clusters. This new model successfully replicates the observed distribution of riots in Santiago but also predicts patterns of disorders in other clusters that were not actually affected by the riots. Ultimately, this research highlights the challenges of modeling complex, unpredictable events like riots and highlights the need for future, more detailed data to enhance understanding of such phenomena. This project's model, data, and results are available at https://github.com/Maximus102004/2023-ChileanRiotsModel. This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions, expanding basic patterns by integrating intersection and complement operators and incorporating regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this approach acknowledges the extended features and character sets in its calculations, bypassing the necessity to translate to automata equivalents and utilizing instead a symbolic rewriting system to solve inequality problems with regular expressions. This approach is based on an equivalence between a regular expression and a symbolic expression describing the regular language recognized by a regular expression, established using regular expression to automata and antimatal translation in combination with reverse engineering. This approach directly addresses the containment issue, bypassing the intermediate step of comparing two regular expressions and instead directly examines the relationship between one regular expression and the complement of another, enabling more efficient calculation by avoiding the generation of intermediate symbolic expressions. This approach is particularly effective for handling complex regular expressions and large character sets, for which it provides an expeditious and precise solution to the containment issue, whereas for simpler cases it offers comparable performance to standard methods. This approach has been successfully tested on numerous examples and instances of regular expression containment problem settings. This research is an extension of a previous study on comparing regular expressions with complement operator, but unlike the predecessor approach, this research does not require the presence of the complement operator. This approach has the added benefit of simplicity in its algorithm and a lower computational load compared to its predecessor. This research introduces a novel interpretation of regular expression matching on infinite character sets, distinct from the standard intersection with universal set, and demonstrates its applicability in multiple contexts. This research has been applied to the evaluation of regular expression containment issue in settings with specific character sets, most notably the set of integers, for which it enables the containment issue assessment without the need to compare vast automata and provides an alternative solution to the containment problem that compares two regular expressions, identical to the approach presented in a previous study but with a more efficient algorithm. This research has been incorporated into the expansion of multiple regular expression comparison algorithms presented in a previous study, offering an alternative solution to the containment problem that compares two regular expressions identical to the approach presented in a previous study but with a more efficient algorithm, and has been utilized in the comparison of regular expressions with the complement operator, for which it provides an expanded and more efficient version of the algorithm. This research has been successfully put to use in multiple regular expression comparison contexts, most notably the comparison of regular expressions with the complement operator, the containment problem for regular expressions with complement operator for finite character sets

Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular the deep learning-based VIO ones, offer the potential to provide pose information without the need to craft custom algorithms. Presently, the majority of VIO models using learning techniques, often rely on recurrent models that fuse multimodal information and process signals, although they have difficulty training and efficiency limitations. In contrast, neural network architectures that are more efficient have limited VIO applications, and specifically the Inertial Envelope (IE) technique, which simplifies the input signal to remove unnecessary frequency components, hasn't been integrated into VIO. This paper introduces a novel and efficient VIO model, the so-called Sensory odometry network, that leverages the Inertial Envelope technique and the efficient neural network, to enhance the fusion of visual and inertial information, and to reduce overfitting. Experimental results, conducted using a monocular camera and an inertial sensor mounted on a mobile agent, show that the proposed model achieves comparable performance to the state-of-the-art VIO models, yet with a significant decrease in computational requirements. This makes the proposed model highly suitable for real-world applications of VIO. In addition to that, the paper includes an in-depth analysis of the impact of the Inertial Envelope technique and the efficient neural network on VIO performance. This analysis provides valuable insights that can be beneficial for future VIO model developments. Experimental results were conducted using a research vehicle as the mobile agent. This vehicle was equipped with an OdysSEE Xsens inertial sensor and a Mieye Nova mono camera. The data collected during these experiments complies with the Visual-inertial odometry (TUMVI) dataset standards, which means it is publicly available for use with other VIO models and algorithms. This dataset is hosted at the Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) dataset webpage. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By constructing a 3D solid-state model with honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings, we both theoretically and experimentally verify the exotic SHOWS state, thereby paving the way for realizing the square-root topological properties in 3D solid-state systems. This study investigates the numerical solution to a problem of reconstructing incomplete boundary data for the time-varying Maxwell equations based on electric field measurements, where the goal is to recover missing information on an inaccessible boundary segment using data from the accessible part of a confined domain. A non-iterative approach to solving the problem is examined and different hybrid mathematical formulations are introduced. Key aspects, such as stability, convergence and smoothness of solutions are demonstrated through rigorous analysis. Edge finite elements are employed to discretize the problem. Computational results, covering two- and three-dimensional cases and accounting for noisy input data, showcase the method's effectiveness. A notable finding highlights the difference in solution smoothness when using edge versus nodal finite elements. A comparative assessment of these two element types is also presented. A priori error estimates for both elements are established, whereas an extra criterion based on the mesh size is required to guarantee the stability of the edge element system. A notable advantage of the edge elements becomes apparent in solutions representing curved wavefronts. A relevant practical application is then presented, involving the reconstruction of boundary data from incomplete measurements in a scenario where a coil probe is placed inside a confined domain and used to measure the electric field through the process of induction, based on a theoretical model verified by experimental means. A real-world example is also provided, involving the recovery of boundary data from incomplete measurements in a scenario inspired by a coil probe placed inside a confined domain and used to measure the electric field through induction, based on a previously validated numerical model. This paper presents the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) approach, a method that enables the creation of a robust, shared model by asking participating institutions to contribute data relevant to specific classification issues. Unlike traditional federated learning methods, FedSA does not involve sending updates to the shared model but rather selects relevant data from its local dataset to contribute to the shared model, thus reducing data sharing costs. To facilitate efficient data contribution, the authors developed a novel ranking-based approach that matches participant institutions with classification issues, thereby creating a framework that addresses issues of data privacy, censorship costs, and the complexity of feature sharing. To evaluate FedSA's effectiveness, the authors conducted several experiments using real-world datasets, comparing its performance to traditional federated learning and found that FedSA yields comparable results with significantly reduced data transfer costs. Moreover, the FedSA framework has practical applications, as evidenced by the successful deployment of a comparable method at Google, known as the Federated Selective Data Approach. Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal activity, are used extensively in various fields. A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. We have investigated a nonparametric Bayesian approach to estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process parameters, obtaining results on the concentration rates of the posterior distribution. Additionally, this has implications for the convergence rates of Bayesian estimators. Another significant aspect in the study of event-data involves uncovering the graph that represents the connections and interactions between events, or the Granger connectivity graph. We have established the consistency of Bayesian methods in estimating this graph, particularly showing that the posterior distribution converges to the correct adjacency matrix, as does a Bayesian estimator based on a suitable loss function. We have tested our methods on both simulated and real disaster data. The R code for the examples is provided in the supplement. The R package called RNBHAWK, which implements these methods, is available on CRAN. The code, along with the RNBHAWK package, allows users to conduct Bayesian estimation of nonlinear Hawkes processes, calculate the concentration of posterior distributions, estimate connectivity graphs, and reproduce the results presented in the study's figures. The RNBHAWK package can be used for Bayesian nonlinear Hawkes process models and related methods, not just the specific data sets used in the study. The code and package are suitable for replicating the results and facilitating potential future work. The R code and RNBHAWK package can be used for Bayesian estimation of nonlinear Hawkes processes in any context, extending beyond the presentation of process parameter concentration and connectivity graph consistency in the paper. We propose a novel type of plasma waveplate based on a specific magneto-optical property when subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field, allowing it to function under extremely high laser intensities. This component can modify the laser pulse polarization while simultaneously increasing the peak power, which has been demonstrated numerically with simulations. It shows that a high-intensity linearly polarized laser pulse can be converted to a higher-powered circularly polarized pulse. This conversion process achieves nearly complete efficiency, with about $98\%$ of the initial energy successfully converted. The required waveplate thickness was found to be inversely related to the electron density in the plasma and the strength of the magnetic field, which, for a specific plasma and field, was found to be approximately 1 cm. This type of plasma waveplate can serve a pivotal role in the effective deployment of multi-petawatt laser systems. It was also discovered that this component can produce a distinctive polarization pattern when interacting with a linearly polarized pulse, which could serve as a sensitive technique for probing the plasma density and the magnetic field through the illumination of a target with a linearly polarized pulse and the analysis of the resulting polarization patterns. We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main conclusions. Firstly, we show that for code rates less than half, there is a diverse class of rank metric codes capable of accurately decoding any symmetric error, even those that are maximal. Moreover, this code class includes, as a subset, the family of Gabidulin codes with rates less than half. Secondly, we propose a method for correcting symmetric errors with a specific parameter, which enables us to decode a class of rank metric codes with rates greater than half. Both of these decoding strategies rely on the solution to a system of linear equations with the code's parity check matrix and the symmetric error matrix. If the system has a unique solution, the symmetric error can be recovered exactly. In contrast, if the system lacks a solution or has multiple solutions, the error still needs to be estimated from the received data. Our approach utilizes a general method for estimating the error as the solution to a system of linear equations with the code's parity check matrix and the symmetric error matrix, which provides an opportunity for further optimization to refine the error estimation. Our research also introduces several decoding algorithms for both systematic and non-systematic rank metric codes, which can handle both optimal and sub-optimal estimation of the error. Our work is motivated by an error control application in the spread spectrum paradigm known as anti-forensics. This technique aims to prevent the detection of a message's existence and its contents from being revealed to third parties, even in the presence of an error-prone transmission channel, as long as the errors made are below a certain, code-dependent threshold. This condition ensures that the error matrix is symmetric, making our decoding algorithm suitable for this critical error control task. Our code design guidelines result in a higher symmetric error threshold, which, in turn, allows for higher code rates, larger spreads in the spread spectrum paradigm, and higher code lengths. Our innovative codes can be applied to various anti-forensics scenarios and error control channels with symmetric errors. We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo, a hydrogen-poor Type II supernova with an exceptionally short duration of about 15 days, extreme asymmetry, and a remarkably fast rise to maximum brightness. Initially classified as a Type Ic supernova, SN~2020jfo's spectra eventually revealed a Type II feature, indicating a complex and evolving progenitor. By modeling the supernova's light curves and spectra using a two-component radiative transfer code, we found that SN~2020jfo was composed of a rapidly expanding, optically thin supernova remnant surrounding a dense, optically thick optically blank sphere. The remnant's radius expanded at a speed of about 3400 km/s and the supernova's total energy was estimated to be around 6.5 x 10^51 erg. Based on SN~2020jfo's narrow helium II line and the absence of SN~2020jfo's precursor SN~2019jq, it's likely that the progenitor had a mass range of about 12 to 16 solar masses and was a non-rotational hydrogen-rich supergiant. Furthermore, the detection of SN~2020jfo's precursor SN~2019jq, with a long duration of about 140 days and a bolometric magnitude of about -1, suggests that SN~2020jfo resulted from a second supernova in the same star, a phenomenon observed in about 1% of Type II supernovae. SN~2020jfo's characteristics are consistent with the "failed" pair-instability supernova scenario, where a massive star experiences a partial explosion leaving a large amount of hydrogen-rich material in the form of a supergiant progenitor, which then experiences another supernova. SN~2020jfo's evolution over time provides a unique opportunity to study the interplay between the two supernovae and its surrounding environment. Additionally, SN~2020jfo's short duration and extreme asymmetry make it an excellent addition to the small group of rapidly evolving, highly asymmetric supernovae with a possible link to hypernovae and gamma-ray bursts. Specifically, we demonstrate that this partial version is equivalent to a specific Uemara-Huisken type flow equation and related parabolic and elliptic equations. Furthermore, we outline the steps for constructing viscosity solutions to these equations within the realm of partial uniform ellipticity. This is achieved by employing level set methods and the properties of the underlying geometry. A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. Moreover, this method has been demonstrated to achieve comparable performance on demanding, real-world tasks with as little as a tenth the usual amount of annotated data. Our approach and associated methods have been open-sourced by Google, and are now available online. Our research and associated tools also include novel active learning strategies, a specialized dataset, and a comparative analysis of different active learning techniques. Research suggests that these aspects influence economic productivity and innovation, though the specific mechanisms remain unclear. This paper examines the effects of street encounters and social connections on the economic success of cities. We use data from 103 World Bank member countries and account for correlations, causation, and potential external factors. The results indicate that higher levels of social connections and street encounters correlate with increased GDP per capita and innovation, as measured by patented technologies. Furthermore, we find that these positive outcomes stem from the direct impact of social connections and indirect effects of street encounters on social connections. Additionally, in developed countries, the positive effects of social connections on GDP per capita and innovation are more pronounced. In contrast, in developing countries, the effects of social connections and street encounters on GDP per capita and innovation are similar. We also discover that higher levels of trust, lower income inequality, and better governance amplify the positive effects of social connections and street encounters on GDP per capita and innovation in both developed and developing countries. Ultimately, our research underscores the significance of public spaces and social connections for the economic and innovative growth and development of cities worldwide. This migration can occur in different forms, either as a result of an external perturbation, or due to the self-supporting instability of the disk. The resulting accretion patterns take various shapes, ranging from sudden spikes to prolonged periods of increased accretion. Key features of these bursts take into consideration factors such as the properties of the stellar core, the characteristics of the surrounding disk, and the migration of objects within the disk. The simulation shows that the shape of the accretion curve can be influenced by both the rate of migration and the size of the objects within the disk. The duration of these bursts can extend from hours to weeks, and their amplitudes can reach up to a hundred times the normal accretion rate. In this proof, a modified Stokes formula for differential forms is demonstrated on a specific class of locally convex spaces. To establish this result, the surface layer theorem is utilized as a key tool. Additionally, an expression for the operator associated with the Stokes formula is obtained. This leads to an examination of the Stokes operator on certain spaces of differential forms. Consequently, this investigation into the Stokes operator enables the extension of several of its properties to this new context. Finally, the modified Stokes formula is applied to solve the boundary value problem for the Laplace equation in a specific class of locally convex spaces. This involves demonstrating that this modification results in the operator being invertible. This invertibility enables the solution to the boundary value problem to be represented precisely, thereby extending several of its known properties. This includes the smoothness of the solution, the composition property, and the surjectivity of the operator associated with this boundary value problem. This investigation also introduces the concept of weak extension of differential forms and connects it with the surface layer theorem. This enables the application of the regularity theory to a greater extent. Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the navigation of indoor environments using a mobile robot with a sonar sensor, either singly or in combination, within a layer that can be considered 'foggy' or 'occluded'. By redefining the sonar sensor's field of view in relation to the robot's movement, researchers have successfully created and tested a control system that uses a model-based approach, capable of compensating for the reduction in available sensory data. As a result, the robot is able to successfully complete a series of tasks, including the avoidance of obstacles, the creation of indoor maps, and the execution of predefined navigation routes. Furthermore, compared to other sensing technologies, the sonar-based system requires significantly less data to function, making it an attractive option for real-world applications. Experimental results validate the effectiveness and versatility of this innovative navigation system. A mobile robot equipped with this sonar-based sensing system has the ability to safely navigate a wide range of indoor spaces, even in the presence of heavy rainfall, as demonstrated in a subsequent experiment. A version of this work was previously presented at the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems in 2021. The associated code can be found on https://github.com/robotology/iros2021_foggy_ping. A related video can be found on https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a58I6d3v1gA. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages transformer-based language models to counter one of their inherent drawbacks, allowing our CMTR-BERT framework to combine diverse text representations and mitigate the negative impacts of certain words on the news verification process. Experimental results reveal our approach surpasses the performance of existing methods utilizing traditional approaches. Furthermore, we conduct an in-depth analysis of our model's performance through representation exploration and feature importance, showing its capability to effectively distinguish between genuine and fake news. When applying dimensionality reduction techniques to datasets with anomalies, L1-PCA has been a well-liked alternative to conventional PCA due to its robustness in recent years. This study focuses on an under-explored version of rotationally invariant L1-PCA and aims to find its optimal solution using sparse PCA methods. Unlike the general case where only one eigenvector is sought, this paper delves into the study of finding the optimal pair of rotational invariant eigenvectors associated with the two largest eigenvalues of the sample covariance matrix. This is achieved by formulating an optimization problem that incorporates the L1-norm and results in a method for recovering the optimal rotational invariant eigenvectors. This approach is further extended into a statistical analysis of the procedure's performance, coupled with the estimation of specific risk metrics. Moreover, this paper demonstrates an applicable example where a method based on rotationally invariant L1-PCA can be utilized for identifying outliers in time series data. This example is accompanied by numerical examples and theoretical support, as well as proxy experiments for outsourcing risk to existing robust estimators. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for public use. Excitingly, the project has been designed as an entry point for students and robotics enthusiasts to learn about mapping and navigation through hands-on experience. With continued development, the project aims to refine the HiTMap representation and enhance the navigation stack in preparation for real-world applications. One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. In scientific simulations and linear algebra applications, a common obstacle is parallelizing band matrix operations, given the sparse nature of these matrices and the limited memory bandwidth. To address this challenge, we introduce an efficient algorithm for dense matrix-vector multiplication using narrow banded matrices, and optimize it for GPU execution. The proposed method employs a novel data layout that minimizes memory access conflicts and caching issues, and features a unique combination of direct and indirect addressing modes to leverage cache efficiency. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects possess a spin magnetic moment of 1$\mu_B$, while being located 1.68 Angstroms from their nearest titanium atoms. Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through intense laser interactions with solid materials, specifically at the interface between the material and its plasma. To better understand the formation of positrons, simulations examining the polarization of an intense laser in relation to a solid material interface have been conducted. The models account for the polarization's influence on electron interactions with the laser, other electrons, and photons. By comparing simulations with experimental data, their accuracy was validated. Further analysis reveals that the positron polarization degree is significantly affected by the laser intensity, electron temperature, and density of the target, though it's largely influenced by the thickness of the plasma interface. In fact, even when the intensity is as high as 10 to the power of 24 Watts per square meter, the degree of polarization remains remarkably low, never exceeding 0.01 unless the plasma interface is extremely thin, where the degree of polarization reaches over 0.9. This thin interface requirement can be difficult to achieve in experiments, however it's crucial for efficiently generating positrons, especially in monoparticle production studies. Therefore, it's crucial to consider the polarization of electrons at the plasma interface in studies of intense electron emissions caused by high-power laser interactions with matter. Additionally, a degree of polarization model has been developed for electrons with a broad energy range, spanning from a few electron volts to a few million electron volts, based on simulations and experimental data from various sources. This model also takes into account the dependence on the laser polarization, electron density, electron temperature, and the thickness of the plasma interface, making it a valuable tool for simulating and studying electron emissions in various experiments. Published in Physical Review X, a research paper delves deeper into this analysis, further by examining the polarization of electrons with specific energies, as well as electron distributions, while also studying the decay channels of highly excited states of atoms, specifically in the case of helium-like ions. Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two. This work also presents an infinite sequence of groups with a constant diameter whose size grows cubically in accordance with their generating set size. Additionally, it is demonstrated that for any prime number p, there are finite groups with a constant diameter whose generators' order is p, and whose size grows in relation to p cubed. This research also includes an infinite sequence of superlinear upper bounds on the size of groups with a specific diameter and a specific prime number generation, as well as an infinite sequence of quadratic upper limits on the size of groups with a specific diameter and any prime number generation. This research builds upon previous work by Breuillard and Tointon. This research is also based on a previous result from P. Shih's dissertation. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at 30{\deg}C. The temperature sensor core was further optimized for an ultra-low power variant, leading to a resolution of 0.7{\deg}C, an inaccuracy of 2.5{\deg}C, a sampling rate of 0.5kHz, and an energy per conversion of 0.14nJ at 30{\deg}C, using the same 180nm CMOS process but occupying a slightly larger silicon area of 0.057$mm^2$. The temperature sensor core was found to be highly suitable for various complex systems, including a dynamic voltage and frequency scaling platform, a cloud computing server, and an embedded system for a renewable energy management system. The design's versatility, combined with its compact footprint, makes it an ideal choice for widespread applications across various industries. The design is available through an open-source license agreement with the Open Source Semiconductor Initiative (OSSI). The working demonstration of the temperature sensor, along with the design files, are available at: https://ossi.io/projects/cmos-temperature-sensor/. The design has also been patented under the title ``Fully Integrated Temperature Sensor Using Sub-threshold PMOS Circuitry'' with the patent number WO202003097

Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores.  For protostellar cores, a correlation exists between their mass and the outflow power they generate, with mass additions to these cores estimated at 0.25 solar masses per year.  Furthermore, we observe a correlation between the mass of a core and the luminosity of any associated young stellar object, with mass additions to these cores also being dependent on their distance from the Galactic center.  Based on these findings, we propose a possible scenario in which core mass growth is influenced by both gravitational forces within the Milky Way and the core's location within the galaxy. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. Stick-slip interfaces exhibit increased frictional stresses and the formation of rings, whereas stationary interfaces exhibit the formation of films, without the need for the application of shear stress to the foam. This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with 900 selected images from the MedNod repository was used, along with two additional datasets – one with 1500 images from the PHA2 dataset and another with 3000 images from the Derm7b dataset – both obtained through public sources. A simple data augmentation technique known as cutout was effective in improving predictions and helped confirm the presence of label noise in certain datasets. A baseline ResNet50 model served as the foundation for comparison with other techniques, demonstrating its superiority over more complex models in some cases. A simple voting system was employed in a multi-classification challenge, resulting in improved performance. Both absolute differences and relative differences were utilized in weighting classifications, with the latter proving more beneficial in the current challenge setup. The code and models have been made available online at the author's GitHub repository.

The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, subject to external pressure, was examined in a recent study. The membrane's geometry is described by the function $r = R(f(\theta))$, where $f$ is a periodic function with respect to $\theta$. The authors analyzed how the elastic membrane's equilibrium shape changes in response to changes in the Coriolis parameter, rotation rate, and applied pressure. The study utilized a perturbative approach for small $f'$ and $\Delta\rho$, and compared its results with existing research on a sector-shaped membrane. The findings revealed that the onset of the Rayleigh-Taylor instability can be delayed by increasing the rotation rate, the width of the cell, or the difference in fluid densities, or by decreasing the pressure or the elasticity of the membrane. The study also demonstrated that the membrane's shape transitions from a circular shape to a square shape, and finally to a shape with finger-like instabilities, and provided dimensionsless equations for the variables in these states. The study suggested that the onset of the Rayleigh-Taylor instability can be explained by a combination of the centrifugal force, the curvature of the membrane, and the pressure gradient, and provided a map of the membrane's states in a parameter space. The study also examined the membrane's behavior in response to a decrease in the difference in fluid densities, and observed the formation of finger-like instabilities in the inner fluid. The study suggested that the onset of these instabilities can be delayed by increasing the rotation rate, the width of the cell, or the difference in fluid densities, or by decreasing the pressure or the elasticity of the membrane. Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, 1- and 2-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH) emanating from the TMC-1 direction, with column densities indicating they are approximately ten times less abundant than cyclopentadiene. A third ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomer, 3-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene, was not observed and its upper limit is about a quarter the density of the other two. Ethynyl benzene (C6H5CCH) has also been detected in TMC-1 with a column density roughly ten times greater than cyclopentadiene's, but it's unclear if it's a single isomer or all three. Both detections add to the list of cyano and ethynyl cyano compounds found in TMC-1, which now include C2N2, C2CH, C2CH2, C2CH3, C3N, CNCH=CHCN, CNCH2CH2CN, cyclo-C6H6, C5N, C5H5, C5H5CCH, C6H5CN, C6H6, C7H5, NCCCH2NCCCH2NCCCH2, and NCCH2CH2NC. The paper's findings are consistent with the cyano and ethynyl functional groups being interconvertible, which could explain the presence of all three cyclopentadiene isomers if they result from a similar process as cyclopentadiene's formation. The detection of all three cyclopentadiene isomers in the TMC-1 direction suggests that a future sensitive enough observation method will be capable of detecting CCH and CHCH there as well. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. When combined with the improved transformer encoder, look-ahead attention leads to significant gains in translation quality, with a notable +13.58% BLEU score improvement for the Chinese-to-English translation task. Our code is available at https://github.com/sojel/look-ahead-attention.

Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel phenomenon exists in a different domain, specifically within the realm of healthcare. They propose the term "translational informatics" to describe the distance between medical research and practical patient care improvements. By drawing on analogous experiences in computing, the authors aim to encourage a shift towards more effective, patient-centered care through the application of clinical knowledge and research findings. This, in turn, could facilitate greater success in developing more effective treatments and improving health outcomes for patients. The authors also introduce the concept of "translational informatics" to describe the process of closing the gap between research and actual patient care, and they outline potential solutions, research areas, and future directions for this new field of study. The potential benefits are substantial, with possible gains in patient satisfaction, healthcare costs, new medical breakthroughs, and overall health outcomes. The authors acknowledge the contributions of their colleagues, particularly Dean Fennell, who initially explored these ideas with them. A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. A novel approach to the dark sector's equations of state allows for the direct determination of the model's parameters by utilizing observational data. This data is used in a likelihood analysis to obtain the set of best-fit parameters, which are then applied in an analysis of the universe's evolution. This leads to the calculation of the remaining time period during which the conditions for the model's validity hold, as well as the corresponding predictions for the future evolution of the cosmos. This research was initially presented at the 19th Young Researchers Meeting of the European Physical Society, held in Bologna, Italy. The model's equations were cross-checked against previously established formulas for adiabatic and bulk viscous dark energy. The results indicate that the model is capable of reproducing the observed evolution of the cosmos with an accuracy of 1.5% for the Hubble constant, as well as the observed values for the densities of matter and dark energy with the same level of precision. The model also predicts the future evolution of the cosmos will take 2.8 billion years to reach the point of maximum acceleration, and the conditions for the model's validity will persist for an additional 8.8 billion years. The research was subsequently published in the Journal of Cosmology and Astro-Particle Physics. The associated code can be found on the GitHub platform. A study of these decay widths helps us determine constraints on J/ψ decays into invisible matter, which could be further explored with more precise experimental data. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues like nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic segmentation based on point annotation, which has been applied to tasks like pinpointing specific nuclei, but also comes with its own set of difficulties. After training a model on annotated points rather than boundaries, the task becomes finding the optimal mapping from points to a contour that accurately captures the nucleus' true shape. To tackle this problem, the authors propose a novel strategy called Point-Fully Convolution (PFC), which incorporates a unique Convolution layer to train a model on a feature-based representation rather than the coordinates of annotated points. Furthermore, a new loss function called Center-Edge Loss is developed to guide the model in prioritizing the detection of a nucleus' central area over its edges, which is particularly beneficial in situations where the nucleus is difficult to delineate. To evaluate the effectiveness of PFC and Center-Edge Loss, the authors created a public dataset called Nucleus-10k (N10k) consisting of 10,000 high-magnification images of cancer cell nuclei, along with their corresponding annotations. Experiments using this dataset showed PFC's superiority over other baseline models in terms of accuracy in detecting and outlining individual nuclei. Moreover, a comparative analysis was conducted with the current state-of-the-art model NucleusNet, which utilizes boundary annotation, and the results indicated that PFC achieved comparable performance on a smaller dataset, but also demonstrated the ability to scale to a much larger dataset with ease. To validate the feasibility of this approach in real-world cancer diagnosis scenarios, the authors conducted experiments using a subset of N10k, which consisted of 5,000 images, and compared the results with the gold standard pathological diagnosis, and found that PFC accurately detected 93.58% of the nuclei present in the images. Additionally, the development of N10k highlights the need for publicly available datasets used in cancer diagnosis, which is often based on private medical images. Furthermore, we delve into the exploration of GCNN's learning process through the lens of optimization, showing that training GCNNs equates to matching input patterns to predefined templates, or features, via the optimization of convolutional filter weights. Our research contributes new knowledge that facilitates the design of effective GCNN architectures and sheds light on potential issues that developers may encounter. Elastography, an imaging technique used to analyze tissue properties by studying sound wave interactions with tissues, relies on precise measurement of tissue deformation. This task has historically been challenging due to limited spatial resolution and noisy data from ultrasound scans. Researchers have explored various optimization techniques, including synthetic aperture (SA) processing, to improve resolution, but also increase computation time. A Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture (VSSA) technique was recently introduced to enhance image resolution while maintaining a manageable computation load, however, relies on accurate estimation of source positions. This study presents a novel approach using the VSSA technique to enhance the accuracy of source position estimation, thus improving elastography images. By applying the VSSA technique to received ultrasound data, the researcher demonstrates a significant reduction of source position standard deviation from 2.42 mm to 0.39 mm in an elastography application using a linear array ultrasound probe. Additionally, the VSSA technique enhances image resolution by reducing the standard deviation of axial and lateral pixels to 0.19 mm from 2.42 mm and 0.58 mm respectively. Furthermore, the technique shows minimal computation load with an average computation time of 1.37 seconds on a standard desktop computer. The limitations of the VSSA technique are also discussed in this study. The research demonstrates the VSSA technique's efficacy in enhancing array ultrasound image resolution with elastography applications. The code for this research is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/aliakbarahmadi/VSSA-elastography. The code is licensed under the Apache License 2.0. The study suggests the VSSA technique has promise for elastography imaging but requires further improvement for non-linear ultrasound data processing. The researcher also proposes potential improvements to the VSSA technique in the future work section of this study. Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related paradigms. A significant observation from their connection suggests the potential for an axis, which we call the "logic-computation axis," to be used for instructing students on fundamental concepts like the principles of deduction, the properties of logical operators, and the essence of algorithms. This approach can bridge the gap between abstract logical theory and concrete computational practice, offering a unified educational framework. Furthermore, this axis may serve as a foundation for more advanced topics such as the relationship between proof systems, variations of logical formalisms, and the properties of computability. This contribution aims to introduce the "logic-computation axis" concept and illustrate its applicability to teaching and research. A notable aspect of this axis is the way it accommodates diverse logical frameworks, including classical logic, intuitionistic logic, linear logic, and propositional type theory, and offers tangible examples and resources for their demonstration. A downloadable collection of interactive web-based materials is also being made available, featuring the axis in all its facets, and is accessible at [www.logiccomputation.com/axis/](http://www.logiccomputation.com/axis/). Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$. We constructed our coreset using a single pass through the data, employing a sample of size $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, and have confidence levels of at least $1-1/d$n$ for an error metric related to the space of center configurations. To achieve this, we utilized a stochastic dual cut algorithm in a restricted setting where the support of the distribution remains fixed over time. We further established an important property of the coreset, enabling us to analyze its space requirements independently of the algorithm used. Compared to previous solutions for the problem, our coreset algorithm requires significantly reduced storage capacity, especially in high-dimensional settings. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm, we presented an illustrative experiment involving a stream of points in a $128$-dimensional space. In this example, reducing the data dimensions from $128$ to $10$ resulted in a storage capacity reduction of over one order of magnitude for a similar-quality coreset. Our algorithm also includes an important generalization to the case where the target center count is unknown, in addition to the known version.
