We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. Furthermore, it offers innovative insights into the optimal design of the hierarchical framework, revealing that the selection of macro-states significantly affects the game's dynamics and solution space. Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptonic colliders. A vectorized effective field theory, SCET$_{\text{SM}}$, is developed to provide a suitable description of such weak boson colliders at their leading level of approximation. This description is particularly effective for describing scattering processes off particles, particularly those involving the exchange of a weak boson. A key aspect of SCET$_{\text{SM}}$ is the introduction of a novel "anti-collinear" field notation that aids in the derivation of a distinctive set of collinear operators. These operators exhibit a distinct behavior under the renormalization group, exhibiting a non-trivial interplay between their renormalization and mixing. A thorough investigation of these operators within the context of SCET$_{\text{SM}}$ reveals a range of novel cross-scales mixing effects that pose significant challenges for the development of reliable predictions for observable quantities. A systematic exploration of these challenges is undertaken, accompanied by a cross-reference to the established body of knowledge within the SCET framework. A key finding revealed through this analysis is the presence of previously unreported contributions to the renormalization of the weak boson mass splitting from the light of the effective theory itself. This discovery is further supported by an explicit calculation of the renormalization group equations for the SCET$_{\text{SM}}$ operators, accompanied by a critical assessment of the scope and limitations of an often-cited approximation commonly referred to as the "small mass" approximation. A distinctive feature of this approximation is the introduction of an arbitrary scale-dependent mass parameter with an undefined origin, which is revealed to be a misinterpretation of the true effective description provided by the SCET$_{\text{SM}}$ framework. Consequently, a timely reevaluation of this approximation is undertaken, followed by a demonstration of the precise effective description captured through the use of the weak boson mass splitting within the context of the SCET$_{\text{SM}}$ effective theory. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task with a dynamics ensemble network can yield substantial
gains. Our proposed approach is supported by both theoretical and empirical
evidence, as informed by the analysis of the learning process and explicit
assessments of the knowledge being shared. Our experiments demonstrate the
effectiveness of our method on a range of both simulated and real-world multi-
task reinforcement learning scenarios. Leveraging our framework's insights, we
also obtained a significant improvement in the performance of our proposed approach
by simply increasing the size of our ensemble from 2 to 64. Our work provides
new understanding of the dynamics ensemble method's behavior in multi-task
reinforcement learning. Our code is available at https://github.com/lyt2000/medrmt. We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques. We demonstrate that the entire collection of these theorems can be derived from a singular axiom, which we call the Incompleteness Axiom. We also explore some of the axioms' implications, such as the fact that any formally defined 'formal system' is necessarily incomplete or inconsistent, and that the concept of undecidability is an inherent aspect of the relationship between the set of theorems and the set of provable statements within any formal system. Furthermore, we outline the connection between Godel's first incompleteness theorem and the halting problem, which was previously observed by Emil Post in 1939, and also the connection to the syllogism rules proposed by Alan Turing in 1938, known as the 'bare little schema'. We conclude by discussing the potential applications of the Incompleteness Axiom within the context of modern computer science, mathematics, and philosophy. Additionally, we outline some possible future research directions inspired by the Incompleteness Axiom, including potential connections to the Curry-Howard isomorphism, the concept of 'totality' in category theory, and the relationship between type theory and the fundamental theorem of algebra. We also explore the possibility of generalizing the Incompleteness Axiom to encompass more intricate forms of self-reference, as well as its potential implications on our understanding of the relationship between mathematics and metamathematics. We also touch upon the idea that the Incompleteness Axiom itself may be seen as being generated by the Curry-Howard isomorphism, which in turn generates the fundamental theorem of algebra. This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space. Additionally, we obtain an estimate for the number of Riemannian balls that can be used to replace three complex disks in Hadamard's original theorem. Furthermore, we obtain an upper bound for the number of balls, n, which can be expressed as 3 for n=1, 4 for n=2, 6 for n=3, and √7n for an arbitrary positive integer n. We also establish that this upper limit can be achieved when using a specific type of ball, known as a polar ball, within the R^n+1 space. We utilize these results to re-examine some previous estimates found in the literature. Furthermore, we extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to a general setting known as the m-Borshten-Levin theorem, which can be found in the Appendix. We also provide an introduction to the concepts of monogenic functions and Clifford analysis in the paper's initial sections. We further explore related topics, the m-Borshten-Levin theorem and polar balls, in the paper's final sections. We also discuss some related open problems. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore degraded or incomplete data by formulating a minimization problem with constraints based on prior information. This results in a solution that represents a sample from the posterior distribution. Sampling from the posterior is a critical step, yet its efficiency varies significantly depending on the specific technique used. To improve the restoration process, a common strategy is to divide the data into non-overlapping segments and solve separate inverse problems for each segment. This strategy, known as non-local, has been demonstrated to produce more accurate restorations when the data contains repetitive elements. However, it entails solving more complicated and time-consuming inverse problems for each segment. To accelerate non-local solutions, an approach called the Gaussian blur operator is proposed, reducing the required number of iterations when applying a prior constraint, without sacrificing restoration quality. This approach takes advantage of a property known as the closure property, where the application of a Gaussian blur to a solution follows the same posterior distribution as the original solution. As a result, the parameters of the blur can be incorporated into the data, enabling more efficient segmentation of the data before solving the inverse problems. This enables non-local solutions to be used for various types of repetitive data, such as text, grid patterns, and images of rotating objects. The proposed method is applicable to both continuous and discrete data domains, and its effectiveness is validated through numerical experiments involving both gradient-based algorithms and the coarse-to-fine method, in addition to direct comparisons with state-of-the-art techniques. The resulting software is an open-source toolbox available online. The advantages of the proposed approach are further highlighted by comparing the source Gaussians used to generate synthetic data with the actual reconstructed sources. This comparison showcases the accuracy of the proposed method in solving inverse problems for segmented data, even in the presence of significant noise. The associated software toolbox can be accessed at this website: https://www.cfdpy.org/docs/gaussianblur/. The corresponding code for the numerical experiments can be found at this repository: https://github.com/numateam/nonlocal_prior. The name of the toolbox is CFDpy, which can also be used for solving various forms of PDEs, in addition to the proposed Gaussian blur operator. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Twenty-four screens were identified within the Earth's line of sight to the pulsar, with dimensions ranging from approximately 0.01 to 0.1 AU. These screens were divided into two categories: small screens, likely associated with the presence of companions in binary systems, and large screens linked to the presence of neutron stars in binary systems, and both types were found to exhibit irregular movements. The large screens were found to exhibit irregular movements similar to those observed for the pulsar itself, suggesting they are connected and share a common origin, with the Earth observing only a small portion of the entire distribution of screens. Albeit limited, estimates suggest the entire distribution contains screen sizes ranging from approximately 10 to 100 AU, with distances between screens ranging from approximately 0.1 to 10 AU. Furthermore, the screens appear to be aligned with the velocity vectors of the pulsar and the surrounding stars, hinting at a three-dimensional distribution that is both extensive and intricate, with the Earth observing only a minuscule portion, denoted as the 'inner screen sphere'. This concept is comparable to an 'atmosphere' proposed by Gruel (1988), albeit with a significantly broader scale. This study also delves into the variability of scintillation patterns and screen movements, with findings suggesting that the interstellar medium screens exhibit behaviors both analogous and dissimilar to those observed within a solar system. This study's extensive database remains the largest collection of scintillation patterns associated with a single-pulsar to date, with future observations across various frequencies poised to expand current understanding of the interstellar medium screens. This knowledge can be further refined with future observations across various frequencies, with potential applications in fields like navigation and frequency management. This study's extensive database stands as the largest collection of scintillation patterns linked to a single-pulsar to date, with potential for expansion through future observations across various frequencies, offering insights into the interstellar medium screens, as well as potential uses in fields like navigation and frequency management, with the potential to shed light on analogous phenomena within a solar system. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Moreover, QPNet surpasses existing WaveNet-based generators in low-frequency band reconstruction tasks. Additionally, QPNet extends the WN pitch control range and yields comparable results to state-of-the-art models in speech synthesis. The code for QPNet is available at https://github.com/zhengzhongzhong/qpnet.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Additionally, this analysis leads to an interpretation of the THH of a monoidal category as the shadows of its underlying bicategorical structure, thus providing a more general explanation for the observed similarity in Berman's work and the earlier findings of the first author and his collaborators. Moreover, feasible criteria for distinguishing between non-equivalent bicategories are established, culminating in the discussion of an idea for constructing the THH of a symmetric monoidal category as the shadows of its underlying bicategorical structure, expressed in a manner analogous to the well-known interpretation of the Eilenberg-MacLane algebra of a presheaf valued in sets as the functor that it represents. Given that the THH of a monoidal category is defined through the application of the THH functor to the monoidal structure, rather than the underlying category, this analysis yields the implication that this construction inherently incorporates information about the symmetries present in that monoidal structure. Consequently, the absence of non-trivial symmetries in the THH of a certain monoidal category can be taken as sufficient evidence for the non-existence of a certain type of self-dual object within that category, exemplified through the explicit discussion of the THH of the category of finite abelian groups equipped with the tensor product as monoidal structure. Ultimately, this analysis may be viewed as a starting point for further exploration of the relationship between the symmetries present in a monoidal structure and the absence of certain self-dual objects within a associated category, presented as the main argument for conducting thorough investigation of this particular topic within the larger context of the shadows theory. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips with sound sources. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale and accuracy. Our algorithm also demonstrates outstanding performance on this new dataset when compared to a strong baseline network. Our code and datasets are available for public use at https://github.com/MCG-UU/sound-source-localization. 

To evaluate sound source localization algorithms, researchers rely on post-processing methods like connection and region proposals. However, these approaches disregard crucial video characteristics, including spatial-temporal patterns and object relationships, which are crucial for accurate sound source localization. In reality, sound sources are often embedded within complex backgrounds, making the task even more challenging. In this research, we introduce a novel, end-to-end connection-aware network that leverages both spatial and temporal connection-aware maps to enhance the accuracy of sound source localization. Our network employs a unique connection-aware module that detects interconnected regions and prioritizes them for further processing. Additionally, we introduce a distinction-aware module that differentiates the target source from other connected objects or backgrounds. Our algorithm achieves the best results on existing datasets, including Flickr SoundNet and VGG-Sound Source, when compared to state-of-the-art baselines and algorithms. Our code is available at https://github.com/MCG-UU/sound-source-localization.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to state-of-the-art GCNs under both Euclidean and non-Euclidean geometries, showing that LGCN is a highly effective solution for graph learning tasks. The code is available at https://github.com/Xiaofan-Li/LGCN. The model has been found to be particularly successful at learning hierarchical structures from graph data, as shown in the accompanying figure. This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of the one-dimensional wave equation for the structure and the acoustic wave equation for the fluid. A unique solution to this problem exists based on an assumption of a single impulse source, following which the solution becomes steadily periodic. In this case, we can invert the forward operator by analyzing the periodic solution. In order to accomplish this, we first establish the uniqueness and the existence of the adjoint operator for the source term, the adjoint operator being linked to the periodic regime's stability. In addition, we derive the adjoint operator's explicit form, which involves the use of the PDEs' adjoint systems as well as the adjoint of an integral operator linked to the fluid's acoustic equation. Ultimately, we outline an enhanced nonlinear least-squares reconstruction framework that incorporates the use of the adjoint operator. In order to demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, we apply it to a simulated test case featuring a non-uniform source. The results obtained indicate a significant enhancement in the source reconstruction accuracy when utilizing the adjoint operator. The impact of the source target's location on the accuracy of the reconstructed source is also examined in the current test case, which reveals a negative correlation. The negative effect of the source's time-shifted self-interaction on the accuracy of the reconstructed source is further analytically proven. In order to tackle more complex and multi-dimensional inverse problems, we propose extending this research using the adjoint operator-based nonlinear least-squares method to the case of a plane wave structure, which would provide a simpler model with a direct relationship between the source and the measured data. In this instance, we validate the proposed method against actual experimental data collected using an acoustic wave tank. The results obtained indicate a direct proportionality between the reconstructed source and the measured data, which supports the feasibility of extending this method to a three-dimensional structure source reconstruction. In addition to the nonlinear least-squares method, we also investigate two alternative inversion strategies. In order to resolve the issue of the source's time-shifted self-interaction, which causes the reconstructed source to become increasingly inaccurate over time, we test two alternative approaches. When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.  This approach can also be applied to bimetric and quasi-symmetric massive gravity theories.  This document serves as an introductory overview to these complex topics rather than a comprehensive research contribution.  This work originated from discussions held during the 12th Parisian Winter School on Theoretical Physics, "Gravity and Quantum Geometry", held in February 2020. This perspective paper will be published in the journal PoS. This work is also related to two collaborative research projects, one with H. Gomes and another with T. Dienert, M. Pardo, and M. M. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. A case study involved utilizing the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that specializes in producing authentic chest X-rays. This enabled the development of a simple, three-component system to create artificial X-rays specifically designed for lung infection detection. By inputting a vector with random values, the pre-trained StyleGAN produced a distorted X-ray, which was then corrected using the f-style technique. The resulting image was subsequently used in a machine learning model to improve its ability to identify pneumonia with an F1-score that's 0.13 higher than the original score. Furthermore, this technique allowed for artificial X-rays creation with specific conditions like pulmonary infections, which Boosted the F1-score by 0.23 when training the model with synthetic data. This study showcases the exciting possibilities GANs present for medical imaging, which demands further research. The code for this project is available online at the author's website. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies. The software is particularly suited for
experts in the field but also offers a basic level of usability for individuals
without a statistical background. ViDaExpert is available for Windows operating
systems. The source code for Linux and Mac OS X can be obtained upon request.
